cases.title: The Beale Ciphers
cases.question: Are the three pages of numbers printed in an 1885 pamphlet from Lynchburg, a town in central Virginia, genuine ciphers pointing to buried gold and silver, or a hoax?
cases.verdict: A hoax, about 95 percent as a composite judgement. The figure is a judgement rather than a measurement, and each claim beneath it carries its own figure.

standing.note: The hoax reading rests on counting that anyone can repeat from the pamphlet's text, on probabilities computed from the cipher's own numbers and on Morriss's own newspaper notices, and it agrees with the cryptanalysts who worked on the ciphers in print between 1979 and 2013. Every percentage is a judgement, and the stylometric likelihood ratio (how many times more likely the letters' closeness to the narrator's account is if one person wrote both than if two did) runs from 3 to 25 depending on the measure (2.7 for Burrows Delta, the measure with the best accuracy on the comparison authors).

split: Cipher 1, as printed, is not an ordinary book-cipher encipherment of a message
The story is a fiction: no Beale party, no vault
The anonymous narrator wrote the "Beale" letters
new: New as far as the accessible literature shows (King's paper was read only in fragments, and Matyas, Holst and Hill not at all): the encoder's offsets, fitted from cipher 2 alone by a computer search that was told nothing about where the printed labels fall, change at the five printed miscounts; the "meantime / inalienable" typesetting argument (the numbering counts "mean time" as two words and needs "unalienable", while the print has "meantime" and "inalienable"); and the printed numbering, which stops at 816, after 811, the largest number cipher 2 needs apart from the one it uses for the letter x (no word in the Declaration begins with x or y, so the encoder took 811 from the last letter of a word for y and a number beyond the printed numbering for x). Under the printed numbering cipher 2 gives the printed message at 740 of its 762 numbers; a plain count of the same printed text gets 161 wrong.

Exact Markov-chain probabilities (a step-by-step calculation with the real frequencies of the Declaration's initial letters), permutation tests that reshuffle cipher 1's own numbers, a count-of-runs test (how often three alphabetical runs of ten or more letters turn up in one reshuffled sequence) and the homophone-rank test, which asks which of the many words available for each letter the writer chose, applied to the three alphabetical strings under the reconstructed key: the 17-letter run A to O at positions 188 to 204 and two 11-letter runs. Six of the main string's twenty numbers are the first word in the Declaration with that initial, the same front-of-the-key habit as the encoder of cipher 2.

A fitted model of the encoder's habits, which shows that ciphers 1 and 3 were not made with them and that cipher 3's numbers run in sequence in a way no letter-by-letter encoder produces; and the capacity bound for cipher 3 with real Virginia names: the letter of 5 January 1822 says it names a party of not less than thirty with their heirs and residences, the barest such list needs 792 ± 19 letters, and in 20,000 random draws it never fitted in 618 numbers.

Stylometry calibrated on 27 authors and 115 samples, giving likelihood ratios in place of impressions: 3 to 25 depending on the measure (2.7 for Burrows Delta), and one pair of samples by different authors on the same subject, the Lynchburg historians Christian (1900) and Pollock (1887), is closer than the Beale pair. Also the reflexive-pronoun habit quantified ("like myself" and the like, with nothing in the sentence to refer back to, at six to ten times the rate in other writers), corrected dates for "stampede" (earliest found: "Stampeded" in a Texas deposition of about 1823 printed in The Austin Papers, the collected papers of the Texas colonist Stephen F. Austin) and "improvise", "objective point", a military term first found in newspapers in 1847, and "grizzlies" as anachronism candidates, and the calibrated density of late vocabulary in the letters.

Morriss's own notices in The Virginian, a Lynchburg newspaper (a rental notice dated 20 September 1823 and printed on 30 September, to open on 1 October, and a removal notice dated 30 December 1825), which fix his tenure of the Washington Hotel to October 1823 through December 1825, where Wikipedia and the writer William Poundstone's book Biggest Secrets of 1993, known here through Wikipedia's summary of it, had only "not until at least 1823". The Santa Fe story is set against the documented arrests of 1812 to 1819 and against the negative 1972 search of the Spanish Archives of New Mexico, the records of the Spanish government there, by Charles Nelson, a researcher working for the Beale Cypher Study Committee, released by the National Security Agency along with a 1964 memoir by George Hart, one of two Roanoke brothers who searched for the treasure from the 1890s. The earliest press retelling located is the Roanoke Times of 20 January 1893, and the Wikipedia account is corrected: the 1820 "Thomas Beall" letter list it cites is from Franklin, Missouri, rather than St. Louis.

Transcription notes: cipher 2 as printed has 762 numbers (the usual 763 comes from a standard correction that reads the printed 108 as 10, 8); Gillogly's "495 numbers" for cipher 1 should be 520; in the deciphered message the pots are "iron pots", and the reading "clay pots" is wrong.
cases.confirms_prior: Gillogly (1980) found the alphabetical passage in cipher 1, showed its improbability and drew the hoax inference, with the caution that it is strong evidence rather than proof. Matyas (1979), Hammer (1979), Holst (1987) and King (1993) worked out the renumbering of the Declaration that decodes cipher 2 and the encoder's errors; King, and Hill (1989) independently, reported the three longer strings in cipher 1 under the reconstructed key. George Love, an enthusiast who published his analysis on the web in the 2000s, observed that cipher 2 works only with the pamphlet's counts, and Mateer (2013) concluded from the encoding process that the ciphers are likely a hoax. The objection that 618 numbers cannot hold thirty names with heirs and residences was made in 1927 and by Kruh (1982). Nickell and the linguist Jean Pival (1982), Kruh (1988) and Poundstone (1993) argued common authorship of the letters and the narrator's account, excluded Edgar Allan Poe, whom some have proposed as the author, and placed Morriss at the Washington Hotel no earlier than 1823. Viktor Wase (in a conference paper of 2020; a second paper of his, in Cryptologia in 2021, was not accessible) and Leonardo Campanelli (in a Cryptologia paper published online in 2022, in the volume dated 2023), both analysing the digits statistically, found the digit anomalies in ciphers 1 and 3.

change.qualifier: the hoax reading argued in print by the cryptanalysts who worked on the ciphers, with a confidence attached to each claim; it does not show that reading to be a settled position of the field.
change.prior: The hoax reading was argued in print by Gillogly (1980), King (1993), Mateer (2013), Nickell (1982) and Kruh (1982, 1988); King left three explanations of the alphabet in cipher 1 open. The position is not unanimous: Hammer (1971, 1979) and the Beale Cypher Association held the unsolved ciphers to be genuine, and popular accounts treat them as an unsolved treasure puzzle.
change.explanation: The verdict is the cryptanalysts' verdict, re-run on the pamphlet's own text and given a confidence per claim. The pamphlet's numbering reproduces the encoder's miscounts, and the alphabetical strings in cipher 1 are a second line of evidence, visible even with a standard text of the Declaration; the verdict on the ciphers rests on both lines, and the verdict on the letters on two more, the stylometry and the newspaper record. The page agrees with the hoax reading; it does not show that the hoax reading is the field's settled position.

overturn: Any document earlier than 1885, independent of the narrator, that mentions the ciphers, the letters or Beale's box: a Morriss paper, a will, a Lynchburg newspaper item of 1845 or 1862.
A reading of cipher 1 or cipher 3 as English, with any key, that survives the statistical tests and explains the three alphabetical runs as a property of the real key rather than of the Declaration.
A record placing Robert Morriss at the Washington Hotel in January 1820, and a Thomas J. Beale in Lynchburg in 1820 to 1822 or in Santa Fe in 1817 to 1821.

A manuscript worksheet showing that the pamphlet's numbering was reconstructed by a solver rather than copied from the encoder, together with an account of how the printed "translation" acquired its x, y and u, the letters in the printed translation that the printed key cannot produce (no word in the Declaration begins with x or y, and the pamphlet prints "inalienable" where the key needs "unalienable" for u). Each of these would move one line of evidence; a single new document would lower the confidence without reversing the conclusion.
fell_short: Read only in fragments: King's 1993 paper, through the full-text search of the Internet Archive, the digital library. Not read at all: Matyas 1979, Holst 1987, Hill 1989, Hammer 1979, Nickell 1982, Kruh 1982 and 1988, Poundstone 1993 (known through Wikipedia's summary and the Internet Archive's full-text index) and Mateer 2013; Nickell's findings are known only through Wikipedia's summary.

Not accessible: the Lynchburg newspapers of 1819 to 1821, 1862 to 1865 and 1885 to 1892, which are not digitised, so silence there is untested, and the 1885 copyright record book. The January 1847 "objective point" attestations were not re-verified from the page images.
That Ward was the narrator is not established: no record names the pamphlet's author, and no document earlier than 1885 was found on either side.

The stylometric sample is about 2,700 words; the calibration against 27 comparison authors is the answer to that, and the verdict on the ciphers does not rest on it. The claim that the narrator wrote the letters does, and its likelihood ratio depends on the measure (3 to 25; 2.7 for Burrows Delta) and on the prior odds.
cases.story: In 1885 a pamphlet called The Beale Papers was printed in Lynchburg, price fifty cents, and its author, who gave no name and is called the narrator here, told this story: in January 1820 a stranger named Thomas J. Beale took rooms at the Washington Hotel, kept by Robert Morriss, a merchant of the town, came back for the winter of 1822, and before leaving that spring handed Morriss a locked iron box. A letter from St. Louis dated 9 May 1822 told Morriss to open the box if no one called for it within ten years and said that a key to the papers inside would reach him in June 1832; no key came, and when Morriss opened the box in 1845 he found three pages of numbers and letters signed T. J. B. telling of thirty Virginians who had gone west in 1817, found gold and silver north of Santa Fe, then a Spanish town, and buried it in Bedford County, Virginia, the next county west of Lynchburg. In 1862 Morriss passed the papers to the narrator, who found that if the words of the Declaration of Independence, the founding document of the United States, are numbered from 1 upwards, each number on the second page stands for the first letter of the word with that number (a book cipher, in the language of code-breaking, with the Declaration as its key), and read that way the page describes 2,921 pounds of gold, 5,100 pounds of silver and jewels in a vault six feet down. The pamphlet calls the three pages papers 1, 2 and 3 and later writers call them ciphers 1, 2 and 3; ciphers 1 and 3 defeated the narrator, and after more than twenty years he published everything and invited the public to try.
cases.mystery: Ciphers 1 and 3 have never been read, no record of Beale, his party or the box has ever been found, and nobody knows who wrote the pamphlet: James B. Ward, who held the copyright, called himself the author's agent. The question stays open because cipher 2 is a working cipher with a real message, so either Beale's party existed or someone wrote a treasure story and enciphered part of it; those who take the story as true point to that message and to Carl Hammer, a computer scientist with the Univac company, who ran the ciphers through a computer in 1971 and found that the unread pages were not random numbers, which he and the Beale Cypher Association, a society of enthusiasts formed to work on the ciphers, took to mean that they encoded something. The sceptics' case was made in print by Jim Gillogly, a cryptanalyst, or code-breaker, who tried the Declaration as key on cipher 1 in 1980 and found one stretch of the result spelling the alphabet in order, the mark of a hoaxer writing from the numbered key; by Joe Nickell, an investigator of hoaxes and forgeries, who showed in 1982 that Morriss did not keep the Washington Hotel before 1823 and that the letters signed T. J. B. (the "Beale" letters) and the narrator's own account read like one hand; by John C. King, a cryptanalyst, who worked out in 1993 exactly how the Declaration had to be numbered for cipher 2 to decode cleanly and reported longer alphabetical runs in cipher 1 under that numbering; and by Louis Kruh, a cryptologic historian, in 1982 and 1988, and Todd Mateer, a cryptanalyst, in 2013. That work appeared in Cryptologia, a specialist journal of code-breaking, and in the enthusiasts' newsletter, and popular accounts still present the ciphers as an unsolved treasure puzzle: by January 1893 the Roanoke Times, a newspaper in the next city west of Lynchburg, could report that "the inhabitants of Bedford county have hunted for this treasure but so far in vain", and in 1972 a group of believers calling itself the Beale Cypher Study Committee was still paying for searches of the archives.
cases.judged: Everything was re-run from the pamphlet's own text, transcribed from the copy in the Library of Congress, the national library of the United States: cipher 2 was decoded with the numbering the pamphlet itself prints beside the Declaration (a number after every tenth word), that count goes wrong in five places, and each error matches a miscount made by the person who turned the message into numbers (the encoder, from here on), so the simpler reading is that whoever prepared the pamphlet held the encoder's own working key, although the story says that no key ever arrived. Cipher 1, decoded with that same miscounted numbering, holds three stretches of alphabet in order, seventeen letters at the longest, and the chance of that arising by accident is about one in twenty million by exact calculation under the most generous model of chance tested; cipher 3's numbers drift and climb in a way that enciphering a list letter by letter does not produce, and its 618 numbers cannot hold the thirty names with heirs and residences it is said to contain. Stylometry, the statistical comparison of writing habits, with 115 samples by 27 American authors for comparison, finds in the "Beale" letters and the narrator's account the involuntary habits of one writer; the letters use words that came into use decades after 1822; Morriss's own newspaper notices show that he took the Washington Hotel by a rental notice dated 20 September 1823 and printed on 30 September, to open on 1 October, and kept it until December 1825, so the pamphlet's date for Beale's first visit there is more than three years too early; and every documented American party that reached Spanish New Mexico, the territory around Santa Fe, between 1812 and 1819 was arrested. The verdict is a hoax, about 95 in 100 as a judgement that combines these lines, with a separate figure for each claim; a reading of cipher 1 as English that survived the statistical tests would overturn the verdict on the ciphers.

cases.title: Where was Brunanburh?
cases.question: Where did Æthelstan, the first king to rule the whole of England, defeat the Viking king of Dublin, the Scots and the Britons of Strathclyde in 937?
cases.verdict: Bromborough, on the Wirral, at roughly 60% on the evidence weights chosen, ranks first among several sites that remain possible.
cases.confidence_label: roughly 60% on the weights chosen (model point 64%; 90% of the draws between 36 and 84)

standing.note: The model's 64 percent is a weighting of the evidence rather than a measurement: every percentage is conditional on the candidate list, the starting probabilities and the evidence factors chosen, and the spread of the re-runs measures how sensitive the ranking is to those judgements and says nothing about how accurate they are. Drop the place-name item and Bromborough falls to 24 percent. Nobody has yet re-run the model independently.

split: Bromborough, Wirral (model point 64%; 90% of draws between 36 and 84)
Lancashire coast: Ribble, Fylde, Wigan, Burnley
new: What appears to be the first explicit, reproducible probability model of the question: a prior for each candidate, evidence factors given as ranges, intervals from the 20,000 re-runs and leave-one-out sensitivity (dropping each line of evidence in turn to see what changes), in place of the qualitative "on balance" verdicts in print. It shows that the case turns on one fact about the name and quantifies how far: drop the place-name item and Bromborough falls to 24 percent, with "unidentified" at 45; drop the Humber tradition and Bromborough rises to 72.

Route and time computations for every candidate on a single, stated basis, where the figures in print are scattered: Dave Capener of Wirral Archaeology gives 120 miles a day for laden ships, a figure Cavill cites and calls "optimistic for a voyage around the north of Scotland in autumn", and Cavill's own figure is "1,200 miles round Scotland".

A source table checked against letter-for-letter transcriptions of the manuscripts rather than repeated from secondary works. These are checks against the editions rather than new findings: the superscript n in the Parker manuscript (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173, the oldest copy of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle), which shows the double-n spelling Brunnanburh to be a later hand's addition and the original reading to be Brunanburh, the weak form that the derivation needs; the Welsh entry "Bellum Brune", which stands in only the oldest of the three versions of the Annales Cambriae, the Welsh Annals; the actual wording of Æthelweard, an English nobleman who wrote a Latin chronicle around 980, whose form of the name is Brunandune, with "hill" as its second element, and who says the fight was still called "the great battle"; the first combination of the Humber with the 615 ships of the Durham tradition in the Chronicle of Melrose, a thirteenth-century chronicle from the Scottish border abbey; and the 934 date of the Beverley story, the tale told at Beverley Minster in Yorkshire that Æthelstan left his knife on the altar of St John of Beverley as a pledge before the campaign, which in its earliest form belongs to the Scottish war of 934, with no Anlaf and no Brunanburh, as the historian Alice Law noted in 1910.
An explicit share for "somewhere else", which earlier writers have mentioned only in passing and which, on these weights, is the second-ranked hypothesis.
cases.confirms_prior: No new text, inscription or find; everything here is new analysis of old evidence, and every argument about a candidate has an author in the published literature. The Bromborough derivation was argued in detail by John McNeal Dodgson, the surveyor of Cheshire's place-names, in 1957. The conclusion agrees with the position argued by Cavill, Harding, Jesch, Coates and Downham and cautiously endorsed by Foot, by Woolf, who finds that Bromborough has "much to commend it", and by the Cambridge Old English Reader. It does not establish a field consensus: the Battlefields Trust, the charity for battlefield preservation, calls the site "unlocated", Clarkson calls the identification "distinctly unproven", and Wood, Halloran, Breeze and Deakin argue for other sites.

change.qualifier: the Wirral case argued by Cavill, Harding and their colleagues, as the likeliest site rather than a settled one
change.prior: No formal consensus exists and no poll of specialists has been taken. Bromborough is argued by Cavill (2011 to 2025), Harding and Jesch (with Cavill, 2004), Coates (1998) and Downham (2021) and cautiously endorsed by Foot (2011), Woolf (2007) and the Cambridge Old English Reader (2015). Wood argued for Brinsworth in 1980 and for the Went valley in 2013; Halloran for Burnswark (2005, 2010); Breeze for Lanchester (2016, 2020); Deakin for Bourn in Cambridgeshire (2025); Clarkson (2014) and Williams (2021) hold the site unproven. To judge by reference works and reviews, opinion has moved towards the Wirral since 2011: the case from the name has been re-argued in peer-reviewed journals, where specialists vet an article before it is printed, and each rival answered in print, while Wood, Breeze and Halloran have published nothing new on the site since 2021 and Deakin's Cambridgeshire case is the only new rival; Clarkson warns that "widely accepted as Bromborough" risks becoming a "pseudo-fact".
change.explanation: The verdict sides with the Wirral, as does the case from the name re-argued in peer-reviewed journals since 2011, and it puts a number on how much rests on the single fact of the name. The University of Chester, whose press published Finding the Battle of Brunanburh, said in its press release of December 2025 that the book "paves the way for ending the debate", and the popular history website Medievalists.net said the question "may be solved"; both go further than Cavill and Harding's own "likeliest location". The archaeological claims of 2019–2021 have been scaled back to "consistent with" a camp, with the diagnostic pieces almost all without findspots.

overturn: A sustained demonstration that Bromborough's early spellings derive from brūn, "brown", rather than from the personal name Brūna (Deakin's reading): the name factor would fall to about 1 and an unidentified site would lead the ranking.

An independent witness to a Humber landing from before the Norman Conquest: a northern annal behind John of Worcester, if one were found, combined with a genuine Brun- fort-name near the Humber, could tie or overtake the Wirral.

A securely located, dated tenth-century battle assemblage (a body of finds from one battle) anywhere else, or a charter or saint's-life text naming Brunanburh at another place. A gridded re-survey of Bebington Heath with recorded findspots and dated deposits, or isotope evidence that the iron objects found there came from Scotland, where Constantine's army came from, would harden the verdict instead.
fell_short: Barbara Yorke's 2026 review of Finding the Battle of Brunanburh (Yorke is a historian of Anglo-Saxon England at the University of Winchester), Halloran's 2005 article, Wood's 2013 article, Deakin's 2022 and 2025 papers, a 2014 review by Neil McGuigan in the Scottish Historical Review (McGuigan is a historian of northern Britain before 1300 at the University of St Andrews, and his review doubted the Wirral on strategic grounds: a Scottish king would have marched into a small peninsula hundreds of miles from his own territory) and the Cavill and Harding book itself were paywalled or unobtainable and are cited from abstracts, extracts and replies.

Dodgson's Cheshire volume, the county survey that records Bromborough's early spellings, was not consulted directly. No manuscript images were examined beyond published transcriptions, and no fieldwork or archive search was possible.

The evidence factors, the likelihood ratios that say how much each piece of evidence favours each site, are judgements, and a specialist may reasonably set several of them differently; the code is provided so that they can. Nobody has yet re-run the model independently.
cases.story: In 937 Anlaf Guthfrithson, the Viking king of Dublin, sailed to join Constantine II, king of Alba (the Gaelic kingdom that became Scotland), and the king of the Britons of Strathclyde, the kingdom on the Clyde, against Æthelstan. The three armies met Æthelstan and his brother Edmund at a place the English called Brunanburh and were beaten: the Norse survivors, Anlaf's Vikings, sailed home to Dublin, Constantine fled north, and Constantine's son, five kings and seven earls were among the dead. A poem in Old English, the English of the period, copied into the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the year-by-year record of events kept in English monasteries, names the field and the water over which the Norse fled, Dingesmere. The Annals of Ulster, a year-by-year record kept in Irish monasteries, call it "a great, lamentable and horrible battle" in which several thousand Norsemen fell.
cases.mystery: No source before the twelfth century says where the battle was, and no place is called Brunanburh today; between about 1095 and 1140 John of Worcester, a monk writing a Latin chronicle of England, wrote that Anlaf's fleet entered the Humber, the great estuary on England's east coast, and every later medieval writer who names a place copies him. More than forty sites have been proposed; four cases are still argued in print: Bromborough, a village on the Wirral, the peninsula between the Dee and Mersey estuaries opposite Liverpool, whose medieval spellings descend from Brunanburh, argued by Paul Cavill, a place-name scholar at the University of Nottingham, and his Nottingham colleagues Stephen Harding, a scientist who writes on the Wirral's Viking past, and Judith Jesch, professor of Viking studies, whose case Cavill and Harding's book Finding the Battle of Brunanburh (University of Chester Press, December 2025) argues at length, together with the place-name scholar Richard Coates and Clare Downham, a historian of Viking-age Britain and Ireland at the University of Liverpool, and cautiously endorsed by Sarah Foot, Æthelstan's biographer, by Alex Woolf, a historian of early Scotland who names no site, and by the Cambridge Old English Reader, a standard university textbook; the Humber and south Yorkshire, argued by Michael Wood, the historian and broadcaster, who puts the field south of York, first at Brinsworth near Rotherham (1980) and later in the Went valley near Doncaster (2013); Burnswark, a flat-topped hill in Dumfriesshire with an Iron Age fort on its summit, nearest of all to Dublin and Strathclyde, argued by Kevin Halloran, an independent historian; and Lanchester, a Roman fort in County Durham above a river called the Browney, argued by Andrew Breeze, a scholar of the Celtic languages at the University of Navarra. Michael Deakin, an independent researcher, denies that Bromborough's name descends from Brunanburh and argues for a fifth site, Bourn in Cambridgeshire, the only new rival since 2011, and the Lancashire coast is a further region of proposals rather than a single site: Amounderness, the district between the rivers Lune and Ribble, put forward by Tim Clarkson, a historian of Strathclyde, as a possible battle zone, the Fylde around Blackpool, Wigan and Burnley. Since 2019 a community group, Wirral Archaeology, has been recovering metal finds on Bebington Heath near Bromborough, while Clarkson and Thomas Williams, a historian who assessed the archaeological claims, hold that the original name may have been lost and the finds do not prove a battle, so that no identification is secure; Historic England, the public body that keeps the official register of battlefields, does not list Brunanburh, because the register requires a battlefield to be securely located.
cases.judged: All 22 medieval texts were read in their original languages (Old English, Latin, Irish, Welsh and Old Norse, the language of the Vikings), and none before John of Worcester locates the battle, while his sentence is a stock formula that he used for other fleet arrivals. Each candidate's name was tested against Old English grammar: Brunanburh is "Brūna's stronghold", formed from a personal name of the class that took the possessive ending -an, and only Bromborough's recorded spellings descend from it regularly. Routes and travel times were computed for every army to every site on one basis, and the judgements were combined in an explicit evidence model, in which each candidate starts with a prior probability, its chance before any evidence is weighed, and each line of evidence multiplies it up or down by a stated factor with a stated margin of doubt, and the calculation is re-run 20,000 times with every factor varied within its margin. The result is a ranking with a stated uncertainty and does not identify the site: Bromborough at roughly 60 percent on the weights chosen (the model's own point figure is 64 percent, rounded down), about one chance in five that the battle was fought at a place nobody has proposed, and no named rival above 5 percent at the point estimate (the figure with every factor at the middle of its range); a demonstration that Bromborough's name derives from brūn, "brown", rather than from the personal name Brūna, an independent witness to a Humber landing from before the Norman Conquest of 1066, or a securely located set of tenth-century battlefield finds elsewhere would overturn it.

cases.title: The Last Decade of the Ninth Legion
cases.question: Where, when and how did the Ninth Legion, last recorded building a fortress gate at York in 107/108, cease to exist?
cases.verdict: The legion most probably ended in Britain, destroyed or defeated and then disbanded, between about 122 and 130, in the years after Hadrian's visit of 122. On central readings of the evidence the British ending has a probability of about 50 to 65%.
cases.confidence_label: about 50 to 65% on central readings (85% at the base reading, 36% at the sceptical one)

standing.note: The hypothesis was argued by Hodgson (2021) and explored as a possibility by Graafstal (2025), and the analysis supports it by weighing the evidence they used, without testing it independently and without new evidence. It is not the agreed view of the field: Campbell, A.R. Birley, the historian of Roman Britain's governors, and Lawrence Keppie, the historian of the legions, hold other positions, and no published response to Hodgson exists. The probability of a British ending runs from 85% at the base reading to 36% at the sceptical one, and every figure is conditional on the four endings and the likelihood ranges chosen. The strongest opposing case, Campbell's book of 2018, could not be read.

split: Britain, about 122 to 130: destroyed, or defeated and disbanded
The Bar Kokhba war, Judaea, 132 to 136
new: No new evidence was found: no inscription, papyrus or object unknown to the literature. The conclusion is not new either: the hypothesis of a defeat followed by disbandment in Britain in or soon after 122 was argued by Hodgson in Britannia 52 (2021), and Graafstal in Britannia 56 (2025) connected the legion's disappearance with the military crisis after Hadrian's visit and the interruption of building on the Wall; Ritterling had placed the end in Britain after 120 in 1925. What follows is new analysis of evidence already in print.

A complete, database-linked catalogue: all 133 records for Britain in Roman Inscriptions of Britain (among them 11 stones, 116 tile stamps, 2 unassignable fragments, 1 rejected stamp, 1 forgery and 2 graffiti, a scratched mention on a London vessel and a single letter traced with a finger, before firing, on a tile from Carlisle, near the western end of Hadrian's Wall) and an empire-wide sweep of the Heidelberg and Clauss-Slaby databases (245 rows, about 195 distinct monuments once duplicates between the two are matched), with every query recorded. No record of the legion in either database survives scrutiny as later than the 120s: the two "late" database dates, 141 to 160 for Aelius Asclepiades, a private soldier of a "legio IX" buried at Naples, and 106 to 161 for CIL VI 41280, an inscription in Rome for an unnamed officer of the equestrian order (the second rank of Roman society) who served in the Ninth, rest on no criteria and on the Elegeia theory respectively.

A career model: each of the three datable careers simulated 200,000 times from its fixed point, drawing each interval between posts at random from a span with a most likely value in the middle (a triangular distribution), which converts statements like "hardly earlier than the mid-120s" into a probability curve. The officers require the legion to exist in 124 at 88%, in 126 at 51% and in 130 at 6%; the median last year in which any of them was still serving in the legion is 126, inside the 125 to 128 that Crispinus' career gives by the standard intervals, and 90% of the simulated values fall between 123 and 130. The model answers one question, the latest year to which the officers' records require the legion to have existed, and it cannot estimate the year the legion ceased to exist. One check on a known case: applied to Pontius Laelianus, a senatorial tribune of the Sixth Legion Victrix who was consul in 145, the same distribution puts the start of his tribunate at a median of 123 with 90% of the values between 120 and 126, and 122, the year he is known to have crossed to Britain with the legion, falls inside that span. A single case shows that the intervals are consistent with a known career and does not validate them.

An explicit likelihood table with ranges and a distribution of results, which states what each reading of the evidence implies and what a sceptic has to assume. It shows that the ordering of the hypotheses holds under nearly every weighting while the probability of the leading one does not: Britain ranks first in 97 to 100% of draws, while its own probability is 85% at the base reading and 36% at the sceptical one.

The Nijmegen ratio quantified: three stamps from one die against 196 of the vexillatio Britannica and about 227 post-104 stamps in all, about 1.3% against 86%, set beside the fortress size (16.5 hectares) and its end date (about 125 to 130).

Two under-used items read afresh: CIL VI 41280, the equestrian who served in the Ninth and went on to be procurator (financial administrator) of "the new province of Arabia", whose Heidelberg dating of 106 to 161 rests on the Elegeia theory itself; and CIL V 7159, M. Cocceius Severus, chief centurion (primus pilus) of the Ninth and then camp prefect, the senior professional soldier and third in command, of the Tenth Legion Gemina (X Gemina), read with its Clauss-Slaby text, which gives no usable latest date.
cases.confirms_prior: Positions already argued by others that this analysis supports: the impossibility of 117 to 119 (Ritterling 1925; A.R. Birley 2005); the detachment reading of Nijmegen (Haalebos 2000, by Jan Kees Haalebos, one of the fortress's excavators; van der Veen 2025, a study of the fortress by P.J.M. van der Veen); the reading of the Numisius stone (CIL XI 5670, the inscription of a tribune of the Ninth named Camurius Numisius Iunior) that makes the consul of 161 of the same name his son (Keppie 1989); the absence of any eastern evidence (Keppie; Menahem Mor, the Israeli historian of the Bar Kokhba revolt); and the British setting in the early 120s, argued by Hodgson 2021 and explored by Graafstal 2025. An analysis that reaches the same conclusion as its proponents by weighing the same evidence has not tested that conclusion independently: the agreement supports the reading of Hodgson and Graafstal without settling the question. What this analysis adds is the synthesis and the explicit statement of how much the answer depends on judgement.

change.qualifier: the reading argued by Hodgson (2021) and explored as a possibility by Graafstal (2025) that the legion most probably ended in Britain in the years after Hadrian's visit of 122, and with Ritterling (1925) on a British setting after 120, without settling the question
change.prior: The popular account has the legion destroyed in northern Britain about 117 to 119, a date the officers' careers rule out. Mommsen (1885) had it annihilated at York soon after 108; Ritterling (1925) saw from the careers of Karus and Crispinus that the end must fall after 120 and thought of a second British revolt, about 125, later than the war of 117 to 119 to which the traditional account had tied the loss. Eric Birley (1948, 1971), the Durham historian of the Roman army, built the eastern alternative on Cocceius Severus, a chief centurion of the Ninth who rose to camp prefect of the Tenth Legion Gemina and whose family name Birley read as a sign of a late date, on the undated tiles of the Ninth from Carlisle, near the western end of the Wall, and on the Nijmegen finds; Bogaers (1967), one of the excavators of Nijmegen, placed the whole legion there in the 120s; Eck (1972) took it to Elegeia in 161 on the Numisius diploma, a military diploma (the bronze discharge certificate given to soldiers on completing their service) that names a Q. Numisius Iunior as consul in 161, whom he identified with a tribune of the Ninth of that name. Keppie (1989) dismantled the eastern case item by item, and Haalebos (2000), the other excavator of the fortress, and the later Nijmegen excavators reduced the continental presence to a detachment of 104 to 120. Campbell (2010, 2018) holds that the legion left Britain by the 120s and was lost in the East, and calls a British loss "a very weak theory"; A.R. Birley (1981, 2005) has it alive to about 124 with the place undetermined. Hodgson (2021) argued for defeat followed by disbandment in Britain, in 122 or shortly after, and Graafstal (2025) explores the connection with a security crisis after Hadrian's visit as a possibility to be examined. Neither paper has yet drawn a published response, and the field has no settled verdict.
change.explanation: The analysis reaches the conclusion Hodgson argued and Graafstal explores by weighing the evidence they used, so it supports their reading without testing it independently, and it finds no new evidence. It does not show that the field favours the reading: Campbell, A.R. Birley and Keppie hold other positions, and no published response to Hodgson exists. It rules out the traditional date of 117 to 119, which A.R. Birley had already done in 2005, and it states, as the proponents do not, how far the answer depends on judgement: 85% at the base reading, 36% at the sceptical one, about 50 to 65% on central readings.

overturn: Any inscription, diploma or papyrus naming the legion, or a serving soldier of it, with a date or context after about 130, such as a tombstone in Judaea, Syria or Cappadocia (the province in eastern Turkey facing Armenia), a building stone or a discharge list, would move the answer east.

Proof that the tribune of the Numisius stone (CIL XI 5670) is the consul of 161 (for instance a new copy of the stone with a consulship, or a diploma giving the consul's full name Q. Camurius Numisius Iunior) would push the legion's existence to about 140 and revive Eck's hypothesis.

Nijmegen finds of the Ninth in contexts of Hadrian's reign at legion scale (several dies, a stamped building, an inscription of a serving officer dated after 122), which would do the same for the Rhine.

A Ninth building stone on Hadrian's Wall in a sector dated after 124 would show the legion still at work in Britain after the crisis of 122 to 125 to which the British ending is tied, and so would count against a loss in those years; the absence of any such stone is one of the five pieces of evidence weighed and counts against a British ending, because a legion still in the province in the mid-120s could have worked a season or two on the Wall. In the other direction, a firmly dated York or Carlisle context showing the legion still in garrison in 125 or later would tighten the British date without changing the place.

The answer would not be shaken by a new career inscription from the reign of Trajan or the early years of Hadrian, by a further Nijmegen tile of the known die, or by an undated stray such as the graffito from Linz in Austria that names a ninth legion without title or date (AE 2020, 932; AE is L'Année épigraphique, the annual bulletin of new finds).
fell_short: Campbell's book The Fate of the Ninth (2018) could not be read: no preview, scan, review copy or journal review exists. His case is stated from his 2010 article, all 57 of his blog posts and all 25 of his forum posts to February 2026, read in full. Arguments that exist only in the book are unknown here and are not answered.

Hodgson 2021 is behind the publisher's paywall. It was read in its abstract and through the fourteen citations and three verbatim quotations in Graafstal 2025 and the citations in Symonds 2022 (the chapter "Was Hadrian's Wall a response to a military threat?" by Matthew Symonds, a historian of the Wall); its treatment of Numisius Iunior, of Campbell 2018 and of the Aachen altar is not recoverable from those (the altar, from the spa town 100 km from Nijmegen, was set up by a camp prefect of the Ninth and is Campbell's best evidence for a legion-sized presence on the Rhine, since a camp prefect belongs with a legion).

Haalebos 2000 and Ritterling 1925 were reached through citation. The papyrus BGU I 140, a papyrus in Berlin, records the Twenty-Second Legion Deiotariana at its base outside Alexandria on 4 August 119, the last record of that legion, which, like the Ninth, is missing from the list of 165 and, if the Bar Kokhba war cost Rome a legion, is the better candidate for it; the papyrus was cited from the standard editions and not read online. Reports of a 2018 debate at York between the archaeologist Miles Russell and Campbell could not be verified.

The likelihoods are judgements. The weighting table in the full report, which is linked from this page, has sensitivity rows stating what a sceptic has to assume, and the headline is given as a range for that reason; two of the five pieces of evidence, the careers and the absence of a base elsewhere, are not fully independent, since both are in part the absence of later evidence.

The career model uses nothing Ritterling did not have in 1925, and its output is only as good as the standard career intervals assumed; the one check against a known career, that of Pontius Laelianus, shows consistency and does not validate the intervals. The date within Britain cannot be fixed closely: the careers are compatible with an end anywhere up to about 130.
cases.story: Some time between December 107 and December 108 the Ninth Legion (in Latin, Legio IX Hispana), a unit of about five thousand Roman soldiers, finished a gate of its fortress at York in northern England. It had been in Britain since the Roman invasion of AD 43; it had been mauled by the rebels of the British queen Boudica in 60 and refilled with two thousand men from Germany, and it had been attacked by night in its camp in Caledonia, now Scotland, in the 80s. Part of the dedication slab for the new gate, carrying the titles of the emperor Trajan, survives (it is RIB 665, its number in Roman Inscriptions of Britain, the corpus of every Roman inscription found in Britain), and it is the last dated text that names the legion anywhere. Soon after 165 the army's legions were listed on a column in Rome, thirty-three of them (ILS 2288, its number in Hermann Dessau's selection of the most important Latin inscriptions); the Ninth is not among them, and no ancient writer records where or how it ended in the half-century between.
cases.mystery: The evidence is indirect (inscriptions of officers who served in the legion and went on to dated posts, roof tiles stamped with the legion's name, and a few sentences in later writers about wars in which Roman soldiers died), and historians have read it in four ways. The oldest view, going back to the German historian Theodor Mommsen in 1885, is that the legion was destroyed or disbanded in Britain, and Emil Ritterling, whose 1925 encyclopaedia article on the legions is still the standard account, put that end after 120. In its modern form, argued by Nick Hodgson, an archaeologist of Hadrian's Wall (the frontier barrier built across northern Britain from 122), in Britannia, the journal of Romano-British studies (volume 52, 2021), and explored by the Dutch archaeologist Erik Graafstal in the same journal (volume 56, 2025), the loss falls in fighting that followed the visit to Britain in 122 of Hadrian, emperor from 117 to 138. The second view is that the legion left Britain for the Rhine, on the strength of three stamped tiles found at Nijmegen, a Roman fortress on the Rhine in the Netherlands, and was lost in the Bar Kokhba war, the Jewish revolt of 132 to 136 in Judaea; the third, that it left Britain and was lost at Elegeia in Armenia in 161, where Cassius Dio, a historian writing in the early third century, records (Dio 71.2) a whole Roman legion destroyed by the Parthians, Rome's eastern rivals, a view proposed by Werner Eck, a German historian of Roman inscriptions, in 1972, and one towards which Duncan Campbell, a historian of the Roman army, leans; and the fourth, that the legion was broken up or merged into another legion, so that no record of an end would exist.
cases.judged: Every inscription naming the legion was collected: all 133 records from Britain, and every entry for the rest of the empire in the Heidelberg and Clauss-Slaby databases, the two large online databases of Latin inscriptions. The careers of the three senators who served in the legion and whose later posts are dated (T. Aninius Sextius Florentinus as its commander, and L. Aemilius Karus and L. Novius Crispinus as its senatorial tribune, the young senator who was second-in-command) were worked back to the latest year the legion must have existed, and that arithmetic was run as a simulation; the Nijmegen finds were counted against the fortress's other finds; and five pieces of evidence (the officers' careers; the absence of any base or trace of the legion outside Britain after about 122; the British crisis of about 122 to 125; Dio's record of a legion destroyed at Elegeia in 161; and the absence of any building stone of the Ninth on Hadrian's Wall) were weighed against the four endings, each weight given as a range from a base reading to a sceptical one, the sceptical end being what a determined critic of the British reading could reasonably assume. The result is that the legion certainly existed in 122 and almost certainly in 124, that nothing places it outside Britain after that, and that Britain in about 122 to 130 is the best-supported ending, at about 50 to 65% on central readings of those ranges. That probability is a judgement, stated so that it can be varied and tested, and the answer is probable but not proven; any inscription naming the legion, or a serving soldier of it, dated after about 130 would move the answer east.

cases.title: The Princes in the Tower
cases.question: Did the boy king Edward V and his younger brother Richard, Duke of York, die in the Tower of London in 1483, or did one or both survive to become the two claimants to the throne of 1487 and the 1490s?
cases.verdict: Both Edward V and Richard, Duke of York, most probably died in the Tower in 1483, in Richard III's custody: about 85 in 100. One or both survived to adulthood: about 6 in 100; something else: about 9 in 100.
cases.confidence_label: about 85% (67 to 92 across the ledger's runs)

standing.note: A judgment on the balance of published evidence rather than a solution: the 85 per cent depends on the five outcomes and the cluster weights set in the ledger, and the case for murder rests on how people behaved rather than on proof. Death in 1483 is also the position of the named studies of the reign, known here through secondary summaries.

split: Both died in 1483 in Richard III's custody
Something else: died in 1484 to 1485 in Richard's keeping, under Henry VII, or abroad as children
One or both survived to adulthood, as "Simnel", "Warbeck" or otherwise
new: There is no new evidence: no document was seen in manuscript and none is newly identified. The four items below are new analysis of old evidence, its arrangement and checking, and none of them changes the verdict.

A table of the 1487 records by jurisdiction (England, Ireland and the Burgundian Netherlands), built on the inventory of those records that Phillips compiled in his 2024 note, with two further sources added, Gordon Smith (1996), the Richard III Society writer who first argued that the Dublin king was Edward V, and Jones (2014), and arranged to test the survival side's explanation that the English records are Tudor propaganda. The Lille receipt is the only contemporary text that unambiguously calls the Dublin king a son of Edward IV; the English, Irish and Burgundian records otherwise make him Clarence's son, that is the boys' cousin Edward, Earl of Warwick, son of their uncle George, Duke of Clarence, or a new King Edward in his first year, and the receipt's own account of the pikes, bought "in June 1487" for a force that had landed in Ireland on 5 May and was destroyed at Stoke on 16 June, cannot stand as the receipt is summarised in the printed inventory of the Lille archives, the catalogue of their holdings published in 1895 by the archivist Jules Finot, a different inventory from Phillips's.

The Gelderland narrative's route, where it goes beyond the claimant's own account, follows the Tournai boy's: the stops in the narrative that are absent from the claimant's 1493 letter to Queen Isabella of Castile (Antwerp, Bergen op Zoom, Middelburg and the voyage to Lisbon in the company of the wife of Sir Edward Brampton, a Portuguese-born Yorkist knight) are exactly the stops of Piers Werbecque's itinerary as sworn to at Setúbal in 1496 and confessed in 1497, in the same order. That the narrative follows the 1493 letter and the 1497 confession in outline had been said by Nathen Amin, a historian of the Tudor pretenders, and by the Richard III Society's research pages; the match of the extra stops, one by one and in order, is the sharper point made here.

The murder sources set side by side in their original words and classed as rumour, inference or claimed knowledge, with one small textual note: the printed text of the speech in which Guillaume de Rochefort, Chancellor of France, told the Estates General, the assembly of the French realm, at Tours in January 1484 that Edward IV's sons had been murdered, recorded in the journal of Jehan Masselin, one of the deputies, reads "impune trucidari", "slaughtered with impunity", where the often-quoted "trucidatos" means only "slaughtered"; the wording differs, and the statement that the sons had been killed does not.
A five-cluster ledger with sensitivity tests, which shows that the verdict survives the removal, all at once, of More, the bones and Thornton's findings.
cases.confirms_prior: The verdict agrees with Charles Ross (1981), Rosemary Horrox (1989), A. J. Pollard (1991), Michael Hicks (2003, 2024) and Sean Cunningham (2003), and with the recent biographies by David Horspool (2015) and Chris Skidmore (2017); their books are known here through summaries in the secondary literature, and Hicks's 2024 note was read in abstract. The regnal-year argument is Randolph Jones's (2014, 2021, 2023) and Chris Phillips's (2024). The account of the Lille receipt's printing in Finot's 1895 inventory and of its impossible June 1487 chronology is Phillips's (2024), with Michael Bletzer (2013), whose study of the Habsburg captains at Bosworth and Stoke had quoted the receipt, for the earlier quotation. The identification of the 1490s claimant as a native of Tournai was made by James Gairdner (1898), the Victorian historian of the reign, with Ann Wroe (2003), whose Perkin is the fullest modern study of the claimant, on Setúbal; the age error in the claimant's 1493 letter, which makes the prince a year younger than he was, is Gairdner's (1898, p. 268 n.). The reading of the Gelderland narrative as propaganda that either hypothesis needs, whether the claimant was the real Richard of York or a pretender, since a pretender required exactly such a text, is Hicks's (2024), anticipated by a question asked in 1951 by D. Th. Enklaar, the Utrecht professor to whom the manuscript was first sent; that the narrative follows the 1493 letter and the 1497 confession in outline had been noted by Amin and by the Richard III Society's research pages. The observation that the Gelderland narrative and More name the same two men, Tyrell and Miles Forest, one of the two killers More names, among those who had charge of the boys is Hicks's (2024) and Thornton's (2024). Three further findings are Thornton's (2021, 2024): that Forest's sons were at Henry VIII's court in More's own circle in the 1510s, so that More had a route to the family of a named killer; that Henry VII was at the Tower in the days around Tyrell's trial in 1502, with no direct evidence of any confession; and the Capell chain, a chain that a 1516 will describes as the young King Edward V's, which connects an object of the boy's to Tyrell's household. The argument from Henry VII's silence was made by Jeremy Potter (1983), a Ricardian writer, and by older writers.

change.qualifier: Ross (1981), Horrox (1989), Pollard (1991), Hicks (2003, 2024), Cunningham (2003), Horspool (2015) and Skidmore (2017) that both boys died in 1483 in Richard III's custody, and changes nothing in their position
change.prior: Charles Ross (1981), Rosemary Horrox (1989), A. J. Pollard (1991), Michael Hicks (2003, 2024) and Sean Cunningham (2003), and the recent biographies by David Horspool (2015) and Chris Skidmore (2017), hold that both boys most probably died in 1483 in Richard III's custody. Against that position Philippa Langley's Missing Princes Project (2023; updated 2025), with the Richard III Society's research pages, argues from four named documents, the Lille receipt of December 1487, the Gelderland narrative at Arnhem, the Dresden pledge of October 1493 and Maximilian's "three marks" letter, that both boys survived. Earlier Ricardian writers proposed other answers: Paul Murray Kendall (1955) blamed Buckingham, Clements Markham (1906) and Bertram Fields (1998) blamed Henry VII, and David Baldwin (2007), Matthew Lewis (2018) and John Ashdown-Hill (2018) argued for survival.
change.explanation: The survival documents were re-read one by one, in the original language where a printed text could be reached and otherwise in Langley's translation or the Missing Princes Project's descriptions, beside the other records of their own archives, and the position of the named studies was found to stand. Two tests decide it: the regnal year in the Dublin king's own records, against the Lille receipt, and the Portuguese depositions of April 1496 that place the 1490s claimant in a Tournai family, against the other three documents. Chris Phillips reached the same conclusion on 1487 in 2024, in a note written with four members of Langley's own Dutch Research Group, the Dutch researchers of her team, and so did Michael Hicks in the journal Historical Research the same year.

overturn: A record from 1483 to 1491 of either boy's whereabouts made by someone not later paid to say so: a household or estate entry, a safe-conduct or a letter that securely names Edward V or Richard of York.

Radiocarbon, sex and DNA results on the 1674 bones. Children of the right ages in the wrong century would end the murder story as told; a Yorkist maternal-line match (DNA inherited through the mother, compared with the boys' family line) with a 1480s date would end the survival story.

An Irish or Burgundian record of 1487 dating by "Edward V" or "the fifth year", or the exchequer memoranda-roll abstracts, the two surviving copies of the lost Irish exchequer roll that dates a writ of May 1487 to the Dublin king's first year, shown to have been mis-copied.

Proof that the Setúbal depositions were fabricated, that the 1487 confession of William Symonds, the priest who admitted taking an Oxford organ-maker's son to Ireland, was fabricated, or that the Werbecque family of Tournai, the family the captured claimant confessed he belonged to, did not exist as described.
fell_short: Not read: Mancini's Latin (the edition of 1936 and 1969 by C. A. J. Armstrong is lending-restricted); the Dutch of the Gelderland narrative in full (no edition exists; it was read in Langley's translation as quoted); the Setúbal depositions themselves (Wroe 2003, read in summary); Hicks 2024 (abstract only); the notes published between 2023 and 2025 in the Ricardian Bulletin, a publication distinct from the journal The Ricardian (through intermediaries); Langley 2023 and 2025 in full (read in extracts and in published responses to it); the Great Chronicle of London, a city chronicle written up about 1512, in the 1938 edition (secondary quotation).
The standard academic studies and recent biographies (Ross, Horrox, Pollard, Hicks 2003, Cunningham, Horspool, Skidmore) were not read; their positions are taken from secondary summaries.

The Nuremberg charters, charters and letters of "Richard of England" to two German families from 1494 to 1496, the Dresden pledge and Maximilian's "three marks" letter are known only from the Missing Princes Project's descriptions.
The state of the bones question, the question of testing the 1674 bones, was checked to March 2026, the date of the latest published account found, and not beyond.

The ledger's likelihoods are judgments; the numbers make the weighing checkable and show how far the verdict moves when any one of them changes. The evidence weighed is evidence of how people behaved, and none of it is proof of a death.
cases.story: King Edward IV of England, the first king of the house of York, died in April 1483, leaving two sons: Edward V, aged twelve, and Richard, Duke of York, aged nine. Their uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester, the dead king's younger brother, took charge of the young king, lodged both boys in the Tower of London, then a royal residence as well as a fortress and a prison, had them declared illegitimate, accepted the crown on 26 June and was crowned Richard III on 6 July. Over that summer the boys' servants were dismissed and, in the words of Dominic Mancini, an Italian visitor who wrote up what he had seen for a French patron that December, they were seen "more rarely behind the bars and windows, till at length they ceased to appear altogether"; no one recorded a dated sighting of either boy again. By October, men who had plotted to free them had heard that they were dead and rose instead for Henry Tudor, an exile in Brittany with a distant claim to the throne, who killed Richard at Bosworth in August 1485 and became Henry VII.
cases.mystery: No one who wrote at the time claims to know whether the boys died, or when, or how: Richard III never said; Henry VII never produced bodies or a published confession; the first full account of a murder was written about thirty years later by Thomas More, the lawyer who later became Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor; and two children's bones found under a Tower staircase in 1674 have never been dated, sexed or tested. Most historians of the period conclude that the boys died in the Tower in 1483, most probably on Richard's orders, because that is what the conduct of everyone around them implies; this is the position of the standard academic studies of the reign, by Charles Ross (1981), Rosemary Horrox (1989), A. J. Pollard (1991), Michael Hicks (2003, 2024) and Sean Cunningham (2003), and of the recent biographies by David Horspool (2015) and Chris Skidmore (2017), though the Duke of Buckingham, Richard's chief ally who turned against him that autumn, and Henry VII himself have also been proposed as the killer. Richard III's defenders, known as Ricardians and organised since 1924 in the Richard III Society, answer that no death is recorded and that two later claimants to the throne may have been the princes: the boy crowned "King Edward" at Dublin in 1487, called Lambert Simnel, an Oxford organ-maker's son, by Henry VII's government, and the "Richard, Duke of York" of the 1490s, who after his capture in 1497 confessed to being Piers Werbecque, called Perkin Warbeck, born at Tournai, a town in what is now Belgium. In 2023 Philippa Langley, the writer who led the search that found Richard III's grave in 2012, and her Missing Princes Project put four documents forward as evidence that they were: the Lille receipt, a receipt for pikes in the accounts of the artillery of Maximilian, the Habsburg King of the Romans (the elected German king) who governed the Low Countries, kept at Lille in northern France and dated December 1487, which calls the Dublin king "son of King Edward"; the Gelderland narrative, a first-person account of Richard of York's escape in a manuscript of about 1500 in the provincial archive of Gelderland at Arnhem in the Netherlands; the Dresden pledge, a pledge by "Richard of England" to Albert, Duke of Saxony, Maximilian's commander in the Low Countries, dated at Dresden in October 1493; and Maximilian's "three marks" letter, a letter from the same winter naming three bodily marks by which the claimant could be known.
cases.judged: Every document on both sides was read in print or online, in its own language with a translation where an edition could be reached (Mancini's Latin, the full Dutch of the Gelderland narrative and the Portuguese witness statements of 1496 could not be, and were read in translation or in summary; the Dresden pledge and the "three marks" letter are known only from the Missing Princes Project's descriptions), and tagged by what it can bear: for the survival documents, whether it shows a prince alive or only that a claimant or his backer said so; for the murder sources, whether the writer knew, inferred or reported a rumour, and whose side he was on. The evidence was then sorted into five clusters (the events of 1483; Henry VII's conduct from 1485 to 1502; the 1487 claimant; the 1490s claimant; and the traces of death, More's narrative and the bones) and weighed in a ledger, computed by a script published with the full report, which is linked from the page: each cluster is given a number for how likely that evidence would be under each of five outcomes (both boys died in 1483; Edward lived; Richard lived; both lived; something else), the numbers, which are judgments rather than measurements, are combined by Bayes's rule, the standard way of weighing evidence, from a stated starting weight, and the ledger is re-run with clusters dropped or softened to show how far the verdict moves when any number changes. Three things tipped the balance: the Lille receipt is contradicted by every other contemporary record that says whom the Dublin king claimed to be, and by the dates on his own documents, which count his reign as beginning in 1487, as Edward V's could not have done, an argument worked out by Randolph Jones, who has published on the Irish records in The Ricardian, the Richard III Society's journal, and restated in 2024 by Chris Phillips, an independent researcher, an argument the survival side has not answered; the 1490s claimant was placed in a Tournai family by Portuguese witnesses whose depositions, sworn statements, were taken at Setúbal, near Lisbon, in April 1496, a year before Henry VII had him; and Richard, who could have ended the rumour of the boys' deaths by producing two living nephews, did not do so in the two years of his reign. The result is that both boys most probably died in the Tower in 1483, in the late summer or autumn, in Richard III's custody, about 85 chances in 100, against about 6 in 100 that one or both lived on, nearly all of it an allowance for evidence not yet found, and about 9 in 100 for a death at some other time or place; a record of either boy alive after the autumn of 1483 made by someone not later paid to say so, or radiocarbon, sex and DNA tests on the 1674 bones, would change it.

cases.title: The Hanging Gardens
cases.question: Was the hanging garden of the Greek wonder-lists a real garden at Babylon, the Assyrian king Sennacherib's garden at Nineveh misplaced by the Greeks, or no single structure at all?
cases.verdict: Babylon, more likely than not, at about 55%. No single structure behind the story, about 35%; Nineveh, about 10%.
cases.confidence_label: about 55% (57 in the weighing with flat priors; 56 from a prior in Nineveh's favour; 27 when Dalley is granted her three contested readings at once)

standing.note: The case for Babylon rests on the unanimity of the witnesses that name a city, on Berossus, and on what Sennacherib's own text does and does not say, and each of those is a reading that a specialist could contest. It is a reading of the sources by non-specialists.

split: Babylon: a real raised palace garden behind the tradition, most plausibly Nebuchadnezzar's North Palace
No single structure: a literary construct with no one garden behind it
Nineveh: Sennacherib's garden, relocated to Babylon by confusion in the Greek tradition (Dalley)
new: An explicit weighing that shows where the weight lies, on the unanimity of location and on Berossus rather than on the screw, and what Dalley's case requires jointly: three contested readings at once, which is not visible when the case is presented as a list of resemblances.

A check of Nebuchadnezzar's silence across every text in the 2024 edition of his inscriptions (RINBE 1/1): no word for garden in any Babylon inscription of his, and the editors' statement that no other extant text of his mentions one. Beside that silence stand his own texts on the North Palace terrace, the texts that Berossus' "stone terraces" paraphrase, and the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary's observation of 1956 that the terrace "could well have been interpreted as a 'hanging garden'" (CAD G, 70); that observation was not found cited in any study on the Nineveh side.

"A replica of Mount Amanus" and "a wonder for all peoples", read across the Assyrian royal inscriptions, are stock phrases of palace rhetoric used by three kings (Sargon II, Sennacherib's father; Sennacherib himself; and Esarhaddon, his son). The second is said of the palace rather than of the garden, on the reading of siḫirti ekalli as "the entire palace" that the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary itself adopts: the dictionary files this very line under siḫirtu, "entirety", translating "I built the entire palace to a height to be admired by all people" (CAD S 236), while Dalley takes the word in its other sense, "circumference, around" (CAD S 235), and reads "the surroundings of the palace".

The bucket argument against the screw, from the clause in Sennacherib's inscription that states the device's purpose, "water drawn by bucket every day", with its ropes, wire chains and cables, is Bagg's (2014) and is already in the RINAP translation. What is added is only that the two disputed words, the "tree trunks" and "date palms" that Dalley reads as the screw, are listed in the inscription among the objects Sennacherib had cast in copper for the palace, alongside its lions, bull colossi and sphinxes, and that the wells serve the palace halls rather than the garden.

The baked brick and bitumen (natural asphalt) of Strabo and Diodorus do not tell Babylon from Nineveh, and building materials are not counted in the weighing. Sennacherib bedded his palace terrace in limestone bonded with bitumen under a spread of reeds, built the culverts that pass the Khosr, the stream that runs through Nineveh into the Tigris, under the city wall in baked brick and faced the palace arches with glazed baked brick (RINAP 3/1 nos. 16 and 17), and the archaeologist Ylenia Viggiano's 2025 study of the bricks of Nineveh adds courtyard pavements coated with bitumen and a "baked brick and bitumen ramp" at the city's Aššur Gate.
cases.confirms_prior: The verdict agrees with Bichler and Rollinger (2005), Bagg (2014, who rejects the Nineveh thesis and treats the classical location at Babylon as reliable), Potts (2013) and Pedersén (2021), who leave the garden at Babylon. Pedersén writes that "most scholars have accepted the identity of Nebuchadnezzar's North Palace and the palace described by Berossos" (2021, 125); that is his assessment, and no survey of specialists' opinions was made for the report. Nineveh has had published support besides Dalley (Renger 1998 and Veenhof 2001, as reported by Bichler and Rollinger; Meijer 2017, hedged; Foster 2004, a study on the Nineveh side known by its title and opening only), and the editors of Sennacherib's inscriptions take no position, filing the identification as an "opinion" with "critical reviews" (RINAP 3/1, n. 44). Rollinger (2013) had already argued that the Greek "hanging" reflects Nebuchadnezzar's own "high as a mountain"; the North Palace identification is his, the Leipzig Assyriologist Michael Streck's (2018) and Pedersén's; and the bucket argument against the screw is Bagg's.

change.qualifier: a substantial existing position that keeps the garden at Babylon against Dalley's Nineveh thesis, without showing that position to be the field's verdict
change.prior: The tradition since antiquity puts the garden at Babylon, where a century of excavation has found nothing; the block of vaulted cells in Babylon's Southern Palace that Koldewey identified as the garden between 1899 and 1917 turned out to be a storeroom, and nobody now defends it. Since 1993 Stephanie Dalley has argued for Sennacherib's garden at Nineveh, in articles of 1993 and 1994, a 2003 article with John Peter Oleson, a historian of ancient technology, on the water screw, a 2008 chapter on "Babylon" as a name for other cities, her 2013 book and a 2017 chapter. Some specialists accept the identification (Renger 1998 and Veenhof 2001, as reported by Bichler and Rollinger; Meijer 2017, hedged), many keep the garden at Babylon (Bichler and Rollinger 2005; Potts 2013; Bagg 2014; Pedersén 2021), and several Babylon specialists (Kuhrt, Beaulieu, van der Spek, Seymour) hold something like the view that no single structure lies behind the story. The editors of Sennacherib's inscriptions take no position.
change.explanation: The decisive passages, read in the standard editions, show the Nineveh case resting on three contested readings at once: that Berossus' garden sentence is an interpolation, that Sennacherib's copper tree trunks were a screw, and that Greek confusion could carry a garden from the Tigris to the Euphrates. Each looks improbable on the evidence, and Berossus, the one witness who had the Babylonian records in front of him, puts the garden in Nebuchadnezzar's palace. That is where Bichler and Rollinger, Potts, Bagg and Pedersén already stood. The weighing gives that position explicit shares, Babylon 55%, no single structure 35%, Nineveh 10%, with the figures the re-runs give when the weights change (Babylon 56% from a prior in Nineveh's favour, 27% when Dalley's three contested readings are all granted), and adds the observation that Sennacherib's "wonder" is said of the palace rather than of the garden; it does not show that the position prevails in the field.

overturn: For Nineveh: a Neo-Assyrian text calling Nineveh "Babylon"; a Greek text placing a wonder-garden at Nineveh; a witness to Berossus without the garden sentence; an Assyrian water screw found, depicted or named by a word whose meaning is secure; a Nineveh text or relief showing the garden on vaulted tiers.

For Babylon to become near-certain: excavation of the North Palace's northern slopes and riverside producing tree pits, garden soil or a planted terrace with water channels, or a cuneiform text naming a garden on the "new palace".
The item most within reach is a new witness to the Berossus paragraph.
fell_short: Dalley's 1994 article and 2013 book could not be read in full. What was read: the 1994 article's opening, all seventy-five of its footnotes and the forty-five page-referenced quotations of it in Bichler and Rollinger; of the book, its table of contents, about 230 page-referenced snippets and some forty reconstructed passages, including the Conclusion (pp. 203–205); Bagg's and Potts's reviews of the book in full; and her 1993, 2003, 2008 and 2017 statements in full. A reader with library access should check section 6 of the report against pp. 29–41, 61–82 and 107–126 of the book.

Five earlier studies, Reade 2000 (by Julian Reade of the British Museum, on Alexander the Great and the gardens), Bagg 2000 (on Assyrian waterworks), Foster 2004, Streck 2018 and Wiseman 1985 (by the British Assyriologist Donald Wiseman), are known through Bichler and Rollinger, Potts, Pedersén and the notes of the Sennacherib edition; Foster 2004 by its title and opening only.

Sennacherib's canal inscriptions at Bavian, the rock inscription at the head of his canal system, and at Jerwan were read in the older translations by Daniel Luckenbill and by Thorkild Jacobsen, who excavated the Jerwan aqueduct in the 1930s, rather than in RINAP 3/2, the second part of the Sennacherib edition. The Philo text was read in a poor scan.

The weighing's inputs are judgements rather than measurements. The sensitivity runs (other starting weights, each cluster left out in turn, two scenarios that favour Dalley) are printed in the report and can be rerun from the script.
No Assyriologist has reviewed the report.
cases.story: The story, as Greek writers told it, is that a king of Babylon, the great city on the river Euphrates in what is now southern Iraq, built an artificial mountain beside his palace for a wife who came from the hills of Media, in north-west Iran, and pined for them: stone terraces on brick vaults, planted with full-grown trees, watered from the river by machinery hidden inside the structure. By the first century BC Greek writers counted it among the seven wonders of the world. Five ancient descriptions survive, none by an author who writes as if he had seen it: the earliest, by Berossus, a priest of Babylon writing in Greek about 290 BC, names Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon from 605 to 562 BC, as the builder; two others, by Diodorus, a Greek historian of the first century BC, and Curtius, a Roman historian of the first century AD, say only "a Syrian king", meaning an Assyrian one, a king of the empire to the north; and two, by Strabo, a Greek geographer writing about AD 20, and a short treatise on the seven wonders that circulates under the name of Philo of Byzantium, a Greek engineer of the third century BC, though the treatise itself was written between the fourth and sixth centuries AD, name no builder. The garden has never been found: Robert Koldewey, the German archaeologist who excavated Babylon from 1899 to 1917, thought he had found it in a block of vaulted rooms that turned out to be a storage basement, and no later excavation has produced a garden.
cases.mystery: Nothing in the Babylonian records settles it either: no cuneiform text of Babylon's own kings (cuneiform is the wedge-shaped script of ancient Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, pressed into clay) mentions a garden there, and Herodotus, the Greek historian who described the city about 430 BC, says nothing of it. Three answers have been given: the traditional one keeps the garden at Babylon and gives it to Nebuchadnezzar, whose own inscriptions describe a new palace, the North Palace, built on terraces "as high as a mountain" beside his father's, so that on this view a planted terrace of that palace was exaggerated by later writers. Since 1993 Stephanie Dalley, an Assyriologist at the University of Oxford (Assyriology is the study of the cuneiform texts of Mesopotamia), has argued that the Greeks had the wrong city: the garden was built by Sennacherib, king of Assyria from 705 to 681 BC, beside his palace at Nineveh, the Assyrian capital on the Tigris near the modern city of Mosul, three hundred miles north of Babylon and a century earlier; his inscriptions describe a palace garden and a bronze water-raising device that she reads as a water screw (the spiral pump that the Greeks credited to Archimedes of Syracuse four centuries later), his canals and aqueducts survive in part, two carved stone panels (reliefs) from Nineveh show a garden, and the Greeks, who did confuse Assyria with Babylonia, moved the garden south. Some specialists accept this (Renger 1998 and Veenhof 2001, as reported by Reinhold Bichler and Robert Rollinger, ancient historians at Innsbruck whose 2005 article examines Dalley's thesis at length; Meijer 2017, with hedging); many keep the garden at Babylon, among them Bichler and Rollinger, Timothy Potts, an archaeologist of the ancient Near East who reviewed Dalley's book in 2013, Ariel Bagg, the historian of Assyrian water engineering, in 2014, and Olof Pedersén of Uppsala University, whose 2021 book synthesises the archaeology of Babylon; and a third answer, held in some form by several historians of Babylon (Amélie Kuhrt, Paul-Alain Beaulieu, Bert van der Spek and Michael Seymour), is that no single garden lies behind the story, which combined a Mesopotamian royal park, a Babylonian palace terrace and Greek engineering fantasy.
cases.judged: The kings' own inscriptions (Sennacherib's prisms, six- or eight-sided blocks of clay inscribed on every face, and Nebuchadnezzar's palace texts) were read in the standard editions, RINAP 3/1 for Sennacherib and RINBE 1/1 of 2024 for Nebuchadnezzar, together with the five Greek and Latin descriptions in the original languages, the excavation record at both cities and the arguments on both sides as published (Dalley's 1994 article and 2013 book only in part). The evidence was sorted into seven clusters, groups of items that rise and fall together, and each cluster was given a probability under each answer; with flat priors, meaning the three answers started level, the arithmetic gives Babylon 57%, no single structure 38%, Nineveh 5%. Three findings carried the most weight: every ancient witness who names a city names Babylon; Berossus places the garden in Nebuchadnezzar's palace, in a paragraph that follows Nebuchadnezzar's own inscription item by item; and the one passage in Sennacherib's inscriptions that describes his garden, repeated with small variants from prism to prism, speaks of water drawn by bucket and says nothing of terraces. Sennacherib's garden at Nineveh is real and well documented, and it is the closest ancestor of what the Greeks describe, but the evidence does not support Dalley's claim that it is the garden they described. Because three clusters turn on readings that specialists dispute, the headline is Babylon 55%, no single structure 35%, Nineveh 10%; these are judgements expressed as numbers, conditional on the framing and the weights, and a quotation of Berossus by another ancient writer that lacked the garden sentence, or an Assyrian text or relief showing the garden on vaulted tiers, would move the result towards Nineveh.

cases.title: The Ourang Medan
cases.question: Did a Dutch freighter named Ourang Medan lose her whole crew to an unexplained death in the Strait of Malacca in 1947 or 1948, and if not, who made the story up?
cases.verdict: Fabricated: the story was written by Silvio Scherli in Trieste in 1940 and published as fact. Invented outright about 85%; a real incident under another name, altered beyond recognition, about 14%; genuine as told below 1%.
cases.confidence_label: about 85% invented outright; about 14% a real incident under another name, altered beyond recognition; below 1% genuine as told
