standing.note: The story's growth is traced printing by printing from dated texts: the key ones are reproduced as page images, the rest are marked as reported or as search snippets, and every quoted passage was transcribed a second time blind against the images. The registers rule out the ship as described and cannot rule out a real incident under another name; the percentages are judgments.

split: A real incident under another name, altered beyond recognition
Genuine as told, in any of its dated versions
new: The Trieste texts in full: the article of 16 October 1940, the editors' note of 26 October 1940 announcing the story's reprinting abroad (the syndication note) and the sequel of 5 February 1941, read as page images from the newspaper's own digital archive and transcribed. Paijmans had a library copy of the first and quoted its rescue boat; the sequel had been listed by the anonymous 2024 blog on Scherli but not, so far as can be found, read. It shows that the sole survivor, the departure from Singapore, the falsified cargo, the nitroglycerine and cyanide, hold no. 4 and the rats are Scherli's own inventions of February 1941 rather than additions of 1948 or later, and that his three versions disagree on the date of the SOS, the ship's nationality, the exploding hold and the size of the cargo.

Scherli in the records: the decree of 1930 that changed his surname from Scherk to Scherli, with his birth date, parentage and address; the 1933 travel photography; the editors' 1940 reply to a doubting reader; the 1943 marriage and the civil-register entry giving his trade as merchant-navy radio officer; the 1950 report from Gijón, a Spanish port; the 1952 city directory; the 1954 letters to the American Tobacco Company; the 1958 photo credit; his death on 7 March 1985. The often-repeated claim that he wrote about the ship again in Export Trade, a New York trade paper, in 1959 rests on a misreading of a trade report on the port of Trieste.

The earliest open-archive Dutch printing: the Leekster courant, a weekly of Leek in the Dutch province of Groningen, of 24 January 1948 with its explicit credit to Elsevier's Weekblad, and the April 1948 item in the Dutch magazine De schalmei that treats the story as common knowledge; transcriptions of the Leekster and Semarang texts (the reprint in De locomotief, a daily of Semarang on Java in the Netherlands Indies) corrected against the page images. Full-text searches on fifteen distinctive phrases found no other printing of the text in 1947 to 1949 among the papers digitised on Delpher.

The registers, reproducibly: a volume-by-volume full-text check of seventeen Lloyd's Register volumes (fifteen for 1938/39 to 1950 and the 1930/31 and 1936 steamers volumes as controls) and of the Wreck Returns for 1946 to 1949, with page images and the scripts, and the Register entry that fixes the Silver Star as the Santa Cecilia of 1942 of the Grace Line, a New York shipping line, renamed Silver Star in 1946 and Santa Juana by mid-1947. The absence itself was known; the check rules out the ship as described and cannot rule out an incident under another name.

Logged negative searches: the Singapore and Malayan press for 1940 to 1949, the New Zealand press, the radio bulletins of the ANP, the Dutch national news agency, the Il Piccolo group's titles after February 1941, and the Coast Guard's Proceedings for the year after its editorial, which printed no correction and no letter.

The accretions dated: each later "fact" tied to the printing that introduced it, in particular the derivation of the Coast Guard editorial of May 1952 from the feature writer Win Brooks's text in The American Weekly of October 1948, argued from shared wording; the observation that its "February 1948" is the month of the Dutch sequels rather than of any event; and the Brazilian magazine Revista da Semana, of Rio de Janeiro, of May 1950, which names Scherli as narrator two years before the Coast Guard printed the story without a source.
cases.confirms_prior: Scherli's authorship, the Trieste priority of October 1940 (the Trieste printing being the earliest), the Associated Press (AP) cable of November 1940, the Elsevier's Weekblad printing of January 1948 and its editors' disclaimers were established by Theo Paijmans (Fortean Times 402, 2021), which remains the essential account. Estelle Hargraves (2015), Brian Dunning's Skeptoid (2020) and Paijmans showed that the Coast Guard editorial is unsigned and unsourced, that the "CIA document" is a private citizen's letter to the CIA, and that the Silver Star entered the story through the German pulp writer Otto Mielke's booklet of 1954 and Roy Bainton's article of 1999. The absence of the ship from Lloyd's Register was noted by Bainton and by later writers; that Taongi, the Marshall Islands atoll where the 1948 sequel lands its survivor, is uninhabited and has no mission, and that no torpedo boat "W 716" existed, were shown by Skeptoid and Paijmans.

change.qualifier: Paijmans's account of 2021, which traced the story to Scherli's Trieste article of October 1940, and completes its paper trail
change.prior: Sceptical researchers had already traced the tale back to 1940. Estelle Hargraves (2015) published the Associated Press clipping of November 1940; Theo Paijmans (Fortean Times, 2021) established the Trieste priority of October 1940 (the Trieste printing being the earliest), Scherli's authorship and the Elsevier's Weekblad printing of 1948 with its editors' disclaimers; Roy Bainton (1999) had noted the ship's absence from Lloyd's Register; Brian Dunning's Skeptoid (2020) and Paijmans showed that the Coast Guard editorial is unsourced and the "CIA memo" a private citizen's letter. Popular accounts from Frank Edwards (1956) to Bainton (1999) still present a Strait of Malacca mystery of February 1948 backed by the US Coast Guard's magazine of 1952.
change.explanation: The report agrees with the main line of Paijmans's account and overturns nothing; the basic debunking is not new. Its additions strengthen and date that account: the Trieste texts in full, which show the survivor and the chemical cargo to be the author's own inventions of 1941; the author's life from official records; a register check that can be repeated by anyone; and each later "fact" tied to the printing that introduced it, so the version that looks documentary can be taken apart printing by printing.

overturn: An entry for a vessel named Ourang Medan (or Orang Medan) in any Register Book of Lloyd's Register, the Netherlands or Netherlands-Indies ship registers, the Indonesian registry after 1945, or a Lloyd's casualty return, in any year from 1900 to 1950.

A contemporary news report, from Batavia, Singapore, Manila, Suva, Honolulu or the Marshall Islands (under US administration in 1947), of a derelict found with a dead crew in November 1939 or June 1947, or of an explosion and loss with about 22 or 40 dead.
A rescue recorded in the log or the Grace Line file of the Santa Juana ex Silver Star, or of any vessel, for June 1947.
Scherli's 16 October 1940 text citing a documented source: a named rescue vessel that existed, a port, an owner, a Lloyd's casualty number.
An Italian, Austrian or German printing before 16 October 1940 not by Scherli, which would at least show that he was retelling rather than inventing.

None of these has turned up in eighty-six years, and the first two are now searchable by anyone in minutes. The verdict would weaken, though not reverse, if the still-undigitised wartime Registers (1943 to 1946) or the unsearched Australian press showed a vessel or an incident that fits.
fell_short: Australia and Fiji: Trove, the Australian newspaper archive, and the Fiji Times for 1939 to 1941 could not be searched, though Scherli's 1941 sequel makes the ship Australian, bound for a Western Australian port, and lands the survivor in Fiji. An Australian-registered Ourang Medan, had one existed, would nonetheless be in Lloyd's Register, which lists every Commonwealth vessel over 100 tons, and no such entry exists.

Trieste: the three Ourang-Medan pages of Il Piccolo and a dozen other issues were read; the rest of "I drammi del mare", Scherli's series of sea dramas in the paper, and his 1950 "Bruciatutto" pieces, a later sea story, are reported from the anonymous 2024 blog and from the archive's text layer (the machine-read text behind the scan) rather than read from the page. The historical archive of the newspaper La Stampa, the Rome and Milan national libraries' newspaper portals and Google Books could not be searched.

Austria, France, Britain: the Austrian National Library's ANNO viewer, the British Newspaper Archive and Gallica's full-text pages are gated (closed to search without an account); the Vienna and Karlsruhe printings of October 1940 are known from Paijmans, the Yorkshire Evening Post, a Leeds evening paper, from clipping images, the two items in 7 Jours, a Lyon weekly, from Gallica's search snippets.

The Netherlands: Elsevier's Weekblad and the Dutch weekly Panorama are not digitised; the Elsevier text is known from the Leekster and Semarang reprints and from Paijmans. Mielke's 1954 booklet and Robert V. Hulse's 1953 article in Fate, the American magazine of the paranormal, were not seen.

Registers: the steamers-and-motorships volumes of Lloyd's Register for 1940 and for 1943 to 1946 are not online, nor is the 1942 sailing-vessels volume. A vessel that entered and left the Register only in those years would be missed by the Register check, though not by the 1946 to 1949 Wreck Returns or by the 1947 and 1948 volumes, which carry every ship afloat. Registry absence shows only that no ship of that name existed; an incident under another name cannot be excluded by searches, which is why 14 percent stays with that reading.

Scherli: the crew lists on Ancestry, the genealogy site, the Trieste civil registers and any literary estate were not consulted; the crew-list career is reported from the 2024 blog and Skeptoid. The 1930 decree spells him "Scherk"; the identification is very probable rather than proven.
No paywall or bot gate (a block on automated visitors) was bypassed. Where a source could not be opened it is marked "reported" and attributed to the investigator who saw it.
cases.story: In the version told today, a Dutch freighter called the Ourang Medan sent a distress call from the Strait of Malacca, the sea lane between Malaya and Sumatra, in February 1948: the officers were dead, the crew probably dead too, and the last words were "I die". An American ship, the Silver Star, found her drifting and put a boarding party aboard, who found the crew dead on their backs with faces turned up and mouths open, and even the ship's dog dead. Smoke rose from a hold, the boarding party fled, and the ship exploded and sank. Explanations offered since then range from fumes from a cargo of potassium cyanide and nitroglycerine to carbon monoxide, nerve gas and "something from the unknown".
cases.mystery: No port of registry, owner, rescue log or inquiry has ever been produced for the ship, and no ship of the name is in any list of the world's merchant ships. Those who think something real happened point to where the story appeared: the United States Coast Guard printed it in 1952 in its own safety magazine for merchant seamen, Proceedings of the Merchant Marine Council; a letter about it lies in the CIA's declassified files; The American Weekly, the Sunday magazine of the Hearst newspapers, claimed in 1948 that its research showed the tragedy had happened; and popular accounts from the American broadcaster Frank Edwards (1956) to the British writer Roy Bainton (1999) present it as a documented event. The sceptics, among them the blogger Estelle Hargraves (2015), Brian Dunning's Skeptoid podcast (2020) and the Dutch researcher Theo Paijmans (2021), answer that the Coast Guard item names no source, that the "CIA memo" is a private citizen's letter, and that Paijmans, writing in Fortean Times, the British magazine of strange phenomena, traced the tale to an Italian newspaper of 1940, where it is dated 1939 and set in the South Pacific. Even the sceptics had checked Lloyd's Register, the annual list of the world's merchant ships, by enquiry rather than by reading the volumes, and little was known of the Italian author.
cases.judged: Every printing of the story was read in the order it appeared, from the earliest known, a signed article in the Trieste evening paper Il Piccolo delle Ore Diciotto (Il Piccolo) of 16 October 1940, through reprints in nine countries to the books of the 1950s and 1960s, with every quoted passage transcribed from the page image and transcribed again blind (without sight of the first transcription) as a check. The scanned volumes of Lloyd's Register for 1938/39 to 1950, its quarterly returns of ships lost (the Wreck Returns) for 1946 to 1949, the Dutch fleet databases and the Singapore press were searched in full text; the author was traced through official gazettes, city directories, civil registers and his own letters; and each detail of the modern story was dated to the printing that introduced it. What came out is that the story was written by one man, Silvio Scherli, a ship's radio officer and freelance journalist of Trieste, the Italian port at the head of the Adriatic: he published it in 1940 as an event of 1939 off the Solomon Islands, added a sequel with a sole survivor in 1941, and in 1948 sold both, re-dated to 1947, to the Dutch weekly Elsevier's Weekblad, whose editors printed a note that they had nothing beyond his personal assurance; the Strait of Malacca, the date February 1948 and the Silver Star were added later by American and German writers. What tipped the balance was the texts, the author's shifting dates, places, finders and casualty counts, the re-used photographs and the absence of any independent report, with the registers adding only that no ship of that name existed; the verdict is fabricated, invented outright about 85 percent, a real incident under another name about 14 percent, genuine as told below 1 percent, and an entry in a register or in a return of ships lost, a contemporary news report or a rescue log would overturn it.

cases.title: Dyatlov Pass
cases.question: What made nine experienced skiers cut their way out of their tent on the night of 1 to 2 February 1959 and walk into the dark without boots or coats, and how did three of them come by crushing injuries with no mark on the skin?
cases.verdict: Cold killed six of the nine; a mass of snow, most probably in the ravine, crushed the other three. Natural causes at about 90 per cent: no other people, no weapon, no explosion, no vehicle and no poison is recorded on or around the bodies.
cases.confidence_label: about 90% natural causes (80 to 95 on the weight given to the missing chemical sheets)

standing.note: The evidence for natural causes is strong on the file as read; the trigger mechanism has a leading candidate rather than an answer, the slab at 45 per cent, with its snow requirement, a buried weak layer (a fragile layer of snow crystals on which a slab can slide) on the step above the tent, unmeasured; the place of the injuries is probable rather than demonstrated, resting on the 1959 examiner's statements about mobility and survival. Every figure is a judgement conditional on the nine explanations scored and the weight given to each of the 28 facts; none is a frequency.

split: Natural causes, no human or technological agent (sensitivity 80 to 95)
The three crushing injuries sustained in the ravine rather than at the tent (60 to 85)
Snow on the tent as the trigger for leaving it (50 to 80)
Of which: a small slab avalanche of the kind Gaume and Puzrin modelled (20 to 65)
Of which: drifted snow collapsing the roof
new: A from-scratch reimplementation of the Gaume and Puzrin release model with sensitivity and regime maps, charts of how its outcome changes as each input is varied. With the paper's own snow parameters, delayed release exists only where the weak layer lies between 24.7 and 29.7 degrees; the forensic window, the 9.5 to 13.5 hours the paper allows between the cut and the release, is met only at 26 to 28.5 degrees; cohesion, the bonding strength assumed for the weak layer, of 300, 440 and 450 Pa gives failure at the cut, the published delay and no release; and the time to release is proportional to a wind-deposition rate, the speed at which wind piles snow onto the slab, that nothing measured constrains. Dieter Issler, the avalanche scientist who reviewed the 2021 paper for the journal, called the agreement with the forensic delay "coincidental"; the regime map bears him out.

Injury physics that makes the examiner's statements quantitative. Any 100 to 300 kg of hard snow at 1 to 2 m/s, or 3 to 4 m of static snow on a person against a firm base, gives the rib pattern without breaking skin, so the chest injuries cannot distinguish the tent from the ravine. For Thibeaux-Brignolle's 9 by 7 cm depressed temporal fracture, the 2.5 to 10 kN of the cadaver tests over the depression needs a crushing pressure of 400 kPa or more, which excludes a soft or medium slab as the sole loader but not a hard slab, nor a hard object under the snow.

A 28-fact by 9-explanation matrix, a table with a cell for every pairing and the contradicting sheet named in every red cell, keeping the three slab versions (Gaume and Puzrin 2021, the prosecutors' check of 2019 to 2020, Buyanov 2011) separate because they place the injuries differently.

The darkness and the clock from open data: the moon below the horizon from 11:27 on 1 February to 04:15 on 2 February; full night from 19:40; the tent site in mountain shadow from 14:40; walking time to the cedar 35 to 85 minutes; the readings at Burmantovo, the nearest weather post, in the Lozva valley below the mountains, falling from −8 to −21 °C between 15:00 and 03:00.

The fireballs closed against the General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects (GCAT), the astronomer Jonathan McDowell's launch list: the sighting of 17 February at 06:46 local time is the launch of an R-7, the Soviet intercontinental missile that had launched Sputnik, at 01:46 UTC, five hours behind local time; the sighting of 31 March at 03:53 local time is the R-7 failure of 30 March at 22:53 UTC; and nothing capable of reaching the northern Urals was launched on 1 or 2 February.

A catalogue of 41 places where the standard English transcription of the autopsy acts and interrogations, the version most English-language discussion relies on, differs from the Russian on load-bearing points, among them the "bomb" in Vozrozhdenny's testimony, which in Russian is «воздушной взрывной волне», an air blast wave, with no bomb; "first hour" for «первые часы», the first hours; and knuckle abrasions rendered as the wrist. With it, 16 internal contradictions, 16 gaps, and 17 further translation differences in the scene and search documents.

The legal status of the 2020 conclusions of the prosecutors' check: disowned by the Prosecutor General on 10 August 2020, never published, never ruled on by any court, with the 28 May 1959 resolution still the only decision with legal force and the relatives' demand of 2 June 2026 for a new criminal case unanswered at the date of the report.

A bound on the average slope from a public 30 m digital elevation model, a grid of ground heights at 30 m spacing: 15 to 16 degrees at the cairn-marked tent position, the site three independent Russian researchers agree on, and no candidate above 19.5 degrees. It does not support the 2021 paper's 23 ± 2 degree average, but it says nothing about the 4 to 6 m steps the model rests on, which the authors' 9 cm drone survey shows.
cases.confirms_prior: Ivanov's 1959 resolution that a natural force killed the group, and Vozrozhdenny's statements on mechanism and survival, are the basis of the finding. Sogrin's 15 to 18 degrees and Borzenkov's 16 to 17 for the average slope are what the elevation model gives. The location of the injuries in the ravine is the finding of Andrei Kuryakov, the department head in the Sverdlovsk regional prosecutor's office who ran the check of 2019 to 2020, and of Nikitin, whose 2019 placement of them there is taken as expert opinion in line with the 1959 examiner rather than as new measurement. The 17 February R-7 identification is Buyanov's, made with the space historian Aleksandr Zheleznyakov in 2007. The observation that small slabs on these slopes vanish within an hour, and the finding that steps steeper than 28 degrees run above every candidate tent position, are Puzrin and Gaume's own field results, reported in their 2022 Comment, a follow-up article on the 2021 paper, and not independently checked. Issler's point about the fitted delay was made in peer review in 2020.

change.qualifier: the 1959 verdict of a natural cause and the prosecutors' 2020 placement of the injuries in the ravine, and reads the slab model's two quantitative claims differently: the delay is fitted rather than predicted, and the injury physics is indifferent to location
change.prior: The 1959 investigation closed with "an elemental force the people were unable to overcome" (Ivanov, 28 May 1959). The prosecutors' check of 2019 to 2020 named a small slab plus hypothermia, death by cold, with the ravine injuries from a collapse of the undercut snow bank; on 10 August 2020 the Prosecutor General disowned the press conference that had announced these conclusions, and they were never published or tested in court. Gaume and Puzrin (2021, 2022) supplied a physical mechanism, a delayed wind-slab release on a buried weak layer at a 28 degree step, and field evidence that such steps and such slabs exist nearby. Buyanov (2011) puts the crushing injuries at the tent; Holmgren (2019) argues a katabatic wind, Eichar (2013) infrasound, and Rakitin (2013) a KGB operation.
change.explanation: The finding agrees with the 1959 verdict of a natural cause and with the prosecutors' 2020 placement of the injuries in the ravine, and it agrees with Gaume and Puzrin that the slab mechanism is possible on this slope, treating it as the leading single trigger candidate at 45 per cent. It reads the model's two quantitative selling points differently: the delay is fitted rather than predicted, and the injury physics is indifferent to location. It rejects Buyanov's injuries-at-the-tent version on the examiner's mobility statements, which argue against the tent without establishing the ravine, and closes the fireball, Mansi, KGB, infrasound and katabatic-wind-as-hurricane theories on cited sheets; wind alone survives as a trigger at about 15 per cent. Nothing here overturns a position held by a specialist.

overturn: A snow profile up the step above the 1959 tent position: a buried weak layer under a wind slab would take the slab to about 65 per cent and the snow trigger to about 80; repeated hard, well-bonded snow to the ground would push the slab toward 20.

The 1959 tent position from the prosecutors' 2019 photogrammetry, which fixed the site by comparing 1959 and 2019 photographs, overlaid on the 2021 drone model, naming the step above the cut and its angle and length.
The missing 1959 chemical and histological (tissue) sheets: a toxin would cut the natural-cause figure sharply.
A full exhumation with modern imaging: broad compression fractures would confirm the ravine; localised blows or a weapon would overturn the finding outright.
A range or telemetry record of any launch over 61.8° N 59.4° E, the position of the site, on 1 or 2 February 1959; the published lists contain none.
The hourly 1959 synoptic record, the weather-station log, for Burmantovo, Ivdel and Nyaksimvol, the nearest stations; a recorded fall-wind event would raise the wind-only trigger.
The written conclusions and nine expert reports of the prosecutors' check of 2019 to 2020, held in the Sverdlovsk state archive with restricted access.
The original 26 to 28 February 1959 negatives of the tent and the slope above it, for a crown line or debris lobe, the marks a slab leaves where it breaks away and where it stops.
A dynamic model of the ravine bank collapse: if the collapse cannot deliver the load, the injuries go back to the tent and to Buyanov's version.
fell_short: No field measurement of the snow at the site: every snow observation is other people's (1959, 2010 to 2019, 2021 to 2023) and none is a pit line up the step above the fixed 1959 tent position.

The ravine collapse, the least secure step of the reconstruction, is treated by static and quasi-static calculation only, which take the snow as a resting load; nobody has run a dynamic model of it, one that follows the collapse in motion.

Only volume 1 of the case file and the published radiograms, the search party's radio messages, were read; volume 2, the unpublished 2020 expert reports and the original 1959 negatives were not. The model paper's code and the cadaver-test primaries, the original publications of those tests, could not be obtained; the reproduction used the published equations and the peer-review file.

The weather for the night is reconstructed from three daily stations 100 to 200 km away, the notes of the Burmantovo readings kept by Yevgeny Maslennikov, the experienced hiker who led the search on the ground, and the 2020 microclimate expertise, the weather reconstruction commissioned by the prosecutors, as reported; no hourly 1959 record for the site was obtained.
Tumanov's claim that the rib fractures run on different lines was not checked against the autopsy drawings.
The hour of leaving the tent is inferred within a 2.5-hour window from a digestion estimate, the hours since the last meal, written identically for five bodies.
cases.story: In late January 1959 nine ski hikers, eight students or recent graduates of the Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg) led by 23-year-old Igor Dyatlov, and a 37-year-old ski instructor, Semyon Zolotaryov, set out across the northern Urals. On 1 February they pitched their tent on the open east slope of Kholat Syakhl, a treeless mountain above the pass that now carries Dyatlov's name, about 150 m below the crest and 1.5 km above the forest, on a platform they had cut into the snow; that night all nine cut their way out through the tent wall and walked downhill without boots or coats in the dark, with the air falling toward minus 25 °C. Searchers found the tent on 26 February with everything inside; five bodies, dead of cold, between the tent and a cedar at the forest edge over the following week; and the last four in May, in a ravine stream bed under metres of snow, three of them with crushed chests or a crushed skull and no wound on the skin. The investigator who ran the case, Lev Ivanov of the regional prosecutor's office, closed it on 28 May 1959 with the finding that they had died of «стихийная сила», an elemental force; the closing resolution does not say what the force was.
cases.mystery: Nothing in the 1959 case file explains why nine experienced people left their only shelter at once, or how three of them were crushed 1.5 km from the tent with injuries that Boris Vozrozhdenny, the forensic examiner who performed the nine autopsies, said needed a great force of the kind seen when a person is thrown by a car. The record cannot settle it: the chemical analyses that the autopsy acts, the examiner's written reports on each body, refer to are not in the file, and of the nine bodies only one, Zolotaryov's, has been examined since 1959, privately, in 2018. The explanations fall into five camps, the first of them snow, a small avalanche or a collapse of snow onto the tent: this is the view of the Sverdlovsk regional prosecutors, who checked the case again in 2019 to 2020, of the snow scientist Johan Gaume and the geotechnical engineer Alexander Puzrin, whose 2021 paper gave it a physical model, and of the engineer Evgeny Buyanov (2011), who holds the avalanche view but puts the crushing injuries at the tent; it is opposed by people who have examined the slope and its snow in winter, the aviation engineer Vladimir Borzenkov and the 1959 searchers Vladislav Karelin and Sergey Sogrin, who say the slope is too gentle, the snow too well bonded and the tent too undisturbed for any avalanche. The other four are wind (a katabatic wind, a violent fall wind off the mountain: the Swedish archaeologist Richard Holmgren, 2019); infrasound (panic from low-frequency sound: the American writer Donnie Eichar, 2013); people (hunters of the Mansi, the indigenous people of that part of the Urals, criminals, or a KGB operation, the last from the pseudonymous Russian author Alexei Rakitin, 2013); and weapons (a rocket, a secret weapon or a toxic release, fed by reports of fireballs, glowing spheres seen over the Urals that February, and by radioactive traces on the clothing).
cases.judged: The 1959 case file, volume 1, 392 numbered pages, each called a sheet, holding the search records, the interrogations, the search party's radio messages and the nine autopsy acts, was read in Russian and 459 facts were extracted with their sheet numbers; the slope, the darkness and the cold of that night were computed from public elevation, astronomical and weather data; the Gaume and Puzrin model was reimplemented from its published equations; and the 2018 examination of Zolotaryov's exhumed bones was added. Then 28 of the facts were scored against nine explanations, with the sheet that contradicts each named, and the reimplemented model showed that its release delay is fitted to the forensic clock, the paper's estimate of the time of death from the watches and the hours since the last meal, rather than predicted, and that its injury physics cannot tell the tent from the ravine, so a small slab avalanche, a plate of wind-packed snow sliding off a steeper step in the slope above the tent, is ranked the leading candidate for the trigger, at 45 per cent, without being established. What tipped the balance toward a natural cause is the file itself: the tent was cut open from inside, the tracks show people walking downhill at a normal pace with no track of any other person near them, no document, injury or object points to a weapon, an explosion or a poison, and Vozrozhdenny said that Nikolay Thibeaux-Brignolle, whose skull was crushed, could only have been carried and that Lyudmila Dubinina, whose chest was crushed, lived ten to twenty minutes, which rules out a 1.5 km walk with those injuries and is what places them, most probably, in the ravine. The verdict is cold for six and crushing under snow for three, natural causes at about 90 in 100; snow on the tent as the trigger and the ravine as the place of the injuries are the most probable answers, and neither is established; a snow profile (a pit dug to read the snow layers) up the step above the tent, the missing chemical sheets, or an exhumation of the other two crushed bodies could move the figures.

cases.title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
cases.question: Did Hamelin really lose 130 of its young people on 26 June 1284, and if it did, what became of them?
cases.verdict: Hamelin probably did lose a group of its young people in or close to 1284 (80 in 100); of seven explanations for how, a recruited departure for the new villages of the colonial east ranks first at 42 in 100, and where they went cannot be recovered from the sources.
cases.confidence_label: 80 in 100 that a loss was real; emigration first of seven at 42 in 100 (about 26 to about 46 as the first figure moves between 50 and 90)

standing.note: The 42 for emigration is a plurality among seven explanations rather than a majority, and no source describes a recruitment, a route or a destination; the shares are one reader's judgements, conditional on the hypotheses listed and the weights chosen. The date, the number and the sequence come from witnesses written 150 years and more after the event.

split: Locator-led emigration of young townspeople to the north-east
No single real event; a late tradition built on a date formula
A religious or Midsummer procession that dispersed or came to grief
An accident near the town: landslide, sinkhole or drowning
A military levy or ruse: the Everstein siege of 1284 or another feud
Something else: epidemic, an unrecorded calamity
new: None of the source corrections is new evidence in the sense of an unpublished document; each is a new use or a re-reading of something printed or digitised: Fink's Urkundenbuch of 1903 (the Hamelin charter book, the collection of the town's medieval charters), Prümers's Pommersches Urkundenbuch of 1885 (the Pomeranian one), the Wolfenbüttel facsimile of the Lüneburg manuscript, Udolph's article of 1997.

New use of a printed source. The Minden charter of 6 July 1502 (Urkundenbuch des Stiftes und der Stadt Hameln II, no. 663) documents a Calvary, a devotional Way of the Cross with stations, "before the east gate … to the boundary of Klein-Afferde, commonly 'beneden den Koppen'". It fixes what the inscriptions of 1525–1602 meant by "Koppen", agrees with Samuel Erich's location of 1654, and rules out Kopahn (Dobbertin) and Coppenbrügge or the Ith ridge, thirteen kilometres east of Hamelin (Waltraud Woeller, Gernot Hüsam), as readings of the phrase. It cannot establish anything about 1284: neither that the group went that way, nor that a Calvary existed there in 1284, nor a destination. It is not cited in Udolph 1997, in Alfred Cammann's summary of Dobbertin's theory of 1984, in Wulf's commentary in DI 28 or in the theory literature that could be read; Hüsam's 1993 paper on "Calvaria" and volume I of the Hamelin Urkundenbuch (Meinardus 1882) could not be obtained, so the claim of novelty is qualified.

Checked against the original. Pommersches Urkundenbuch II no. 1308 shows Count Nicolaus of Spiegelberg with his brothers at Stettin on 8 July 1284, twelve days after the tradition's date; the "† 1283" of the Wikipedia genealogy, repeated in recent summaries, is wrong (Dobbertin had the right date, as Cammann's summary of him in 1984 shows). A mounted count could ride the 470 kilometres from Hamelin to Stettin in twelve days; a column of 130 on foot, at 25 kilometres a day, could not. This corrects a date and shows that a channel existed; it does not show that any transfer of people from Hamelin took place.

Checked against the original. The Lüneburg note (Ratsbücherei Lüneburg, the town library, Ms. Theol. 2° 25, fol. 268r), re-read from the facsimile: the text circulating on Wikipedia has no basis for its heading "Fabula exodi Hamelnsis" (a cataloguer's title) or its "fere" ("about", before the number), the scribe wrote "valvam" over a cancelled "portam" (both Latin words for a gate), and the note contains no Latin verses. The eyewitness chain runs through Dean Johannes de Lüde (will 1378), the dean whose mother the note names as having seen the children go; it is the only link the sources offer to a fourteenth-century record.

Correction. The "surnames fed into a computer" story (1998 press) has no counterpart in Udolph 1997, which examines place names and has only a short section on medieval bynames (the added names that preceded hereditary surnames); several of the place names that Udolph traced from the Hamelin region to the east are attested in the east before 1284 (Hindenburg near Prenzlau in 1269, Depenau in 1250), so the names show that a settlement corridor existed; they do not show that the group of 1284 travelled it.
cases.confirms_prior: Christine Wulf's edition of the inscriptions (DI 28, 1989) had already shown that the date "of about 1300" that most retellings give to a stained-glass window in Hamelin is Dobbertin's and undocumented, that the oldest inscription is 1525, and that the "1384: 100 years since our children left" record, often repeated, cannot be traced to any scholarly or early-modern source. Willy Krogmann showed in 1934 that the rats are a south German wandering motif, a story element that travels from place to place, which fused with the Hamelin story in the 1560s. Dobbertin, Udolph, Norbert Humburg, Wolfgang Mieder and the Museum Hameln already rank emigration first; the report agrees, at lower confidence. Bernd Ulrich Hucker's objection of 1985 (a lawful emigration should have left traces) stands as the counter-case, and the accident, procession and levy readings have advocates of their own.

change.qualifier: Dobbertin, Udolph, Humburg, Mieder and the Museum Hameln in ranking emigration first, at lower confidence and without choosing a destination
change.prior: Since the 1950s a substantial line of opinion (Hans Dobbertin from 1955, Jürgen Udolph 1997, Norbert Humburg, Wolfgang Mieder 2007, and the Museum Hameln today) has read the tradition as a recruited emigration to the colonial east; Dobbertin argued for Pomerania and Prussia, Udolph for the Prignitz and the Uckermark, two districts of Brandenburg, all of them lands east of the Elbe. Bernd Ulrich Hucker objected in 1985 that a lawful emigration should have left traces. The accident reading (Waltraud Woeller 1957/61, Gernot Hüsam 1990–2024), the procession reading (Britannica 1911, G. Spanuth 1958, Rumpf 1985) and the levy reading (Fein 1749, Thomas Küntzel 2010) have advocates of their own, and Willy Krogmann (1934, partly) and Rostek-Lühmann (1995) doubt that any single event lies behind the legend. The popular version adds a computer analysis of surnames said to prove the destination, which comes from a 1998 press report.
change.explanation: The report keeps emigration in first place, at 42 in 100 rather than as a settled result, refuses to choose a destination, and removes the surname evidence from the case. It gives the possibility that the tradition records no single event more weight than the specialists do, 18 in 100. The source corrections change dates and readings in the literature and leave the ranking unchanged.

overturn: A charter, a locator's contract or a town book of about 1284–1295 naming settlers "de Hamelen" (of Hamelin) in a new village in Pomerania, the Neumark (Brandenburg's lands east of the river Oder), Prussia or Brandenburg would, on these weights, push emigration above 70 and fix the destination. The Pomeranian charter book's volumes for 1284–1300 contain no such entry; the charter books of Prussia, Brandenburg and Mecklenburg and the earliest burgher books, the registers of townsmen, of Riga, Danzig, Elbing, Stettin and Prenzlau, five towns in the east, have not been searched systematically.

A fourteenth-century Hamelin document mentioning the exodus, in the records of St Boniface's, the collegiate church (one run by a body of canons) that was Hamelin's principal church, or in the "old book" the Lüneburg writer used, would settle whether it happened; a full search of the Hamelin deposit in the Hauptstaatsarchiv Hannover, the Lower Saxony state archive in Hanover, finding nothing would push "no single event" up.
A mass grave of the 1280s at the Koppen (the Afferde hills) or on the Ith would revive the accident theories; nothing of the kind has appeared in seven centuries of quarrying and building there.

Hartmann's 1941 genealogy of the Spiegelberg counts, which could not be obtained, may record Nicolaus after July 1284; if he reappears in Saxony in 1285, the reading in which he himself led the group to Pomerania fails, though the channel remains possible.
fell_short: Not available: Dobbertin's Quellensammlung itself (his collection of the sources), Hartmann 1941, Hüsam 1993 and 2024, Küntzel 2010, Meinardus 1882 (Urkundenbuch I), Wauer 2000 (a name-book of the Uckermark) and Bichlmeier 2024 (a review), so no list of the members of Hamelin's town council of 1284, the men who would have known of a sponsored emigration, could be attempted.
The Landbuch of 1375, the Brandenburg land register, was available only as a scan too poor to search for names. No new document from the thirteenth or fourteenth century was found.

There is no statistics or stylometry (the statistical comparison of writing habits) here; the computation is limited to the calendar and distance checks. The probabilities are one reader's judgement of the tradition's features and add no evidence of their own.
The narrative of the event is the tradition's narrative, and the reconstruction built on it is speculative in the plain sense that no source describes a recruitment, a route or a destination.
cases.story: Hamelin (in German, Hameln) is a small town on the river Weser in northern Germany, some 40 kilometres south-west of Hanover. The story it has told since the fifteenth century: on 26 June 1284, the feast day of Saints John and Paul, a handsome, well-dressed stranger with a silver pipe came in through the gate on the river side, played through the streets, and led 130 of the town's children out through the gate on the far side, towards the hill outside the walls where the town carried out its executions. The children vanished; their mothers went from town to town and found nothing; and the town, the story says, counted its years from that day. The rats, the unpaid fee and the mountain that opened to take the children in first appear in books of the 1550s and 1560s; the lame boy left behind first appears in an English book of 1605, from which the poet Robert Browning took his poem of 1842.
cases.mystery: Nothing written at the time survives: the earliest account is a short Latin note added about 1430–50, some 150 years after the event, to a manuscript now in the town library of Lüneburg, a city about 150 kilometres to the north-east (the Lüneburg note), and its writer says he copied it from "an old book"; the house inscriptions that give the date and the number begin in 1525, and the first printed accounts date from 1556. Historians therefore argue about whether anything happened at all, and if it did, what: Hans Dobbertin, a local historian who collected the sources in 1970, and Jürgen Udolph, a German specialist in place names, hold that the "children" were young people recruited for the German settlement of the lands east of the river Elbe, which was actively under way in the 1280s, a view shared by the Museum Hameln, the town's museum, by Norbert Humburg, editor of the 1985 volume of the Hamelin conference on the legend, and by Wolfgang Mieder, author of the English handbook on the legend of 2007, while the medieval historian Bernd Ulrich Hucker objected in 1985 that a lawful emigration should have left traces. Others read the story as a religious procession of the young that came to grief (the Britannica encyclopaedia of 1911; two later writers, G. Spanuth in 1958 and Rumpf in 1985); as an accident on the hills outside the town (the folklorist Waltraud Woeller in 1957–61, the local historian Gernot Hüsam since 1990); as a levy of young men for a local war (Fein, a garrison preacher, in 1749; Thomas Küntzel, writing in the Hamelin museum society's yearbook in 2010, who pointed to the siege in 1284 of the castles of the counts of Everstein, Hamelin's former lords, near the town); or as a crime, and some folklorists (Willy Krogmann in 1934, in part; Rostek-Lühmann in 1995) doubt that any single event lies behind the tale. The version most often repeated in English, that Udolph proved where the children went by feeding Hamelin's surnames into a computer, rests on a press report of 1998; Udolph published no such study.
cases.judged: The evidence is every surviving witness to the story, meaning each document that records it, read in order of date and, wherever possible, from the originals: the Lüneburg note from the facsimile, the images of the manuscript that the Herzog August Library at Wolfenbüttel has put online; the house inscriptions from Christine Wulf's standard edition of 1989 (DI 28, in the Deutsche Inschriften, the standard German edition of medieval and early modern inscriptions); the sixteenth-century printed accounts from digitised copies; and the medieval charters of Hamelin and of Pomerania, the duchy on the Baltic coast about 470 kilometres to the north-east, from the printed charter books, the volumes that collect such medieval documents. The method is to list what the tradition, the story as the town handed it down, claims and when each claim is first attested, then to score seven explanations against those claims and against the documentary record of the 1280s, and to attach to each explanation a probability expressing an estimate of its likelihood; two documents not previously used for the legend came out of the charter books, a bishop's letter of 1502 that fixes the place the inscriptions name and a Pomeranian charter of 8 July 1284 that puts Count Nicolaus of Spiegelberg, of the family of minor nobles who from 1281 held Coppenbrügge, the next lordship east of Hamelin, at the Pomeranian duke's court twelve days after the date of the exodus, and neither document shows what happened in 1284, since the Spiegelbergs show that a channel to the east existed and no evidence shows that a Hamelin group used it. The result is a ranking of the seven explanations by estimated likelihood, and it does not establish which of them is correct: a real loss of young people probably lies behind the tradition (80 in 100, with the caution that no surviving witness is older than about 1430); a recruited departure for the new villages east of the Elbe, the colonial east, is the best single explanation at 42 in 100, which ranks it first, with the other six together carrying 58; and the sources cannot say where the group went. A charter, a locator's contract (a locator was a contractor who recruited settlers for a territorial lord) or a town book of about 1284–1295 naming settlers "de Hamelen" (of Hamelin) in a new village in the east would push emigration above 70; a fourteenth-century Hamelin document mentioning the exodus would settle whether it happened.

cases.title: Who wrote "A Visit from St. Nicholas"?
cases.question: Did Clement Clarke Moore, who claimed the poem in 1844, write the fifty-six lines the Troy Sentinel printed without a name on 23 December 1823, or did Henry Livingston Jr., for whom his descendants have claimed them since 1879?
cases.verdict: Clement Clarke Moore wrote it. The confidence is about 85 percent: Moore 85, Henry Livingston Jr. 12, someone else 3.
cases.confidence_label: about 85% (85 to 90 on the documents alone)

standing.note: The documents carry the verdict, and most of them were read in transcription, including Holley's 1836 statement on which the earliest dating of Moore's authorship rests; no manuscript from before 1823 survives on either side. The stylometry is weak both ways and every metre-matched result rests on four Moore poems, so the 85 percent is a reasoned judgment, conditional on the weights set out in the full report, which is linked from this page; no calculation produced it.

new: Nothing here is new documentary evidence; all of it is new analysis of texts already known.

Reference profiles built from the anapestic verse of both men only, validated on known poems and then applied to the poem, are the comparison Scott Norsworthy asked Jackson for in 2017. Jackson reported his tests' scores for Moore's four anapests as a control; nobody had built and validated a metre-matched design. It places the poem with Moore on every word and character feature set, on a base of four Moore poems.

The leave-one-out validation of standard profile methods (each known sample held out in turn and attributed by the rest, using the most frequent words or character n-grams) is new to this question. Trained on whole corpora they misfile Moore's own anapests (0 to 2 of 4 correct). Jackson's own lists do better (2 or 3 of 4 with Moore, depending on whether the dividing line between the two men is set from all their verse or from their anapestic verse only), but the poem lies beyond all four on both of his tests. A simulation on 105 pairs of control poets (one poet's samples tested against a reference built from another's to look like Livingston's corpus, 16 anapestic and 21 other samples) shows the mechanism is general: a poet's anapestic samples are misattributed to that Livingston-like reference about twice as often as the same poet's other verse (29 against 16 percent on words, 32 against 15 percent on character 4-grams).

A General Impostors verification against 29 period poets, which no earlier study of this question appears to have run. Neither candidate is verified, and the poem's nearest neighbours are the comic anapestic poets of the period (Byron, Thomas Love Peacock, Thomas Hood, and James and Horace Smith, authors of the parodies Rejected Addresses of 1812).

Jackson's word-list and phoneme-pair tests are replicated on independently built corpora, which no earlier study appears to have done. Both reproduce (poem 51.6 on the word test against Moore 33.7 and Livingston 49.5; 64.6 on the phoneme test against 49.9 and 61.8). On the 14 control poets who wrote enough in both metres to compare, anapestic verse scores 5.5 points more "Livingston" on the phoneme test; the word test is not shifted by metre.

The eight favourite expressions of Moore's that Norsworthy found in the poem and the six that Jackson found absent from it are put on one likelihood scale with Poisson tails (the chance under a Poisson model of a count at least as high as the poem's). "Like" occurs 8 times in the poem's 545 words (14.7 per 1,000) against 8.4 per 1,000 in Moore's anapests and 1.2 in Livingston's. Norsworthy's eight favour Moore by a log likelihood ratio (natural logarithm) of 14, about a million to one on the model's own terms, driven by "like"; Jackson's six favour Livingston by 2.8; words found in only one man's corpus split three and three. The expression evidence is mixed: each list favours the side that compiled it, the words found in only one man's corpus split evenly, and the largest single item, the rate of similes, matches Moore's anapests and has no parallel in Livingston's verse.
cases.confirms_prior: The documentary picture is Scott Norsworthy's: Moore's 1844 letter in the New York American, a newspaper (re-read here from the scan, in which the last digit of the first year Moore gives is smudged), Holley's 1836 statement (read only in Norsworthy's transcription), the pre-1844 attributions, and his identification of T. W. C. Moore, a kinsman of Moore's by marriage who sent one of Moore's handwritten copies to the New-York Historical Society in 1862, as Livingston's first cousin once removed, so that a relative of Livingston's was vouching for Moore's authorship in 1862; Seth Kaller (2004) and Stephen Nissenbaum (2001) had set out the record before him. Foster's "all" marker (his claim that the poem's use of "all" as an intensifier was a Livingston habit) fails on these corpora, the two men's rates being equal. Tom Jerman (2023) and Shlomo Argamon (2023), known here only through secondary accounts, are reported to point the same way as the metre-matched result; neither was replicated. Jackson's own numbers reproduce.

change.qualifier: the traditional attribution to Moore; what changes is the reading of Jackson's numbers
change.prior: The traditional attribution is to Moore. Livingston's descendants have disputed it since 1899, Don Foster since 2000 (Author Unknown) and MacDonald P. Jackson since 2016, whose statistical tests on the poem's words and sounds placed it with Livingston; Jackson's position in 2017 was that the external evidence favours Moore, the internal evidence favours Livingston, and the question may never be settled. Stephen Nissenbaum (2001), Seth Kaller (2004) and Scott Norsworthy have defended Moore on the documents, and Tom Jerman (2023) and Shlomo Argamon (2023) are reported to have found for Moore by computation.
change.explanation: The verdict agrees with the traditional attribution. What it changes is the reading of Jackson's numbers: his Livingston-favouring results are real, but they are close to what any anapestic poem by Moore produces on tests trained on his mostly iambic output. On word and character features the metre-matched design places the poem with Moore; only Jackson's word-list test survives the metre check, and it favours Livingston by a margin the test's own noise nearly covers. Taken together the stylometry is close to even and weak in both directions, and it neither raises nor lowers the documentary figure by much.

overturn: A Poughkeepsie newspaper printing of the poem from before 1823, which the family said existed and which searches since the claim was first published in 1919 have not found; Dutchess County (the county around Poughkeepsie) newspaper files from 1800 to 1822 are where this could be settled.
A dated document from before 1844 in which any Livingston mentions the poem, or a manuscript of the poem in Livingston's hand.
An attribution method that correctly assigns at least nine in ten of both men's anapestic poems on a leave-one-out test and still places the poem with Livingston.
fell_short: Moore's anapestic sample is four poems and 1,797 words, and every metre-matched result rests on it; a percentile (the poem's place among the ranked samples) is coarse when there are four samples.

Livingston's corpus comes from second-hand transcriptions on henrylivingston.com, a website run by one of his descendants, and includes the 1803 Carrier's Address (a newspaper's New Year's poem), which Norsworthy thinks is probably by Isaac Mitchell, a Poughkeepsie newspaper editor; a purged corpus, with that poem removed, was not run.

The phoneme features use the modern American pronunciations of the CMU dictionary, the Carnegie Mellon pronouncing dictionary, and skip unknown words. The impostors test could not verify either man, so every stylometric statement concerns weak signals.

No manuscript was examined, and most documents were read in transcription, including Holley's 1836 statement on which the earliest dating of Moore's authorship rests. Jackson's book was read in excerpt and through page-referenced quotation rather than in full.

Jerman's protocol in JGAAP (an open-source authorship-attribution program) and Argamon's method of repeated comparisons on random subsets of the texts, as the Bloomberg columnist Justin Fox describes it, were not re-run, and the Dutch-forms question (whether the Dutch forms Dunder and Blixem, two reindeer names in the 1823 text, mark the poem as Livingston's because the oath they come from was current in the Dutch-descended society of Poughkeepsie where he lived) was taken only as far as Google Books Ngrams, which counts phrases in printed books by year.
cases.story: Two days before Christmas 1823 the Troy Sentinel, a newspaper in Troy, New York, printed fifty-six lines of verse headed "Account of a Visit from St. Nicholas", with a note from its editor, Orville L. Holley, saying he did not know who wrote them. The poem (it begins "'Twas the night before Christmas") gave St. Nicholas his reindeer, his sleigh and his descent by the chimney, and it circulated for thirteen years without an author's name; in December 1836 a New York anthology printed it under the name of Clement Clarke Moore, a professor of Oriental and Greek literature at the General Theological Seminary in Manhattan, and in 1844 Moore said in print that he had written it years before to amuse his children. The Poughkeepsie Journal, a newspaper in Poughkeepsie, some seventy miles down the Hudson from Troy, had printed the poem anonymously in January 1828, six weeks before Henry Livingston Jr., a local landowner, surveyor and writer of light verse in the poem's metre, died there; nobody in his house is recorded as saying anything about it. From 1879 his descendants wrote, and from 1899 said in public, that he had read the poem to his children years before 1823, that his manuscript had burned in a house fire in Wisconsin, and that a Poughkeepsie paper had printed it before Troy did; neither the manuscript nor that printing has been found.
cases.mystery: For Moore there is a sequence of dated documents: the Sentinel's editor wrote in January 1829 that the author was a New York City scholar and recalled in 1836 (a statement known only in transcription) that he had learned within months of the printing that the author was "a professor in one of our colleges", a student's diary of 1834 describes a costume made "according to the description of Prof Moore in his poem", and Moore supplied the poem to the 1836 anthology, claimed it in 1844 and wrote out signed copies until his death in 1863. On the other side, he said nothing for twenty years, no manuscript from before 1823 survives for either man, and most of his other verse is grave and iambic (the da-DUM of most English verse), whereas the poem is comic and anapestic (da-da-DUM), a metre he used in only four other surviving poems; for Livingston there are two things, the family's memory and the poem's manner: the memory was first written down in 1879, fifty-six years after the printing, the relatives who recorded it disagree about the date, the child and the newspaper, and, as the family said in 1900, no document from his lifetime supports it, while the manner matches the comic anapestic verse he habitually wrote. Don Foster, an English professor at Vassar College, argued the case for Livingston in his book Author Unknown (2000), and MacDonald P. Jackson, a New Zealand scholar of Shakespearean authorship, tested the claim statistically in a book of 2016: on his counts of common words and speech sounds the poem scored with Livingston, and in 2017, answering Scott Norsworthy, an independent scholar who had reviewed that book on his blog Melvilliana, Jackson wrote that the documents favoured Moore and the text favoured Livingston, and that he could not reconcile the two; Moore has been defended on the documents by Stephen Nissenbaum, a historian of the American Christmas, in 2001, by Seth Kaller, a dealer in historical documents, in 2004, and by Norsworthy. Tom Jerman, a retired lawyer, in a 2023 book, and Shlomo Argamon, a computer scientist at the Illinois Institute of Technology, in tests for Bloomberg in 2023, are reported to have found for Moore by computation.
cases.judged: Every dated document from 1823, the year of the printing, to 1920, when the family's claim reached a national magazine, was collected and marked as checked against a scan or known only from a transcription, and the stylometry, which counts a writer's habits, that is, how often particular common words, letter sequences (character n-grams) and speech sounds (phonemes) appear, each kind of count making one feature set, was rebuilt on corpora (collections of text) built for the report: 46 poems by Moore (the 29 in Poems, the collection he published in 1844, proofread against a scan of it, and 17 manuscript poems taken from the transcriptions on henrylivingston.com, a website kept by a Livingston descendant), 66 by Livingston (also from that site's transcriptions, not checked against originals) and 2,756 by 32 other poets of the period (the control corpus, used to test the methods), with every method tested first on poems whose author is known. Standard profile tests, which compare a text with a profile of each man's habits built from everything he wrote, sort the known poems 80 to 89 percent correctly, but the word and letter-sequence tests attribute Moore's own four comic anapestic poems to Livingston most or all of the time (0 to 2 of 4 correct), because the tests learn the metre along with the author; tests built from the anapestic verse of both men only (the metre-matched design) sort Moore's four correctly and put the poem with Moore, inside the range of his four and beyond 94 to 100 percent of the sixteen 56-line samples of Livingston's anapestic verse on every word and letter-sequence feature set (speech sounds are a tie, and four Moore poems are a thin base). Against twenty-nine other poets of the period neither man can be verified as the author at all, and the stylometry is close to even and weak in both directions, so the verdict rests on the documents: nothing written in Livingston's lifetime, or for fifty years after it, connects him with the poem, the editor who printed it placed the author in New York City eleven months after Livingston died, and Moore is put at about 85 percent, Livingston at 12, someone else at 3. A Poughkeepsie newspaper printing of the poem from before 1823, or a dated document from before 1844 in which any Livingston mentions the poem, would overturn it.

cases.title: Nefertiti and Smenkhkare
cases.question: Who ruled Egypt between Akhenaten and Tutankhamun: was the king Ankhkheperure Neferneferuaten a woman, and was she Nefertiti; was Smenkhkare a separate king, and did he reign before or after her; whose body lies in tomb KV55; and which Egyptian king's widow wrote to the Hittites asking for a husband?
cases.verdict: King Ankhkheperure Neferneferuaten was a woman, and she was Nefertiti: about 89% on the readings adopted. Smenkhkare was a separate, short-lived male king (about 94%), most probably before her.
cases.confidence_label: about 89% (50 to 97 across the sceptical and generous readings)

standing.note: The identity verdict agrees with a well-supported position inside a live debate. The percentages are judgements written as numbers: every one depends on which reconstructions were allowed to compete, which 30 pieces of evidence were counted and how each was scored, and the range beside the headline shows how far the figure moves under other readings and does not check the scoring against anything outside it. The identity and the order are probable rather than demonstrated, the Hittite king and his widow remain undecided, and no part of the case is treated as settled.

split: One person: Nefertiti, Neferneferuaten and Smenkhkare the same (Harris, Samson, Reeves)
Neferneferuaten a man, Smenkhkare renamed (Krauss, Hornung, Kemp, Willeitner)
new: New evidence: none. The report did not examine any object, check any inscription afresh against the original, or find any text that the specialists lack. The newest evidence used is other people's (Van der Perre 2012 and 2014, the quarry inscription found by Athena Van der Perre, a Belgian Egyptologist, dated to year 16 of Akhenaten, about a year before his death, which names Nefertiti as still King's Great Wife; Johnson 2020, a join of two carved blocks from Hermopolis, the city across the river from Amarna, by Ray Johnson of the University of Chicago's mission at Luxor, which completes a scene of a female ruler walking beside a king with a small king's daughter behind them, taken by Dietrich as evidence that Akhenaten and Neferneferuaten reigned together; Willeitner 2022; Kemp 2016; Gad and colleagues 2020, Hawass's own team, on the DNA; Reeves 2023 as Dietrich reports it).

A way of weighing the old evidence: the first time all of it has been scored together (13 successions x coregency x KV55 identity x Nibhururiya identity; 30 items; three readings each; five starting weightings; each item removed in turn), with the sensitivity (how far each figure moves under other readings) printed beside the headline.

Within the scoring: the identity verdict does not depend on the Hittite question (the Egyptian items alone give the same identity figures), and it survives the removal of any single item, while the Hittite verdict flips under the sceptical readings.

A suggestion: dockets 35 ("House of Smenkhkare, [justified]") and 36 ("House of Ankhkheperure"), ink labels on jars from Amarna published in City of Akhenaten III, the 1951 volume of the excavation's finds, name two estates, so the plain throne name on its own did not stand for Smenkhkare in the administrative record, if the restoration (the word "justified", the epithet given to the dead, supplied where the label is damaged) holds; if it does, the docket, dated to a year 1, also records Smenkhkare as already dead in a year 1 that was not his own.
Everything else reproduces published scholarship, credited by name in section 9 of the report.
cases.confirms_prior: The identity verdict agrees with the two-ruler Nefertiti position of Aidan Dodson (2009, 2020), accepted by James Allen in 2016 (as footnote 102 of Dodson's 2020 book and footnote 18 of Dietrich's 2024 survey report it) and argued again by Kawai (2023): Nefertiti reigned as King Neferneferuaten, and Smenkhkare was a separate male king, probably earlier. The position was reached in three steps, each disputed at the time. A female ruler in the titulary (the king's formal set of names and titles): Harris 1973, from the regalia (royal insignia) shown with her and the doubling of Nefertiti's cartouche (her name written in two cartouches, like a king's); the feminine t (the -t ending that marks a feminine word in Egyptian) credited to Harris 1974 (by Dodson) or to Julia Samson's ring bezels, the flat faces of glazed finger rings (by Reeves); collected by Krauss 1978, who assigned the feminine writings to a separate queen; settled by Gabolde's 1998 reading of the epithet (the added phrase in her name) "effective for her husband" and the 2004 collations of the coffinettes (the four miniature gold coffins from Tutankhamun's tomb, which Allen and Gabolde each checked against the originals that year). Two rulers: Allen 1988, from the fact that the two name-sets never appear together. The separate female king as Nefertiti: Dodson 2009 and 2020, Allen 2016, Kawai 2023. Harris's own Nefertiti was one person who was also Smenkhkare, a different proposition. On KV55 the verdict sides with the examiners of the bones (Strouhal, Duhig, Ronald Harrison, the Liverpool anatomist who examined them in 1966, and Joyce Filer, who examined them at the British Museum in 2000), Allen's arithmetic on Akhenaten's age at death (a daughter by about his second year and a reign of 17 years put him past the age the bones show), Dodson, Belmonte and Bommas, against the 2010 CT age and Gabolde. On Nibhururiya it leans with Miller 2007 against the Tutankhamun identification that most handbooks print, with low confidence.

change.qualifier: the two-ruler Nefertiti position of Dodson, Allen and Kawai, one side of a live argument among Egyptologists
change.prior: Until the 1970s everything under the name Ankhkheperure was assigned to one young man, Smenkhkare. John Harris (1973) argued for a female ruler and identified her with Nefertiti, but kept Smenkhkare and Neferneferuaten as one person. James Allen (1988) separated the two name-sets into two rulers, a theory that Dodson says met "by no means universal acceptance". Aidan Dodson (2009, 2020), Allen (2016) and Kawai (2023) identify the separate female king with Nefertiti; Charlotte Dietrich (2024) accepts that Akhenaten and Neferneferuaten reigned together and leaves the identity open. Against them, Nicholas Reeves (2001, 2015, 2023) makes Neferneferuaten Nefertiti but Smenkhkare her later name; Marc Gabolde (1998 onwards) and Dimitri Laboury (2002, 2010) make her Meritaten; Rolf Krauss (1978, 2007), Erik Hornung (2006), Barry Kemp (2016) and Joachim Willeitner (2022) keep one male king; Allen's 2009 paper made her the daughter Neferneferuaten-tasherit. On the other two questions, the 2010 CT study makes the KV55 body Akhenaten, and most handbooks make the Hittite king Nibhururiya Tutankhamun; both remain disputed.
change.explanation: The verdict takes a side that named scholars already hold. It agrees with Dodson, Allen and Kawai on the identity, and less firmly on the order, against Gabolde and Laboury, against Krauss, Hornung, Kemp and Willeitner, against Reeves's one person and against Allen's 2009 daughter. That agreement does not test the scoring. On KV55 it sides with the examiners of the bones against the 2010 CT age: the body is probably not Akhenaten, who keeps about 21% on the readings adopted and 32% on the sceptical ones. On the Hittite question it leans with Miller 2007 against the Tutankhamun identification that most handbooks print, but the answer flips under the sceptical readings, so no winner is claimed.

overturn: Any object joining the extended throne name with the name Smenkhkare, or a feminine form with the plain throne name: it would collapse the two-ruler rule and bring the one-person readings back at once.
A dated text of Nefertiti as King's Great Wife after Akhenaten's death, or a queenly burial of Nefertiti: either would move the identity to Meritaten.
Publication of the CT criteria behind the 35 to 45 age for KV55, or an independent re-examination giving an age over 30: either would move KV55 to Akhenaten.

A convincing rebuttal of Miller's Armaa synchronism (a Hittite record in which the Egyptian general Horemheb, who later became king, is still a commander in Syria years after Nibhururiya's death, which sits badly with Tutankhamun as the dead king) together with a Hittite text placing the king's death in winter (the season in which the floral collars in Tutankhamun's tomb place his own death): that would return Nibhururiya to Tutankhamun and the widow to Ankhesenamun.
A year-dated Smenkhkare text later than a year 3 of Neferneferuaten: that would reverse the order.
fell_short: The percentages depend on which reconstructions were allowed to compete, which 30 pieces of evidence were counted and how each was scored; the sceptical and generous readings show how far the answers move when those choices change, and they do not check the numbers against anything outside the scoring. Changing several scores changes the headline figure.

Works known only through other authors: Harris 1974 and Samson 1977 (the credit for the feminine t rests on Dodson 2009 and Reeves 2001 and 2015); Allen 1988 (through Allen 2009 and Dodson 2009); Allen 2016 (through footnote 102 of Dodson's 2020 book and footnote 18 of Dietrich's 2024 survey); Reeves 2023 and Dodson's second paper of 2020, on the Theban temple name (both through footnote 18 of Dietrich's 2024 survey); Van der Perre 2014, the edition of her quarry inscription from year 16 of Akhenaten naming Nefertiti as still his queen (abstract only; the month of that date, which fixes how many months before Akhenaten's death Nefertiti was still only his queen, is left open); Johnson 2020 and Kawai 2023 (through Dietrich); Krauss 1978 and 2007 (through Dietrich, Dodson, Miller, Belmonte and WiBiLex, an online reference work); Gabolde 1998 (through the scholars who reviewed it); Stempel 2007 and Theis 2011, the published rebuttals of Miller's Armaa argument (not read; the sceptical readings of the Hittite items are meant to carry their weight, but they were set without them).

The Willeitner and Dietrich readings of the epithet on the Munich ivory (a small ivory plaque in Munich that Willeitner published in 2022 as a record of a male Smenkhkare) disagree and were not collated (checked against the original).

No object was examined; readings come from published editions; the plates (the photographs and drawings) in Roeder's 1969 publication of the blocks from Akhenaten's dismantled buildings that were re-used at Hermopolis, in Petrie's and in the City of Akhenaten volumes were not seen.

The CT criteria behind the 35 to 45 age for KV55 have never been published, the raw DNA data have never been released, and no laboratory outside Hawass's team has typed the mummies (read the DNA markers used in paternity tests).
cases.story: Akhenaten, the king of Egypt who replaced the old gods with the sun disc, the Aten, and built a new capital at Amarna, died in the seventeenth year of his reign, about 1336 BC, and within a few years the boy Tutankhamun was king and the old gods had been restored. An Egyptian king had two main names, a throne name taken on accession and a personal name, each written inside an oval ring called a cartouche, and between the two reigns the monuments show two pairs of royal names (name-sets) sharing one throne name, Ankhkheperure: one pair belongs to a king Smenkhkare, shown once with Akhenaten's eldest daughter Meritaten, who held the chief queen's title of King's Great Wife, as his queen; the other belongs to a king Neferneferuaten, which had been the name of Akhenaten's chief wife Nefertiti, and some of its writings carry feminine endings. Jar labels at Amarna are dated to years 1 to 3 of a reign that followed Akhenaten's, and an ink inscription in a tomb at Thebes, the old religious capital in the south (modern Luxor), is dated to year 3 of Neferneferuaten and praises Amun, the god Akhenaten had suppressed. In 1907 a small tomb in the Valley of the Kings, the royal cemetery at Thebes, numbered KV55, was found to hold a coffin with its names cut out and the skeleton of a man whose age at death has been disputed ever since, and the Deeds of Suppiluliuma, a Hittite chronicle found in the ruins of the Hittite capital in central Turkey (the Hittites were the other great power of the day), records that the widow of an Egyptian king it calls Nibhururiya wrote to the Hittite king Suppiluliuma asking for a son to marry and make king of Egypt.
cases.mystery: Later kings erased the Amarna period from their records, so no surviving text says who Neferneferuaten was, whether the two name-sets belonged to one ruler or two, in which order they reigned, whose body lies in KV55, or which king's widow wrote to the Hittites, and Egyptologists have disagreed about the answers since the 1970s. Aidan Dodson of the University of Bristol (2009, 2020), James Allen, an American Egyptologist who showed in 1988 that the two name-sets never appear together on one object (the plain throne name goes only with Smenkhkare, the throne name extended by a phrase naming Akhenaten only with Neferneferuaten) and who accepted the identification in 2016, and Kawai, an Egyptologist, in a paper of 2023, hold that Neferneferuaten was Nefertiti reigning as king and that Smenkhkare was a separate man, whereas John Harris, a British Egyptologist (1973), Julia Samson, who worked on the Amarna finds of the excavator Flinders Petrie, and Nicholas Reeves, a British Egyptologist best known for proposing in 2015 that Nefertiti's burial lies behind a wall of Tutankhamun's tomb, hold that Nefertiti bore both name-sets in turn. Marc Gabolde, of the University of Montpellier, who in 1998 read a phrase in her name as "effective for her husband", and Dimitri Laboury, of the University of Liège, make the female king Meritaten; Rolf Krauss, of the Berlin museum, Erik Hornung, of Basel, who with Krauss edited the standard handbook of Egyptian chronology in 2006, Barry Kemp, who has directed the excavation of Amarna since 1977, and Joachim Willeitner, a German Egyptologist, keep one male king and read the feminine writings as his widow's or as misreadings; Allen's 2009 paper proposed a young daughter, Neferneferuaten-tasherit, a view he gave up in 2016; and Charlotte Dietrich, whose survey of 2024 is the most recent map of the debate, accepts that Akhenaten and Neferneferuaten reigned together and leaves her identity open. On the body in KV55, the 2010 CT-scan and DNA study of the royal mummies led by Zahi Hawass, then head of Egypt's antiquities service, made the man a son of Amenhotep III, Akhenaten's father, and the father of Tutankhamun, put his age at 35 to 45 and called him Akhenaten, and Reeves and Gabolde agree, while every examiner who has handled the bones, from the anatomists of 1910 to Eugen Strouhal, a Czech physician and anthropologist, in 1998 and Corinne Duhig, a British specialist in human remains, in 2010, has put the age under 27, which makes him a younger brother of Akhenaten, and Dodson, the chronologist Juan Antonio Belmonte and the Egyptologist Martin Bommas take that side; on the widow, Hans Güterbock, who published the Hittite chronicle in 1956, identified the dead king with Tutankhamun, which makes the widow his queen Ankhesenamun, a third daughter of Akhenaten, and most handbooks follow him, but Jared Miller, a specialist in Hittite texts at the University of Munich, argued in 2007 that the dead king was Akhenaten, which makes the widow Nefertiti or Meritaten, and Gabolde agrees.
cases.judged: The full report, linked from this page, collected 30 pieces of evidence (items), 18 from Egypt, four on the KV55 body and eight from the Hittite texts, and quoted each from its original publication, with a marker beside each modern study saying whether it was read in full, in part, or only through other authors' citations; it listed the thirteen reconstructions of the succession (the order of reigns) that scholars have proposed, added the combinations that no one defends so that the starting weights did not favour the views scholars have argued for, and scored each item for how well each reconstruction accounts for it. Each score was set three times, once as the report's own reading (the readings adopted), once as the reading least favourable to a female king that a named scholar defends (the sceptical readings) and once as the most favourable (the generous readings); the scores for each reconstruction (each from 1, expected, to 0, impossible) were multiplied together and the products scaled to add up to 100, the results were re-run under five starting weightings (the weight each reconstruction starts with before the evidence is scored) and with each item removed in turn, and the full score table, the code and the score file accompany the report. On the readings adopted, Neferneferuaten was Nefertiti at about 89%, and still 50% on the sceptical readings; Smenkhkare was a separate man (94%) and probably reigned first (80%); Nefertiti was probably made king while Akhenaten still lived (68%); the KV55 body is most probably Smenkhkare (61%); and the Hittite king is Akhenaten at 68% on the readings adopted but Tutankhamun at 80% on the sceptical ones, so that question is left open. Removing any single item leaves Nefertiti as the most probable identity; the percentages are the report's judgements expressed as numbers, which depend on the reconstructions admitted and on the scores given, and a single object joining the extended throne name with the name Smenkhkare, or a feminine form with the plain throne name, would collapse the two-ruler rule (that the two name-sets never share an object) and bring the one-person readings back at once.

cases.title: The dancing plague of 1518
cases.question: What made the poor of Strasbourg dance in the streets for weeks in July and August 1518, how many danced, and did anyone die?
cases.verdict: A behavioural epidemic among the poor of a city at the end of two years of dearth, spread by watching and by music, and given its shape by the belief that St Vitus sends the dance and cures it: about 85 percent that the cause was behavioural rather than a poison or an infection, and ergot rejected. Up to fifty dancing at a time by the council's count, more than two hundred over four weeks by a chronicle written at the time, and no death in any text read from the years 1518 to about 1580.
cases.confidence_label: about 85% (55 to 85 across the table of what moves the percentages)

standing.note: Every percentage is a judgment rather than a measurement: it depends on the five explanations weighed and on the weight given to each piece of evidence, and the table of what moves it is printed beside the headline. Backman's book of 1952 was not obtained, Waller's book was read only in library search snippets and Rohmann's book of 2013 was not read, so the opposing works are answered through their articles and through other writers.

split: A psychogenic epidemic: a natural illness, spread by sight and sound among the destitute
The same behaviour as a culturally scripted rite (Martin 1914, Bartholomew 2000, Rohmann 2013)
