Another organic disease: an epilepsy cluster, chorea (a disorder of involuntary movement), encephalitis (inflammation of the brain), heat
A few sick people and a crowd of beggars and impostors
new: "Fifteen a day" has one candidate source: the sentence of 1518 by Wilhelm Rem, a merchant of Augsburg who recorded the outbreak that year, "daß ain tag wol bei 15 menschen ankam", a count of new cases rather than deaths. Martin (1914, p. 114) quoted it only to fix the year. Waller's essay in the medical journal the Lancet (February 2009, "about 15 lives a day"; further reading Backman and Midelfort only) and his book ("fifteen were dying each day") give a death rate; Wikipedia took it from the Lancet on 8 April 2016. The descent from Rem to Waller is an inference from the wording, Waller's endnote and Backman's translation not having been seen. A new reading of a printed text.

200 against 400: the Strasbourg librarian Rodolphe Reuss's 1875 edition of the Imlin chronicle from the manuscript reads "mehr dan 200" (page image checked); the Kleine Strassburger Chronik, an anonymous Strasbourg chronicle of the early seventeenth century, independently has "über 200"; 400 is the reading of 1879 by the psychiatrist Georg Witkowski, carried by Martin (1914), Midelfort (1999) and Waller. A press interview about Waller's book put 400 into the Wikipedia article on the day it was created, 8 August 2008. A new reading of printed editions.

The anonymous Basel chronicle (written before 1537) restored to 1518: its manuscript reads 1518; its editor, the Basel historian August Bernoulli, moved it to 1418 in 1902 because of Schilter's misdated council orders. It is the earliest narrative outside Strasbourg; its wording matches, in prose, six verses from an unidentified Strasbourg manuscript chronicle that Schilter printed in 1698 under the same wrong year; and it is the earliest source for "hundreds" as a round plural (the Imlin chronicle, written at the time, gives the figure of more than 200): its "several hundred" is the formula that the verses give as "many hundreds", a stock expression rather than a tally. A new reading of a printed edition.

The ergot hypothesis tested against reconstructed weather, for the first time in the literature that could be reached: a drought index of −6.8 for 1517 at Strasbourg in the Old World Drought Atlas (third driest summer of 1500–1600), a dry spring and a warm May and June; the cold June of 1518 is the one favourable sign, and it belongs to a crop not yet cut. The climate and price datasets are the one body of evidence not brought to the question before; the datasets are the published work of others, and their application here is new. The extraction from the atlas was run a second time from scratch and gives the same value (−6.787 at the Strasbourg cell).

The outbreak ended in August: "Dienstag post Adolphi" is 31 August 1518 (St Adelphus falls on 29 August), rather than 29 September as Martin read it; the letter of 25 July says the sickness was ending. A calendar correction.

The council's policy was containment rather than encouragement: drums restricted on 22 July, wagons to the shrine on 23 July, on 25 July a cooling diet and string music only, a general ban on 2 August, families and brotherhoods made responsible on 11 August. The platform on the horse market with people hired to dance with the sick, to drums and pipes, is Specklin's, written about 1580. The pilgrimage was imposed by the council (the Instruction of 23 July for the transport to the shrine), which weakens the reading of the dancing as a chosen rite; dancers who chose the rite appear only in Johann Wencker, a Strasbourg magistrate whose chronicle of 1637 copies Specklin. A new reading of the documents Martin printed.

Waller's supporting details corrected: the English sweat of 1517, an epidemic fever of the period, is a misdating of 1529; the "smallpox hospital" is the Blatterhaus, the house for syphilis; the leper house shows no surge (eight inmates and two deaths in 1518 to 1519); the Bundschuh of 1517 (a peasant plot on the Upper Rhine) was a conspiracy scare rather than a series of rebellions. A new reading of published work.

Two bad arguments retired: the claim that ergot alkaloids decay within a year (unsound; Barger 1931), and the 1951 mass poisoning at Pont-Saint-Esprit in southern France as a case of ergot-induced mass behaviour (organic mercury, according to the European Food Safety Authority in 2012). The case against ergot rests on season, weather, form, course, spread, fatality, diagnosis and end rather than on chemistry. Published literature applied.

No Strasbourg record of dancers in 1374, the year of the dancers whom the chronicle of Limburg on the Lahn condemned as devilry and heresy; the fifteenth-century cases on the Upper Rhine sorted (Zurich 1418 or 1428 and 1452, the cluster of 1463 at Metz, Obernai and Eberhardsklausen, dancers in the name of St John rather than St Vitus, and the town law of Rottweil, in Swabia, which in 1485 set a fine for the curse "sant Vitstantz", St Vitus's dance called down on another person). "Strasbourg 1418" is Schilter's error. A new reading of printed editions.
cases.confirms_prior: The verdict is the one Élisabeth Clementz and Georges Bischoff reached for the 2018 exhibition "1518, la fièvre de la danse": about fifty dancers, no contemporary death, Troffea an invention of Paracelsus, ergot rejected. They had already questioned how much contemporary testimony lies behind the familiar story, and this report (the full report is linked from this page) builds on their correction. Erik Midelfort (1999) gave the sober English account, one woman about 14 July, thirty-four within four days, the sick sent to Saverne, deaths only in Kleinlawel. John Waller's premise, a city in dearth and fear, is borne out by the climate and price record, and his account of how the dancing spread, by sight, is the one described in the surviving minutes of the three councillors of 23 July.

change.qualifier: Élisabeth Clementz and Georges Bischoff (2018), Erik Midelfort (1999) and Alfred Martin (1914); shifts the popular account of 400 dancers, dozens of deaths and fifteen dying a day (Waller 2008 and 2009; Wikipedia)
change.prior: Alfred Martin (1914) dated the outbreak to 1518, printed the council's papers and disposed of Schilter's 1418. Erik Midelfort (1999) gave the sober English account, with deaths only in Kleinlawel. Élisabeth Clementz and Georges Bischoff, for the 2018 exhibition, reduced the outbreak to "quelque cinquante personnes", found no death in any contemporary document, exposed Troffea as Paracelsus's invention and dismissed ergot. Martin and Midelfort carried Witkowski's 400 reading of the Imlin chronicle, and Waller took it from them. The popular account, from Waller's book of 2008 and articles of 2009 to Wikipedia, has 400 dancers, dozens of deaths, fifteen dying a day and a council that built a stage to keep them dancing. E. Louis Backman (1952) argued for ergot; Gregor Rohmann (2013) and Robert Bartholomew (2000) read the dancing as a religious rite rather than an illness.
change.explanation: The finding agrees with the Strasbourg historians of 2018, with Midelfort and with Martin, and builds on the 2018 exhibition's correction. It shifts the popular account: 400 dancers become up to 50 at a time and more than 200 over four weeks; dozens of deaths become none recorded in the sources read before about 1580; "fifteen dying a day" has one candidate source, Rem's count of fifteen new cases on one day, and its descent into the modern death rate is an inference rather than a traced citation; the council that staged the dancing becomes a council that contained it, Specklin (about 1580) being the only source for the stage. Ergot (Backman 1952) is rejected on eight counts.

overturn: A document of 1518 that records deaths among the dancers: a hospital or parish register, or the lost account of Sebastian Brant, the author of The Ship of Fools and the city's chancellor in 1518, the full narrative that a note in the council's own register says can be found "in my chronicle", meaning Brant's. Deaths would cut the behavioural share to about 70 percent and reopen the organic causes.

The German original of the council's letter to the bishop of 25 July 1518 (ADBR 12 J 1495, its shelfmark in the departmental archives of the Bas-Rhin), read here only in a 2018 French translation, if it describes burning limbs, gangrene or cramps of the hands and feet.

A chronicle notice of a wet May and June 1517 at Strasbourg: the tree-ring drought value for 1517 is regional and safe because it is extreme, but the seasonal rainfall reconstructions for the sixteenth century are weak, and one wet fortnight at flowering would not show in them.

An ergotism epidemic recorded in Alsace or Baden in 1518, for instance in the accounts of the Antonite house at Isenheim, one of the hospitals of the Order of St Anthony that treated ergotism; none is known to Barger or to the later literature.

Evidence that the sick went to St Vitus of their own motion before the council organised the transport of 23 July, which would move weight from illness to rite without touching the verdict against ergot.
The Imlin manuscript reading 400, which would restore Witkowski without changing the council's fifty or the absence of deaths.
fell_short: Gebwiler's contemporary account (ed. Stenzel 1926) was not read; it is known here through Midelfort and the material for teachers published by the 2018 exhibition.
The letter of 25 July 1518 was read only in the French translation published in 2018; the mandate of 2 August is not transcribed anywhere that could be reached.

Witkowski's paper of 1879 was not found online. Backman's book of 1952 was not obtained (about sixty snippets from a library full-text search). Waller's articles in the journals Endeavour, the Lancet and the Psychologist were read in full, but his book only in about 120 such snippets, so his endnote for "fifteen were dying each day" was not seen. Midelfort's chapter was read from the text of an archive.org scan whose provenance could not be confirmed.

Rohmann's book of 2013 was not read (his 2020 article, reviews of the book and an interview were used); Clementz's transcriptions of the 1518 documents in the 2018 catalogue (pp. 136–152) were not obtained.
The Alsatian economic historian Charles-Auguste Hanauer's price volume of 1878, the source of the Strasbourg rye prices, could not be opened; two later transcriptions disagree on the 1516 rye price.

The gridded climate reconstructions have low skill (they reproduce known weather poorly) before 1659; the drought value for 1517 is safe because it is extreme and regional; the seasonal rainfall figures are not.
Three words in the council's papers are unexplained ("pfrymen", "termen", "brucken" or "beucken").
No parish or hospital register was searched; the absence of deaths is an argument from the silence of every text written at the time.
cases.story: On 14 or 15 July 1518, in Strasbourg, then a free city of the Holy Roman Empire on the Rhine, a woman began to dance in the street and kept it up for days. The city council had her taken to a shrine of St Vitus, the saint believed both to send this sickness and to cure it, in the hills above Saverne, a small town to the north-west; while she was on the road, others began to dance, about thirty-four within four days. The council restricted drums on 22 July, lodged the dancers in guild halls, sent them to the shrine by wagon on 23 July, wrote to its bishop on 25 July that the physicians called it a natural illness of the heat and the stars, banned all public dancing on 2 August, and voted a hundredweight candle for the saint on 31 August. The council's decree speaks of up to fifty dancing at once; the chronicle of the Imlin family of Strasbourg, written at the time, counts more than two hundred over four weeks.
cases.mystery: The cause was not diagnosed in 1518 and is still disputed: the physicians said natural illness; the chroniclers of the next century said a curse, a punishment and fraud; E. Louis Backman, a Swedish physician and historian of religious dance, proposed in 1952 that the dancers were poisoned by ergot, a fungus of rye whose poison causes convulsions and gangrene, and that became the popular explanation; John Waller, a historian of medicine, argued in 2008 for a trance brought on by hunger, fear and belief in the saint's curse, spread by sight; and Gregor Rohmann, a German historian of the Middle Ages, and Robert Bartholomew, a sociologist who studies outbreaks of mass hysteria, read the dancing as a religious rite. The facts are disputed too: the popular story has four hundred dancers, fifteen deaths a day, a first dancer named Frau Troffea (a name found only in Paracelsus, the Swiss physician, who wrote on the sickness about 1526 to 1532) and a council that built a stage and hired musicians and dancers to keep the sick dancing, while the surviving texts give figures from fifty to four hundred (the four hundred rests on one nineteenth-century reading of one word in one manuscript). The first reports of deaths come sixty and a hundred years after the event, from Daniel Specklin, the city architect, writing about 1580, and from Michael Kleinlawel's rhymed chronicle of 1625; the council's own minutes burned with the city library in 1870 and are known only from extracts made in the eighteenth century, though a few originals survive, among them the minutes of the three councillors who questioned the dancers' families on 23 July and the letter to the bishop. The American historian Erik Midelfort (1999) gave the sober account of the sources, and the Strasbourg historians Élisabeth Clementz and Georges Bischoff, in a 2018 exhibition, reduced the outbreak to about fifty dancers with no contemporary death.
cases.judged: Every text that describes the dancing was read in the order it was written, from the council's papers of 1518 to the chronicles of the following century, in the printed editions (above all the medical historian Alfred Martin's study of 1914, which printed the council's papers) and in the page images, with one exception, the account of the cathedral schoolmaster Hieronymus Gebwiler from the early 1520s, known only through later writers; each element of the modern story was traced to the text in which it first appears, the phantom outbreak of 1418 listed in half the modern literature, for instance, to the jurist Johann Schilter, who printed the council's orders under that wrong year in 1698; and the explanations were tested against that record and against three kinds of evidence the earlier writers did not have: the weather of the growing seasons of 1515 to 1518 reconstructed from tree rings and written weather records, the grain prices of those years, and the modern medical case series of outbreaks that spread through schools and villages by suggestion. What tipped the balance was the record of 1518 itself: the texts written that year describe poor people set off by watching others dance or by the sound of a bagpipe, a verdict of natural illness from the physicians, up to fifty afflicted at once and no death, while the four hundred, the daily deaths, the stage and the name Troffea each enter the story later at a date that can be fixed, and ergot fails on eight counts, among them that the rye eaten in July 1518 had grown in the summer of 1517, the third driest of the century at Strasbourg. The verdict is a behavioural epidemic, an outbreak spread by sight and sound rather than by anything eaten or caught, among the poor of a city at the end of two years of dearth (failed harvests and high grain prices), at about 85 percent, with ergot rejected; a document of 1518 recording deaths among the dancers would cut that share to about 70 percent and reopen the organic causes, a poison or a disease.

cases.title: The Man in the Iron Mask
cases.question: Who was the masked prisoner who died in the Bastille on 19 November 1703, who had he been before his arrest in 1669, and why was he kept for thirty-four years?
cases.verdict: The prisoner was the valet whom Captain de Vauroy, an officer of the Dunkirk garrison, handed over at Pignerol in August 1669, entered in the ministers' letters as Eustache Dauger, Danger or d'Angers: 78%. Who he had been before July 1669 nobody knows, and no minister ordered a mask.
cases.confidence_label: 78% (about 42 to 78 across the three link weights)

standing.note: Which of the two Exilles prisoners died in January 1687 is decided by inference rather than by any document, so the headline is a product of three judged weights, printed with its sensitivity. Petitfils 2003 and Sonnino 2016, the two books that defend the current identifications, were not read in full, and no original manuscript was consulted.

split: The valet handed over at Pignerol in August 1669 (Eustache Dauger, Danger or d'Angers)
La Rivière, Fouquet's other valet, as the survivor of Exilles in 1687
Someone else: a prisoner brought from Pignerol in 1694, or a man the record never names
Count Ercole Antonio Mattioli, whose name the burial register echoes
new: No document unknown to the printed editions was found; everything below is a new reading of old evidence.

The whole printed record from 1669 to 1703 (the editions of Roux-Fazillac, Delort, Ravaisson, Iung, Topin, Loiseleur, Lair, Funck-Brentano and Laloy, each made by a historian who printed part of the file between 1801 and 1913, and Mongrédien's 1953 article) transcribed into 180 dated entries with each edition's archive reference, and the variants between editions tabulated, so the chain of custody can be checked line by line.

The weakest link given a probability. Lair and Petitfils state the identity of the 1687 survivor as a fact, and Mongrédien wrote that he had demonstrated it; here it carries a probability and a published sensitivity, and the Bastille identification is given at 78% rather than as certain. Twenty candidates are tested against seven fixed points by a short script, so anyone who disagrees with a cell can change the candidate file and rerun it.

The ministers' unbroken use of "ancien prisonnier" from Saint-Mars's letter of January 1696 to the orders of 1698 as the answer to Brugnon's thesis that the island prisoner died in 1693: a prisoner who had died in 1693 could not be "your old prisoner" in 1697.

The letter of 12 March 1680 on a dead valet's wages read as Champagne's wage arrears rather than as the death of Eustache, against the thesis of Jean-Marc Dabos, who runs the website masque-de-fer.com and publishes photographs of the original letters there, that the masked man was Fouquet himself: an inference from the surrounding letters rather than a documented exchange.

The variant "ce qu'a fait" (Topin) against "ce que fait" (Iung) in Barbezieux's letter of 17 November 1697, flagged as a reading that bears on the argument and that the original, in the French army's historical archive at Vincennes (Service historique de la Défense, A1 vol. 1392, p. 171), would settle. None of these three readings was found in the works consulted, several of which could be read only in fragments.
cases.confirms_prior: Jules Lair (1890) first identified the masked man with the valet of 1669, and Loiseleur had already shown in 1882 that the masked man of 1687 came from Exilles and could not be Mattioli. Georges Mongrédien (1952) eliminated every Pignerol prisoner but Mattioli and the valet, argued that La Rivière died at Exilles in 1687, and declined to choose ("Si oui, c'est Dauger, si non, c'est Matthioli", if so it is Dauger, if not Mattioli, p. 231); Petitfils (1970, 2003), John Noone (1988), Sonnino (2016) and Josephine Wilkinson (2021) decide for the valet. The arrest at Calais, on the Channel coast, is Brugnon's finding (1987); the reading of the name as Danger or d'Angers is Lair's and that of Bernard Caire, who examined the original letters in the 1980s; the deleted words "ce qu'il a vu" (what he has seen) in the ministry's draft, the minute, of 23 December 1678 are Caire's find; the reading of the mask as the jailer's device is Noone's and Petitfils's, and the judgement that the secret was small is Caire's and Petitfils's. The refutations of three other candidates, Martin (a valet of the Huguenot conspirator Roux de Marsilly), Eustache Dauger de Cavoye (a disgraced nobleman who bore the valet's name) and Bulonde (a general), belong to Laloy (1913), Mongrédien (1953) and Batiffol (1894), and the observation that the secret was an employment rather than an identity is Laloy's and Caire's.

change.qualifier: the identification most historians working from the letters have reached since Lair (1890), though the question is still argued, and at a lower confidence than its proponents state
change.prior: Jules Lair (1890) first identified the masked man with the valet of 1669. Georges Mongrédien (1952) reduced the choice to Mattioli or the valet and declined to choose; Petitfils (1970, 2003), John Noone (1988), Paul Sonnino (2016) and Josephine Wilkinson (2021) decide for the valet. Who the valet was is disputed between Petitfils's servant of Madame and Sonnino's valet of Picon. Against or aside: Funck-Brentano (1894) held for Mattioli, the writer Harry Thompson (1987) for Eustache Dauger de Cavoye, a disgraced nobleman who bore the valet's name, the writer Roger Macdonald (2005) for d'Artagnan, and Sarah Madry, in an article of 2016, argues that the word "valet" in the 1669 letter cannot be relied on. The royal brother of Voltaire (1771) and Dumas has no document behind it.
change.explanation: The verdict reaches the man most historians have reached since Lair, at a lower confidence than they give, because one link in the chain, the death of one of two unnamed prisoners at Exilles in January 1687, is decided by inference rather than by any document; Mongrédien treated the point as settled and Petitfils does not discuss it as a difficulty. On the valet's earlier life the verdict declines to choose between Petitfils and Sonnino. On the secrecy it follows Noone and Petitfils, the mask as the jailer's device, with one qualification: the King approved in August 1698 whatever precautions Saint-Mars had proposed for the journey, so the mask, if it was among them, had the King's general sanction from then on.

overturn: Saint-Mars's letter of 5 January 1687, or any Exilles account, naming the prisoner who died. If it names Eustache, the Bastille prisoner was La Rivière and the first two verdict lines change places.

A burial or garrison record of Sainte-Marguerite between 1687 and 1698 recording the death of the prisoner held in the cell newly built on Sainte-Marguerite in 1687, which is what Brugnon's reconstruction of the island register claims to establish.

The original of Barbezieux's letter of 17 November 1697 (Service historique de la Défense, A1 vol. 1392, p. 171) reading "ce que fait" rather than "ce qu'a fait", which would remove one of the three supports for identifying the survivor of 1687 with the valet of 1669.

Any document naming the master or employment of "Eustache" in 1669: Vauroy's reimbursement order in the Mélanges Colbert, a manuscript collection at the Bibliothèque nationale, as Brugnon described it, Fouquet's sealed reply of January 1679 to the King's question about the valet's past, or the Calais notarial records Sonnino cites. It would settle the second question and might change the third.
The minute of Louvois's letter of 19 July 1669 read in a hand other than the scribe's, or the name shown to have been added later, which would bear on whether the name was real.
fell_short: Petitfils 2003 and Sonnino 2016, the two books that defend the current identifications, were not read in full: about 1,050 and 1,000 short passages returned by searching the text of the online lending copies, which show only a few lines around each hit, plus their reviews (by Genet, Venturino, Ruff and Parrott) and interviews in full. The objections raised against them may be answered in pages not seen. Mongrédien 1952 was read in 3,439 page-numbered snippets plus his 1953 article in full; Noone, Wilkinson, Thompson and Macdonald in fragments only; Petitfils 1970 through four contemporary reviews.

Not obtainable: the proceedings of a conference on the Iron Mask held at Cannes in 1987 (Brugnon, Caire), the proceedings of a Pinerolo conference of 1974, Brugnon's 1992 reconstruction of the island register (a typescript at the Arsenal library in Paris), Caire's articles of 1988, 1997 and 1998, Sonnino's 1992 article on Imbert, an agent of the cardinal de Retz, Mazarin's old enemy, and an earlier candidate of Sonnino's, the reviews of Sonnino in three journals (the Journal of Modern History, the Catholic Historical Review and the American Historical Review), Duvivier 1932 (the book that proposed Cavoye), and Bazeries and Burgaud 1893 (the book that proposed Bulonde; known through Batiffol's review).

No original manuscript was consulted. Six letters were checked against the photographs on masque-de-fer.com, and the manuscript newsletter of 4 September 1687 that first mentions a mask was seen only in Dabos's photograph. Vauroy's reimbursement order (Mélanges Colbert 282, fol. 276 v°), the minute of 23 December 1678 with its deleted words, and the royal order of 17 August 1678 concerning Cavoye at Saint-Lazare, a house of correction in Paris, are known only through the authors who report them. Iung, Topin, Lair and Funck-Brentano differ on dates, folios and words, and where they differ the report says so rather than choosing on authority.
The percentages rest on judgements about the weight of the documents. The arithmetic behind the headline is stated so that a reader who weighs the 1691 letter differently can redo it.
cases.story: On 18 September 1698 the new governor of the Bastille, the royal fortress-prison in Paris, arrived with a prisoner whose face was covered by a mask; the governor, Bénigne de Saint-Mars, had guarded state prisoners for the crown since 1665, in the Alps and then on an island off Cannes. Étienne du Junca, Louis XIV's lieutenant at the Bastille, who kept its entry book, wrote that the man's name "is not said". The prisoner died there on 19 November 1703, "always masked with a mask of black velvet", and was buried the next day under a false name, Marchioly, with his age given as forty-five or thereabouts. No paper of the Bastille says who he was.
cases.mystery: The writer Voltaire made the mask iron in 1751 and hinted in 1771 at a brother of Louis XIV, Alexandre Dumas made the prisoner the King's twin in a novel of the 1840s, and some fifty identifications have been offered since 1745 (the historian Jean-Christian Petitfils counts fifty-two): a royal brother, a diplomat from Mantua, the playwright Molière, the musketeer d'Artagnan, the disgraced finance minister Nicolas Fouquet. The evidence is the correspondence from 1669 to 1703 between Saint-Mars and the ministers who had charge of the state prisons (Louvois, the King's war minister, from 1691 his son Barbezieux, and Pontchartrain for the Bastille), kept while Saint-Mars held his prisoners, Fouquet among them, at Pignerol, a French fortress in the Alps (now Pinerolo, in Italy), at Exilles, a smaller fort in the same mountains, and on the island of Sainte-Marguerite off Cannes; the letters, first printed in 1801 by Pierre Roux-Fazillac, a former member of the revolutionary Convention, say where each prisoner was moved and when, never say why this one was held, and are missing at the one point where a name is needed, since in January 1687 one of two unnamed prisoners died at Exilles and the letter that said which is lost. Most historians who have worked from the letters since Jules Lair, Fouquet's biographer, in 1890 (Georges Mongrédien, a historian of the seventeenth century, in 1952, who narrowed the choice to two men and would not decide; Petitfils in 1970 and 2003; the writer John Noone in 1988; the American historian Paul Sonnino in 2016; the biographer Josephine Wilkinson in 2021) hold that the masked man was a prisoner the war minister called "only a valet", a manservant, arrested in July 1669 and brought to Pignerol that August; the nineteenth century's answer, from Roux-Fazillac to Frantz Funck-Brentano, who catalogued the Bastille's papers, in 1894, was that diplomat from Mantua, Ercole Antonio Mattioli, seized by the French in 1679, whose name the burial register nearly reproduces; and the popular answer, from Voltaire to the film-maker Marcel Pagnol, is a brother or twin of the King, for whom no document exists. Those who accept the valet still disagree on who he had been (Petitfils: a servant of Henrietta of England, Louis XIV's sister-in-law, known at court as Madame, during her secret negotiation of 1669 to 1670 with her brother Charles II of England; Sonnino: a valet of Antoine-Hercule Picon, the man who managed the fortune of Cardinal Mazarin, the King's chief minister until his death in 1661) and on why he was kept for thirty-four years.
cases.judged: Every letter and register entry of the correspondence printed between 1801 and 1953 was read, 180 entries in all, with the variants between editions recorded: the letters of Saint-Mars and of the war ministers, Louvois and from 1691 his son Barbezieux, with those of Pontchartrain, the minister who had charge of the Bastille as secretary of state for the King's household, the Bastille registers and the burial entry of the parish of Saint-Paul. Seven dated facts about the man's custody, the fixed points, were taken from them, each resting on a named letter or register entry (arrest 1669, service to Fouquet 1675, confinement with Fouquet's other servant, La Rivière, 1680, move to Exilles 1681, death of one of the two 1687, entry to the Bastille 1698, death 1703), and twenty candidates were tested against the seven; only the valet of 1669 passes every documented point. The undocumented point, which of the two Exilles prisoners died in 1687, is argued from two later letters and the subject matter of the whole file (the ministers' letters from 1669 to 1680 are about the valet, and La Rivière appears in them only as Fouquet's servant) and given a probability, as is the thesis of Stanislas Brugnon, an archivist who reconstructed the island's prison register, that the island prisoner died in 1693 and never reached the Bastille; three links in the chain of custody, put at 99%, 93% and 85%, multiply to the headline of 78%, printed with a table of how it moves as each weight changes. Saint-Mars's lost letter of 5 January 1687 announcing the death, or any Exilles account naming the prisoner who died, would settle the identity either way.

cases.title: The Roanoke Colonists
cases.question: What became of the men, women and children John White left on Roanoke Island in August 1587, whose only message to him when he returned in August 1590 was the word CROATOAN cut on a post?
cases.verdict: The carving names Croatoan as the colonists' seat; their arrival there is inferred, since no witness recorded it. On the weighing of the evidence in the full report, linked below, the main body's principal seat was the Albemarle mainland at about 68 in 100 (range 41 to 77), Croatoan 17, somewhere else 7, the Chesapeake 4.
cases.confidence_label: about 68 in 100 (41 to 77 across nineteen alternative weightings)

standing.note: The possibilities are put in order and none is established. The leading one is a reconstruction from hearsay and from digs that have not been published, and every figure depends on the weights chosen in section 6 of the report, which anyone can change.

split: Albemarle mainland: the Chowan mouth and the Roanoke River country
Somewhere else: the Pamlico, Tar or Neuse interior, or early annihilation
new: No new evidence: every document used was in print by 1888 and every excavation is someone else's. What follows is analysis of old evidence: the weights in the ledger are the report's own, the mile calibration is arithmetic on the distance figures of Ralph Lane, governor of the first colony on the island in 1585 to 1586, and nobody else has run the spelling test.

A ledger, published with its code, that shows how far the mainland reading depends on the announced plan and the Jamestown hearsay, and how close Croatoan runs when those are discounted. The result is Horn's reading at lower confidence, with the alternatives published beside it.

A check of the colonists' "50 miles further vp into the maine" against Lane's own "130 miles" to the Chesepians and to Chawanook, the chief town of the Chowanoc people on the Chowan River: in any reckoning of the mile the phrase stays inside the Albemarle basin (the sound and its shores) and does not by itself pick the Chowan mouth over the middle of the sound.

A check of every archaeological claim of 2024 to 2026 against what has been published, which is nothing: no site report for Site X or Y, no count of the pottery fragments (sherds) for Site Y, no section drawing or radiocarbon table for the hammerscale, and a First Colony Foundation web statement of 4 June 2026 announcing the colony "found" with no new data behind it.

A test of the first Dare Stone's spellings against Hakluyt, Smith and Strachey: its archaic spellings are of the kinds an imitator would choose (an added e, a dropped letter, and stage archaisms such as "mine childe"), and the claim of David La Vere, a historian at the University of North Carolina Wilmington who reopened the case for the stone's authenticity in 2009 and 2010, that "salvage" was used "during only a few years" is wrong; the word is common in all three.

Two small observations: the objects in the 1625 note of Samuel Purchas, Hakluyt's successor as a collector of voyages, which says that Powhatan showed Smith a musket barrel, a brass mortar and pieces of iron that had been the colonists', could, if real, have been picked up on the abandoned Roanoke site where White had seen iron lying in the grass in 1590; and the order given in 1650 to Edward Bland, a Virginia merchant who led a party towards the Tuscarora, to enquire for "an English woman cast away long since" among them attests a living tradition of English people among the southern nations that none of the works read here discusses.
cases.confirms_prior: Quinn, Horn and Philip Barbour, the editor of the Jamestown texts, whose identifications of the place names are the standard ones, read the documents closely first, and section 8 of the report credits each step: Quinn for the reading that Strachey's "at Roanoak" means the colony rather than the island; Horn for the argument that Strachey's own geography rules out the Chesapeake; Helen Rountree, the ethnohistorian of the Powhatans, for the dating of the Chesepians' destruction (Strachey says Powhatan destroyed them for a prophecy; Rountree puts it about 1597 or 1598, before Jamestown); Barbour for the point that the 1609 searchers (the two parties Jamestown sent into the interior in 1608 and 1609 to look for the colonists) never crossed the watershed to the Roanoke River; Lee Miller, a writer (Roanoke: Solving the Mystery of the Lost Colony, 2000), and Kupperman for the reading of the slaughter story (the report that Powhatan's people killed the colonists) as propaganda of the Virginia Company, the London company that financed Jamestown; Oberg for the point that Croatoan could not feed the whole colony; Ewen for the objection that the layers holding the Cape Creek finds are seventeenth-century; Brandon Fullam, an independent researcher, for the caution that the clothed men reported at Ocanahowan, an inland town named in the Jamestown reports, may have been Spaniards. The order of the reports, the single London channel behind the slaughter story (one Powhatan informant, whose story was told in London in the winter of 1608 to 1609 and is repeated by all three London texts that carry it), the late and editorial character of Powhatan's supposed confession of the killing (a note that Purchas printed in a margin in 1625 and that appears nowhere in Smith), the negative result of the 1609 searches (both parties came back with rumours and no survivor), the independence of Lawson's testimony and the weakness of the Lumbee link (the claim, first published in 1888, that the Indians of Robeson County, North Carolina, the Lumbee, descend from the colonists) are all in Quinn, Barbour, Horn, the Lumbee historian Malinda Maynor Lowery, and Lawler.

change.qualifier: the split-and-absorption reading (Horn 2010, Lawler 2018), that the colony divided and was absorbed by the peoples around it, at lower confidence than they state; moves the slaughter story, the report that Powhatan's people killed the colonists, to one London report of 1609 that does not support the Chesapeake
change.prior: Quinn (1974, 1984, 1985), followed by Kupperman, Oberg (2008) and Horn (2005), held that the main body went to the Chesapeake and was killed by Powhatan in April 1607. Since 2010 (Horn, A Kingdom Strange, 2010; the First Colony Foundation; Lawler 2018) the usual reading is that the colony split between Croatoan and the Chowan and was absorbed; Thomas Parramore, a North Carolina historian (2001), had already put the main body on the Albemarle mainland, where on his reading it died in warfare between the Tuscarora and the Algonquian peoples on the western shore of the sound. Dawson and Horton (2016 to 2026), endorsed by DuVal (2025), hold that all of them went to Croatoan. Ewen and Shields (2024) hold that no hypothesis is more probable than another.
change.explanation: The verdict agrees with Horn's split-and-absorption reading at lower confidence than he states: the sources support the direction and the dispersal but not the route, the season, the headcount at Croatoan or the Powhatan raid of 400 warriors that his narrative supplies, and the ledger gives the mainland about two chances in three. It moves the weight of the slaughter story: the instructions sent in May 1609 by the London Council of the Virginia Company, the dedication Hakluyt wrote for a book on Virginia in April 1609 and Strachey's Historie are one London report from one Powhatan informant, Machumps, a man brought to England in January 1609, which itself dates the killing to spring 1607 and places it outside Powhatan's territory, so it does not support the Chesapeake; and Powhatan's "confession" with the musket barrel and brass mortar is a 1625 marginal note by Purchas and appears nowhere in Smith. No witness recorded the mainland move or the dispersal.

overturn: A published, sealed 1580s deposit at Cape Creek with a hearth and slag would raise Croatoan to first place.
A sixteenth-century English burial or house floor on the Lynnhaven or Elizabeth River, where the Chesepian towns stood, would restore Quinn's Chesapeake.
A demonstration that the Salmon Creek ceramics (the Bertie ceramics of Sites X and Y) are of 1607 to 1650 or later would bring the mainland and Croatoan to parity.

The lost written account of a voyage south to Roanoke by one Marmaduke Rayner, heard by the Virginia Company in 1621 (its minute records no finding), or the second part of Strachey's Historie (which Strachey called a decade), if either survives, could decide more than any excavation.
A laboratory result on the first Dare Stone, either way.
fell_short: The modern books (Quinn's Roanoke Voyages and Set Fair for Roanoke; Horn; Lawler; Kupperman; Oberg; Miller; Rountree; Fullam; Dawson) are in copyright and were read in search-inside snippets (the short extracts a search of the digitised text returns, page-numbered where Google Books supplied them), the authors' own articles and full reviews rather than cover to cover. Parramore (2001) and Oberg's review of Lawler were not obtained; Parramore's argument is known from the page-by-page annual index of the North Carolina Historical Review for volume 78, the volume that holds it, and from Fullam. The First Colony Foundation's 2023 volume Excavating the Lost Colony Mystery, edited by Eric Klingelhofer, one of its archaeologists (Klingelhofer ed. 2023), was read in unpaginated Google Books snippets (59 search terms), contents and reviews; Ewen and Shields 2024 as publisher descriptions, contents and interviews.

The Zúñiga chart, a manuscript map of Virginia drawn at Jamestown in 1608 and known from the copy that the Spanish ambassador in London sent to Madrid, was read in three published transcriptions (Alexander Brown's Genesis of the United States, 1890; Barbour 1975; Encyclopedia Virginia) which disagree in wording; Barbour's 1969 diplomatic text (a letter-for-letter transcription) was not obtained.

The Spanish text of the account by Luis Jerónimo de Oré, a Franciscan friar who wrote up the Spanish voyages along this coast, of the Spanish voyage of 1588 that found the Roanoke harbour empty, was not obtained; Maynard Geiger's translation of 1936 is used and Quinn's differing translation noted.

The Virginia Company's instructions of 1609 were read in Susan Kingsbury's printed edition of the Company's records rather than in the manuscript in the Bodleian Library's Ashmole collection; Strachey's Historie in R. H. Major's 1849 edition of the British Library's Sloane manuscript, with the readings of the Princeton manuscript (a second manuscript of the Historie) only as Barbour quotes them.
The case rests on reading alone: no fieldwork and no laboratory result.
cases.story: On 27 August 1587 John White sailed from Roanoke Island, on the coast of what is now North Carolina, to fetch supplies from England; he was governor of a colony of about 115 men, women and children, the first English settlement in America to include families, sent out that spring by Sir Walter Ralegh, who held the queen's licence to settle the coast, and White's daughter Eleanor and her newborn child Virginia stayed behind. War with Spain kept him away for three years, and when he landed again on 18 August 1590 the houses were down, the site was walled with tree trunks, the boats were gone, heavy iron and lead lay in the grass, and the word CROATOAN was carved on a post: the name of an island fifty miles to the south, now the southern part of Hatteras Island, and of the friendly people who lived there. By a code agreed before he left, a cross over the word would have meant trouble, and there was none. A storm cost his ships their anchors before he could reach the island, and the voyage was given up.
cases.mystery: No search reached them, no house, grave or bone of theirs has been identified, and every later report is hearsay from Indians, heard through interpreters at Jamestown, the English colony founded on Chesapeake Bay in 1607, about a hundred miles to the north. The colonists had told White they would move fifty miles inland, to the west, while the word they carved names an island to the south. David Beers Quinn, the historian who edited the colony's documents, held that the main body went to Chesapeake Bay and was killed there in April 1607 by the people of Powhatan, the paramount chief of the Indian nations around Jamestown, and the historians Karen Ordahl Kupperman and Michael Leroy Oberg followed him; since 2010 the usual reading, set out most fully by the historian James Horn and shared by the journalist Andrew Lawler, is that the colony split between Croatoan and the mainland at the head of Albemarle Sound, the shallow water west of the island, where the Chowan River enters it, and was absorbed into the Indian peoples around it, the Algonquian-speaking peoples of the sounds and the Tuscarora, the Iroquoian-speaking people of the interior; and the First Colony Foundation, an archaeological group that has dug on that shore since 2012, announced in June 2026 that it had found the colony. Scott Dawson, a Hatteras native who founded a local archaeological society, and the archaeologist Mark Horton, who have dug on Hatteras since 2009 at Cape Creek, the site of the Croatoan town, hold that everyone went to Croatoan, a reading endorsed in 2025 by Kathleen DuVal, a historian of Native America; Charles Ewen, an archaeologist, and E. Thomson Shields, a literary scholar, both of East Carolina University, hold in their 2024 book Becoming the Lost Colony that no hypothesis is more probable than another; and a carved stone of 1937 claiming to be a message from Eleanor Dare (the first Dare Stone) has its own defenders.
cases.judged: Every surviving document was read in full, in the original spelling where the original text could be reached and otherwise in published translations or transcriptions: the fifty pages in the Principal Navigations of Richard Hakluyt, the clergyman and geographer who collected and printed the English voyages; the Spanish documents; the Jamestown reports of 1607 to 1625, each traced to its first teller, chiefly through the writings of Captain John Smith, the Jamestown leader, and the Historie of William Strachey, the colony's secretary in 1610 and 1611; and the later testimony of 1650 to 1888. The archaeology of three sites was checked against what has been published, as of September 2026, and the possible fates were then set side by side in a ledger, a table of weights that anyone can change, which was run nineteen ways to show how far the result depends on the weights. On that weighing the mainland at the head of Albemarle Sound comes first as the main body's principal seat, with about 68 chances in 100 (range 41 to 77), Croatoan second at 17, somewhere else 7 and Chesapeake Bay fourth at 4, and the answer is a leading candidate rather than a settled one, because no source names the place, no structure or grave has been found, and the two excavations that could decide the question have not been published. A published, sealed (undisturbed) 1580s deposit at Cape Creek with a hearth and slag (the waste from working metal) would put Croatoan first; separately, some colonists were possibly killed by Powhatan's people about 1607 (45 in 100), and the Hatteras Indians who told the surveyor John Lawson, in his book of 1709, that several of their ancestors were white people are more likely than not a trace of them (60 in 100).

cases.title: The Great Chicago Fire
cases.question: How did the O'Leary barn on DeKoven Street catch fire on the evening of Sunday 8 October 1871, at what hour, and can anyone be named for it?
cases.verdict: A flame carried into the barn by a person, about 85 percent; the person cannot be identified from the surviving evidence. Among the possible carriers, Daniel Sullivan and a member of the O'Leary household stand first, close to even. The fire began inside the barn, on the side where wood and shavings were kept, at about 8.40 by the neighbourhood's clocks.
cases.confidence_label: about 85% for a carried flame; leading candidates 22 / 22 / 20 / 15, none above 30 in the central assessment

standing.note: The 85 percent for a carried flame is a judgment with its sensitivity (how far it moves under other readings of the evidence) printed beside it, and the candidates below it are ordered by judgment with ranges: the two leading candidates are close to even and none reaches 30 percent in the central assessment. The inquiry transcript was not read in the original and Bales's book only in fragments, so the ranking rests on the Tribune's reports of the inquiry, the affidavits and Andreas's interviews.

split: Daniel Sullivan, alone or with Dennis Regan
A member of the O'Leary household with a lamp (Catherine O'Leary 15)
Boys, young men, vagrants or a passer-by from the alley
A guest from the McLaughlin party next door
new: Five documents not previously used in the published discussion, as far as could be checked against a book read only in fragments: the entries in Edwards' city directory for 1871 (the annual list of residents with their trades and addresses) showing Sullivan and White as teamsters (drivers) for the same firm, Chase, Hanford & Co., an oil merchant on South Water Street; the Tribune's reports of the inquiry sittings of 29 November and 4 December 1871, on pages missing from the Library of Congress's online newspaper collection (30 November p. 4 and 5 December p. 2) and recovered from another scan; the silence of the Illinois Staats-Zeitung, the city's German-language daily, on the inquiry and the Board's report; the dating of the Evening Journal's O'Leary interview to 21 October 1871; and a second Chicago extra of 9 October 1871 carrying the cow story.

The sightline test: a 3-D model built from the 1891 atlas, the 1906 Sanborn map, the present-day parcel, one photograph and the deeds Bales found in the tract books, run with uncertainty ranges over all four placements of Sullivan already in the record (his affidavit's "a few lots east", the Board's "nearly opposite", Andreas's "in front of his own house", and Bales's midpoint of White's west parcel), 7,200 draws. From the seat Bales chose nothing under about 16 ft above the barn's ridge is visible (median 15.6 ft; 14 to 16 ft across the three eye heights tried); from the parcel his own deeds put Sullivan's house on, a flame within 5 ft of the ridge is visible in 61 percent of the model's draws and the barn itself in 17 percent. The model adds no document to the record.

The three-cluster reading of the 46 time statements, grouped by the clock each rests on, and the 10 to 15 minute offset between the neighbourhood's clocks and the fire department's, a re-reading of the Tribune's and Andreas's reports. By Patrick O'Leary's account he had been in bed about ten minutes (none to twenty) and his wife about forty (thirty to fifty) when the barn caught, on times for which the O'Learys cited no clock. Sullivan's sequence of events is consistent once the clock times he gave are discarded: an hour at the O'Learys' from about a quarter past seven, twenty to twenty-five minutes on the sidewalk, the fire seen at about 8.40.

The inference from computed sunrise that the 5 a.m. milking was in darkness, so a lamp was kept in the barn every day and its remains prove nothing; whether Bales makes the point could not be checked, since his chapter 2 was read only in snippets.

The re-working of the arithmetic in Bales's Appendix B, where he adds up the distance Sullivan ran to the barn: his 193 feet depends on the seat he chose, and a man who had driven a dray (a delivery wagon) for fifteen years on a wooden leg covers it in thirty to fifty seconds.

The finding of Anthony DeBartolo, a Chicago Tribune writer (1997, 1998), that Cohn's recorded will contains no confession is his and is not claimed as new; it is repeated because the contrary is often printed.
cases.confirms_prior: The Board of Police found in December 1871 that the cause could not be determined from the evidence; Andreas restated that in 1885 and Carl Smith in 2011 and 2020. Bales (1997, 2002) showed that the case against Mrs O'Leary was never more than hearsay, and Fred Fedler (1985), a journalism scholar, that the cow story was in print before any reporter could have invented it as later claimed. The Chicago City Council adopted the same view by resolution on 28 October 1997, a legislative judgment on Bales's research that adds nothing to the evidence about the night. DeBartolo found in 1997 and 1998 that Cohn's recorded will contains no confession.

change.qualifier: the Board of Police (1871), Andreas (1885) and Carl Smith (2020) that the cause cannot be determined
change.prior: The Board of Police (December 1871), Andreas (1885) and Carl Smith (2011, 2020) found the cause undetermined, and Musham (1940) affirmed the cow story. Bales argued in 1997 and 2002 from the Chicago Title land records and the houses on the block that Sullivan could not have seen the barn from where he said he sat, that his story covers his own presence in the barn, and that he, perhaps with Regan, started the fire; his case has been repeated in print for nearly thirty years. The Chicago City Council, by resolution of 28 October 1997 introduced by Alderman Edward M. Burke and approved by its Committee on Police and Fire on 6 October 1997 after a hearing at the fire academy that stands on the site of the barn, resolved to "forever exonerate Mrs. O'Leary and her cow from all blame in regard to the Great Chicago Fire of 1871": a legislative judgment on Bales's research, which adds nothing to the evidence about the night.
change.explanation: It agrees with the official finding that the cause cannot be determined and adds no name. It differs from Bales (2002) on Sullivan: his sightline argument holds for the one seat he chose, the midpoint of White's west parcel, and fails for the three other placements the record gives, and his time argument rests on an error about the hour that the official record as a whole makes. Nothing here overturns what historians already think. Bales's refutation of the cow story stands and the analysis here depends on it, and any model of the block depends on his tract-book research.

overturn: The full inquiry transcript, read in the original, holding a statement by Sullivan or Regan about what they saw from the street that fits no placement at all, or an admission by anyone that they were in the barn.

A record of Dalton's house (a builder's contract, an insurance survey, a photograph) fixing its width and height: with the house two feet lower or five feet narrower, the ridge is visible from White's parcel in most draws; with it two feet higher, nothing under ten feet of flame is.
The 1870 or 1872 directory, or a deed, settling whether No. 134, Sullivan's house, was the east half of Lot 18 or the west half of Lot 19.

A text from October to December 1871 in which Mrs O'Leary, or anyone in the house, admits being in the barn; none was found in about 120 issues of 1871 papers, but the Chicago Times of 18 October and the Evening Journal extra of 9 October were read only through later quotation.
Documentation of Cohn's story from before 1942, which would do the same for the alley scenario.
fell_short: The inquiry transcript was not read in the original: the Chicago History Museum's transcription could not be obtained, and Bales's Appendix D, his transcription of the witnesses, could be recovered only in fragments of about 100 characters.

Bales's book could not be read in full: it was read through two search services that return fragments of a book rather than its pages, 128 Google Books queries returning 534 snippets, each tagged with its page number, from 187 pages, and 435 Internet Archive search-inside queries returning 1,439 fragments of about 100 characters joined into 76 passages; his Figures 54, 64 and 78 and his 1997 article were not seen.

Carl Smith's 2020 book was read through its excerpt in American Heritage magazine; the later literature on the fire, Sawislak (1995), Pauly (1984), Miller (1990), Cromie (1958) and Kogan and Cromie (1971), was not obtained; Ahern's and Cohn's originals are known through later quotation. The 1997 resolution is cited from its own text as reproduced by the Glessner House Museum, a Chicago house museum, and from the press of October 1997; the Journal of the Proceedings, the City Council's own record, for 28 October 1997 was not reached.

The barn's orientation is unsettled between Andreas's plan and Musham's, and the heights of Dalton's house, of the O'Learys' two cottages and of the cottage at No. 133 rest on one photograph and typical construction; the model carries these as ranges. It leaves out trees, smoke, the coal shed in the passage beside the cottage and the light of the fire itself. Its result is a range of heights, and it cannot settle a claim that falls inside those ranges.
The 1870 and 1872 directories could not be obtained, nor could several archive holdings; no paywall or bot wall (a block on automated visitors) was bypassed.
cases.story: On the warm, dry evening of Sunday 8 October 1871, at the end of a summer with little rain, a fire started in the cow barn behind the two small cottages of Patrick and Catherine O'Leary, an Irish couple who kept five cows and sold the milk, at 137 DeKoven Street on the West Side of Chicago. By Patrick O'Leary's account his wife went to bed about eight and he half an hour after her; on the neighbourhood's time that put him in bed about ten minutes, and her about forty, when the barn caught, though the O'Learys cited no clock. Their tenants the McLaughlins, who rented the front cottage while the O'Learys lived in the rear one, had company that evening for a cousin newly arrived from Ireland, with two tunes on a fiddle and two dances. Daniel Sullivan, a neighbour from across the street who drove a delivery wagon for a living and had a wooden leg, had sat with the O'Learys until they turned in; some time after half past eight by the neighbourhood's clocks he saw fire in the barn, ran across, shouted fire, cut two cows loose and got out as the loft burned above him. Within half an hour five buildings were burning; the fire crossed the river that night and burned through the centre of the city for two days.
cases.mystery: Nobody saw the fire start, and within a day the newspapers had blamed Mrs O'Leary and a cow that kicked over her lamp, in two extras (special editions) of 9 October, one of them the Chicago Evening Journal's, an afternoon paper, a story that Michael Ahern, a reporter for the Chicago Republican in 1871, boasted forty years later he had made up; the Board of Police and Fire Commissioners, the city board that ran both the police and the fire department, held an inquiry in November and December 1871, questioned fifty-one witnesses and found no proof that anyone had been in the barn after dark. H. A. Musham, whose 1940 study is the longest older account of the fire's first hours, kept the cow story; Richard Bales, a lawyer with the Chicago Title insurance company, which holds the only land records to have survived the fire, argued in a 1997 article and a 2002 book that Sullivan could not have seen the barn from where he said he sat, that he lied to hide his own presence in it, and that he started the fire, alone or with Dennis Regan, another neighbour who had called that evening; and on the strength of Bales's research the Chicago City Council exonerated Mrs O'Leary and her cow by resolution in October 1997. Others have blamed a guest from the McLaughlins' party going to the barn for milk, boys gambling in the loft by lantern light (a claim first made public in 1944 on behalf of Louis M. Cohn, a Chicago businessman who died in 1942 and said he had been one of them), a spark from a chimney, the new hay heating by itself, and fragments of Biela's comet, a comet that had broken up and been lost to sight some twenty years earlier; A. T. Andreas, who interviewed the neighbours and the firemen for his History of Chicago in 1884, and Carl Smith, the Northwestern University historian whose 2020 book is the most recent full history of the fire, both concluded that the cause cannot be known. Three things keep the question open: the witnesses' words survive but disagree with one another by up to an hour; the shorthand record of the inquiry survives only as 1,100 handwritten pages at the Chicago History Museum; and Bales's argument about Sullivan's view, the blocked view, the only evidence that names anyone, has been repeated in print for nearly thirty years without a published re-examination.
cases.judged: The evidence read was the inquiry as the Chicago Tribune, one of the city's morning papers, reported it day by day, the affidavits (the sworn statements of the O'Learys and Sullivan, taken a week after the fire on 15 October 1871), the interviews Andreas printed, Bales's own transcription of the witnesses (read in fragments, since his book could not be read in full), the city directories, an 1891 property atlas, a 1906 fire-insurance map, the present-day lot lines and one photograph of the O'Leary cottage. From the last five the block was rebuilt to the foot, and a 3-D model was run for 7,200 draws (runs with every uncertain dimension set at random within its range) to ask, for each of the four places the record puts Sullivan, whether the barn or a flame above it could be seen; the 46 time statements (what witnesses said about the hour) were tabulated and sorted by the clock each rested on; and every theory was set against the record and given a share, as a judgment, with the shares recomputed under the readings that change them most. Two findings tipped the balance: the yard and barn were in complete darkness, so whoever was inside carried a light or struck one, and Bales's blocked-view argument succeeds for the one seat he chose for Sullivan, the midpoint of the west parcel of William White, a neighbour who owned two parcels of land on Sullivan's side of the street and at whose fence Sullivan said he sat, and fails for the three other places the record puts him, the seats differing by one 25-foot parcel and the outcome changing with about three feet in building height, which is within the uncertainty of every dimension in the reconstruction. The verdict is a flame carried into the barn by a person, about 85 percent, with the fire beginning at about 8.40 by the neighbourhood's clocks, and the person cannot be identified, because in the central assessment (the ranking with each piece of evidence at the weight the report gives it) no candidate reaches 30 percent; the inquiry transcript read in the original, or a record fixing the width and height of the house of James Dalton, the neighbour next door east, which decides what Sullivan could see, would change it.

cases.title: The Bixby letter
cases.question: Who composed the 139-word letter of condolence sent to Lydia Bixby of Boston over Abraham Lincoln's signature on 21 November 1864: Lincoln himself, or his private secretary John Hay?
cases.verdict: The question is unsettled; on a judgement of the documentary record Lincoln composed the letter, about 53 percent; John Hay, about 42; another hand in the office, about 5; Lincoln against Hay alone, 56 to 44.
cases.confidence_label: about 53% (26 to 75 across the likelihood weights)

standing.note: The question cannot be settled on the present record: the lean to Lincoln rests on documentary items weighed as likelihood ratios, any one of which moves him between 26 and 75 percent, and no stylometric method run here separates the two men in this register. The added tests exist in two implementations that agree on the direction and differ on the rate; no one else has rerun them, and neither used the paper's own corpus.

new: No new evidence was found: every document used was already in print, and what is new is the analysis of it.

The first replication of the 2019 study and of its validation, done twice. Under the study's own design (Lincoln before 18 May 1860 against all of Hay) the letter goes to Hay at all seventeen string lengths, as the paper reports. In the first implementation every one of 1,011 known texts of 50 to 400 words (423 Lincoln, 588 Hay) is attributed correctly by the majority vote of the analyses at character-string lengths 4 to 10; in the second, 1,380 of all 1,397 texts in its pools are attributed correctly, the paper's accuracy curve (its F1 score, a standard measure that counts both wrong attributions and missed ones) is reproduced at every length, and the 17 misses fall on texts outside the two men's ordinary prose, Lincoln's verse, his 1842 eulogy, his temperance address and reported speech among them.

Three tests of that design's sensitivity, which its authors had named as untested in their first presentation of the study (Aston University, 13 April 2016). Period: Lincoln's own-hand wartime texts of 100 to 200 words go to Hay 14 percent of the time under a pre-1860 Lincoln pool (18 percent at 50 to 100 words), and the two Lincoln periods are separable at 100 percent. Register: 30 of 63 register-matched Lincoln pieces (about 140 words each, from 30 documents of 1861 to 1865, among them the Gettysburg Address and Lincoln's two surviving letters of condolence, to the parents of Elmer Ellsworth, a young colonel killed in 1861, and to Fanny McCullough, the daughter of an Illinois friend killed in 1862) go to Hay under that design in the first implementation and 19 of 63 in the second, against a Hay set of 57 pieces cut from two eulogies of 1861 and one 55-word condolence; the own-hand design misses 17 of 63 and none of Hay's 57. Edition: 95 Lincoln texts present in both Basler (manuscript) and Lapsley (print) sit 0.010 to 0.016 nearer Hay in print at every string length.

Why the two register rates differ. The gap lies in the Lincoln pool rather than in the code: the first implementation's code on the second's exact pool gives 19 of 63 under the paper's rule for drawing the random samples of each man's writing and under the first's own rule, and 20 in a run with fewer random draws; the second's code on the first's pool gives 26; and the one difference that matters is 19 items from Lapsley's third and fourth volumes, 83,000 words of Lincoln's 1858 campaign speeches and his side of the debates with Stephen A. Douglas, his opponent for the Senate that year, which the second implementation dropped because Lapsley prints a few hundred words of Douglas inside some of them. Without those items the first implementation's code gives 18 to 20 of 63; with them restored to the second implementation's pool, Douglas's words cut out, the second's own code gives 27 of 63. Under the method's equal-size sampling those items dilute Lincoln's sample with oratory (24 against 20 pieces wrong at an equal 159,000 words) and enlarge Hay's sample by a matching amount, to 243,000 words (29 wrong at that size); Hay's sample enlarged alone sends 54 of 63 to Hay. The paper's own Lincoln corpus (1,085 texts, 400,747 words, speeches included) is nearer the larger pool, but neither pool is the paper's corpus, so the range 19 to 30 of 63 (30 to 48 percent) is what the evidence supports.

A corpus design built from Basler's source codes, so that Lincoln's side holds only what survives in his hand from 1860 to 1865 in the three volumes of Basler's edition that could be read, IV, VII and VIII (1,887 items, 125,600 words), and a register-matched Hay set from his 1861 war prose, the two magazine eulogies "Ellsworth" (Atlantic, July 1861) and "Colonel Baker" (Harper's, December 1861), attribution confirmed from both magazines' indexes.

The detection test. Under the own-hand design 18 of the 19 documents in Basler's edition of 50 to 200 words that survive in Hay's hand, three of Hay's four known letters for Lincoln's signature (to the poet George H. Boker, 1863; to the abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison, Congressman John F. Driggs and Charles Butler of New York, 1864 to 1865) and Hay's own condolence letter of 1864 are called Lincoln by the n-gram vote; the calibrated classifier and Burrows's Delta call all five Lincoln. The second implementation finds the same under pools of its own matched in date: all four letters to Lincoln (by votes of 7-0, 7-0, 6-1 and 7-0) and the condolence to Lincoln. The methods cannot detect Hay writing as the President, so a result on the letter under them is not evidence for either man; the stylometric likelihood ratio is taken as 1 (range 1:3 to 3:1).

Under the own-hand design the letter itself splits eight lengths to Hay and nine to Lincoln (the vote at character-string lengths 4 to 10 is Hay, six to one); the calibrated classifier gives a probability of Hay of 0.29 to 0.41, where Hay's own register pieces average 0.66; Delta says Lincoln. Under the second implementation's date-matched pools it splits 5 to 2 for Lincoln on the vote over character-string lengths and 9 to 8 for Hay over all 17.

A word and phrase table across four corpora: "beguile" is Hay's (0 in 338,000 words of Lincoln); "tendering to you", "the files of the War Department" and "should attempt to" occur only in Lincoln's own hand; "the altar of", "solemn pride" and "gloriously" only in Hay, mostly after 1865; "tender" as a verb is Lincoln's (22 to 0 in the wartime corpora).

The documentary record read in full (Bullard's book; Sherman Day Wakefield's pamphlets; the memoirs of Nicholas Murray Butler and John Morley; Kendall Banning's 1922 article; Schouler's history; the 1908 Hay letters and diary; Thayer's biography of Hay; Burlingame 1995 and 1999; Emerson 2006 and 2008; Nickell 1989) and weighed as likelihood ratios with a sensitivity table.

A count of Basler's items for every week of the autumn of 1864: the Bixby week has 15 against a thirteen-week mean of 21, 23 in election week and 35 in the week of the President's annual message. The count gives a number to Bullard's answer to the "too busy" argument (that Lincoln had no time that week to write the letter himself).

The observation that the Phillips letter of 21 November 1864 (Lincoln's other composed letter of that day, to John Phillips, a 104-year-old Massachusetts voter), kept beside the Bixby clipping in Hay's scrapbook at the Library of Congress, survives only in "an unidentified handwriting" that is not Hay's (Basler's edition, the Collected Works, volume VIII, page 118, note), which cuts against reading the scrapbook as a record of Hay's own compositions. No earlier writer is found to have pointed this out.
cases.confirms_prior: The hearsay character of every reported Hay claim, five chains (each a story passed from Hay through one or more people before it was written down), none first-hand, none written down before 1922 (Bullard 1946; Emerson 2008); Hay's letter of 19 January 1904 to William E. Chandler, a former senator from New Hampshire, and what he told Robert Lincoln (Bullard 1946; Emerson 2008); Hay's practice of writing routine letters for Lincoln's signature, four of them in the Bixby week (Basler); the reported claims assembled, "beguile" and the scrapbooks (Burlingame 1995, 1999); the parallels in Lincoln's own letters and the grammatical habits that favour Lincoln, such as his "should" where Hay would write "would" (Nickell and Pival 1989); that the 2019 result reproduces under its own design and passes its own validation (Grieve and colleagues 2019); that n-gram tracing is "highly sensitive to the choice of authors and texts in the comparison corpus" (an earlier test of the method on literary texts by Thomas Proisl and colleagues, computational linguists in Germany, 2018); and that the method's sensitivity to register needed testing, a concern the authors raised themselves at Aston University on 13 April 2016, so that what is new here is the specific test rather than the concern.

change.qualifier: provisionally, the balance within a question that stays unsettled: since 2019 it had tilted to Hay (Burlingame 1995 and 1999; Grieve and colleagues 2019), and with the 2019 study treated as neutral it moves back to near even, leaning to Lincoln; the older view that authorship is unproved (Basler 1953; Emerson 2006 and 2008; Harold Holzer, a Lincoln scholar, 2026) stands
change.prior: That authorship is unproved: Basler's 1953 headnote (the note heading the letter in his edition) called the claim for Hay "unproved"; Jason Emerson (American Heritage 2006; Lincoln Herald 2008) and Harold Holzer (a review on the history website Emerging Civil War, 23 July 2026) still call the question unsettled. Within that unsettled question the balance had tilted to Hay since 2019, on Michael Burlingame's articles ("New Light on the Bixby Letter", Journal of the Abraham Lincoln Association 1995; "The Trouble With the Bixby Letter", American Heritage 1999) and on the n-gram study by Grieve, Clarke, Chiang, Gideon, Heini, Nini and Waibel ("Attributing the Bixby Letter using n-gram tracing", in the journal Digital Scholarship in the Humanities 34, 2019), which called Hay "almost certainly its primary author"; Tyler Dennett, Hay's biographer (1940), and James G. Randall and Richard N. Current, in the last volume of Randall's life of Lincoln (1955), had leaned to Hay earlier. On the other side stood F. Lauriston Bullard (Abraham Lincoln and the Widow Bixby, 1946), Joe Nickell with Jean Pival (Lincoln Herald 1989) and Emerson.
change.explanation: The 2019 attribution reproduces, but its validation does not carry over to texts of the letter's period and register: under the paper's design between 19 and 30 of 63 register-matched Lincoln pieces go to Hay, the Gettysburg Address among them, and the design cannot detect Hay writing as the President. Two implementations of these tests, written independently of each other, agree on the direction (19 of 63 and 30 of 63 on the same pieces; on 97 pieces the second implementation chose itself, 27 by its own code and 28 to 40 by the first's, depending on the pool), and the gap between 19 and 30 is traced to the choice of Lincoln texts: with Lincoln's 1858 campaign speeches restored to its pool, the second implementation's own code sends 27 of 63 to Hay. With the 2019 study treated as neutral, what remains is documentary and near a balance, leaning to Lincoln on judgement weights. It stays provisional because both implementations reconstruct the paper's design on corpora the paper did not use (its own corpus could not be obtained), because the size of the register effect depends on the Lincoln pool, and because no one else has rerun the tests. A rerun on the paper's own corpus by a third party would settle the rate; if it found no register effect, the balance would return to the 2019 tilt to Hay.

overturn: Toward Hay: a draft or copy of the letter in Hay's hand, or a diary entry, letter or memorandum by Hay claiming it; the original manuscript in Hay's hand over Lincoln's signature; a use by Hay before November 1864 of "beguile you from the grief", "the altar of freedom", "solemn pride" or "assuage the anguish"; a first-hand record dated before 1922 from Morley, from Walter Hines Page, the publisher and later ambassador to Britain, or from W. C. Brownell, literary adviser to the publisher Charles Scribner's Sons, the three men said to have heard the claim from Hay; the "unidentified handwriting" of the Phillips copy identified as Hay's.

Toward Hay: a stylometric method that still attributes the letter to Hay after validation on Hay's known letters for Lincoln's signature and on register-matched Lincoln texts; a rerun of the register test, on the paper's own corpus, that finds no register effect.
Toward Lincoln: the original manuscript in his hand with corrections; a statement by Hay, in his hand, that Lincoln wrote it; a use by Lincoln of "beguile" in any surviving document.

What would not move it: more reported confessions of the same kind, at two or more removes and written down decades later, because the story was in circulation by 1904 and the chains share a source; and a further n-gram study under the 2019 design, because both implementations find that design misreading between a quarter and a half of Lincoln's elevated prose.
fell_short: The added tests exist in two implementations, written independently of each other, and no one else has rerun them; neither used the paper's own corpus, which could not be obtained.

The size of the register effect depends on the Lincoln pool (19 to 30 of 63, and 27 of 63 when the second implementation's own code runs with the 1858 speeches restored to its pool); the report gives the range and its cause rather than a single figure.
The Hay side of the register set is three documents, and Hay's condolence writing of the 1860s is one 55-word letter. A proper test of the hypothesis needs Hay condolences that do not exist in print.
No archive was visited and no new document was found; the Hay Papers (at Brown University and the Library of Congress), the Morley papers and the Bixby family papers were not searched.

Basler's volumes II, III, V and VI (1848 to 1863) could be had only as online lending copies, which cannot be read as full text, so they are absent from the Lincoln corpus; the McCullough condolence enters the register set from a printed text.

Burlingame's 2000 chapter in At Lincoln's Side, the fullest case for Hay, and Edward Steers's Lincoln Legends (2007) were not available; the 2000 chapter is cited through Emerson and Burlingame's later summaries. Hay's letter of 25 November 1864 to Charles S. Spencer of New York, who had asked for a letter from the President to read at a banquet, is quoted from Burlingame's quotations of it.
The impostors method, a fourth stylometric check that adds many unrelated writers to the comparison, did not finish and is not in the report.
The likelihood ratios are judgements; a reader who changes several at once can end up on the other side of 50.

Searches for work since 2019 could not reach the online journal and book libraries MUSE, JSTOR, HathiTrust or Google Books; no replication, re-analysis or rebuttal of the 2019 study was found elsewhere.
cases.story: In September 1864 a Boston widow, Lydia Bixby, showed five letters to William Schouler, the Adjutant General of Massachusetts, the officer who kept the state's military records; each reported the death of one of her sons in the Union army, and Governor John A. Andrew of Massachusetts asked the War Department for a letter from the President. On 21 November a letter of 139 words signed "A. Lincoln" was sent to her, and on 25 November, the day it reached her, the Boston Evening Transcript printed it. It has been reprinted and anthologised ever since, and it was read aloud in the film Saving Private Ryan (1998). Its facts were wrong, since only two of the five sons had been killed, and the error was Schouler's.
cases.mystery: The manuscript has never been found: no draft or copy survives, the newspaper text is the only authority for the wording, and the "facsimiles" of the manuscript sold from 1891 onward are forgeries. Lincoln signed the letter, but his 26-year-old private secretary John Hay (later Secretary of State, 1898 to 1905) drafted many letters for Lincoln's signature, and after Hay's death several men said he had told them in confidence that this one was his; none wrote it down in his lifetime, the earliest record is from 1922, and Hay himself wrote in 1904 that "the letter of Mr. Lincoln to Mrs. Bixby is genuine" and told Robert Lincoln, the President's eldest son, that he knew nothing of the letter's source. For Hay: drafting was his job, "beguile", the letter's rarest word, is his and never Lincoln's, and a clipping of the letter is pasted in two of his scrapbooks; the case was built by Michael Burlingame, author of the fullest modern life of Lincoln (1995, 1999), and seemed settled in 2019 when Jack Grieve, a linguist at the University of Birmingham, and six colleagues applied n-gram tracing, a technique that counts how many of a text's short strings of letters and words occur in each candidate's known writing, and found Hay "almost certainly" the author. For Lincoln: he wrote his own condolences (both that survive from his presidency are in his hand), the request came through the Secretary of War with a governor's wish that the President write, and Hay's own statements point away from Hay; the case was argued by F. Lauriston Bullard, a Boston editor (1946), by Joe Nickell, an investigator of questioned documents, with the linguist Jean Pival (1989), and by Jason Emerson, a historian of the Lincoln family (2006, 2008), while Roy P. Basler, editor of the standard edition of Lincoln's writings (1953), printed the letter as Lincoln's and called the claim for Hay "unproved".
