cases.judged: The printed record was read in full, every reported claim was dated and traced from mouth to print, and the documents of the week were counted from the notes in Basler's edition (his source codes) that record where each surviving item comes from and whose hand it is in. The 2019 technique was rebuilt from the paper and checked against the paper's results, which reproduce, then tested in three ways the paper did not (the date of the comparison texts, their register, meaning the kind of writing, and manuscript against print), with a second implementation of the tests (the same tests programmed again from the paper, without sight of the first implementation's code) as a check; the technique and three other standard methods were then tried on the known letters Hay wrote for Lincoln's signature, and none detects them. With the stylometry, the statistical comparison of writing habits, treated as neutral, the documentary items were weighed as explicit likelihood ratios, each a stated weight for how far the item favours one man over the other, with a sensitivity table showing what changing any one weight does, and the result is a lean: Lincoln composed the letter, about 53 percent; Hay, about 42; another hand in the office, about 5. The question stays unsettled, since changing any one weight moves Lincoln between 26 and 75 percent; a draft in Hay's hand, or a rerun of the register test on the paper's own corpus (the collection of known texts it compared the letter with) that finds no register effect, would move it toward Hay, and the manuscript in Lincoln's hand with corrections would move it toward Lincoln.

cases.title: Double Falsehood and Cardenio
cases.question: Does the play Lewis Theobald staged in 1727 as Shakespeare's descend from the Cardenio that Shakespeare's company played at court in 1613, and if so whose writing is still in it?
cases.verdict: Fletcher wrote the second half; Shakespeare probably wrote in the first half, though that is not proven; Theobald did not make the play up. About 64 percent that the play descends from a Fletcher and Shakespeare original.
cases.confidence_label: about 64% (50 to 75 across the readings of the evidence)

standing.note: The 64 is a judgment with its range stated beside it. Fletcher's presence is measured; Shakespeare's is a reading the models cannot verify at scene length, and nobody has yet rerun the computation.

split: A Fletcher play, alone or with another Jacobean partner
new: None of this is new documentary evidence. Each item is a new measurement on texts that were already available, or a new reading of published results; the measurements were checked on plays of known authorship and on two 18th-century plays that contain no Jacobean writing, and nobody has yet rerun them.

The calibration: survival curves from the 39 Restoration and 18th-century adaptations (of 45 in the corpus) whose originals are plays by Shakespeare or Fletcher alone, giving every attribution score a meaning in terms of how much wording survived, plus two 18th-century plays with no Jacobean writing in them as a floor (Nicholas Rowe's Fair Penitent, an original tragedy written in imitation of old plays, and Theobald's Orestes, one of his own plays). None of the studies read for the report measured this.

The equal-corpus test (each candidate author represented by the same amount of text) at scene length against Shakespeare, Fletcher, Massinger, Shirley, Thomas Middleton, John Ford, Webster and Ben Jonson, all dramatists of the period, together with the 18th-century group and Theobald, checked by holding out one play at a time; the Authorship Companion listed it as the gap. Fletcher confirmed, Massinger and Shirley absent, Shakespeare the best fit for 3.2 and undecided for 1.2 and 1.3.

The check of Theobald's four plays, four translations and The Cave of Poverty, his poem written in imitation of Shakespeare, together, with a scanned-copy control: on the impostors test his 125 chunks give Fletcher a mean of 0.19 and a maximum of 0.63 (against 0.79 to 0.84 in the verified scenes), and his 93,000 words contain four instances of "hath" and "doth", one of them the "doth" in The Cave of Poverty.

Shakespeare-unique phrase links, three-word sequences found in Shakespeare's plays and no other author's, do not discriminate at this scale (Fletcher's and Massinger's scenes carry them as densely as Shakespeare's own); Fletcher-unique links do.
The absence of "ye", Fletcher's habitual form of "you", from the play shows only word-by-word modernisation, since three adaptations of Fletcher from 1695 to 1702 also lack it.

Where the later layers sit: 18th-century-only phrasing peaks in 2.1 to 2.3, and 400-word windows put the Shakespeare-like writing in the second half of 1.2, in 3.2 and at the opening of 5.2, agreeing with E. H. C. Oliphant, who surveyed the Beaumont and Fletcher plays in 1927, Brian Nance, who studied the prose of 1.2 in 2013, Taylor, Marina Tarlinskaja, a scholar of verse rhythm, and Pascucci by an independent route.
A null result: the phrase-level comparison with Shelton, Phillips and Motteux shows no preference for Shelton.
cases.confirms_prior: The break at 3.3 and Fletcher after it were established by Bradford (1910), Walter Graham (1916), who later edited the play, Oliphant (1927), Kukowski (1991), Hope (1994), Hammond (2010), Jackson (2012) and Tarlinskaja (2017); the thinness of surviving Shakespeare by Jackson (2012) and Robert D. Hume (2016); Theobald's and the Restoration hands in Act 2 by Oliphant, Richard Proudfoot, the Arden series' general editor, Taylor, Tarlinskaja and Pascucci; the documentary chain as John Freehafer (1969), who traced the play's history, and Hammond (2010) set it out. The three-layer view, a Jacobean original by Fletcher and Shakespeare under a Restoration adaptation and Theobald's revision, is Hammond's (2010) and the New Oxford Shakespeare Authorship Companion's (2017).

change.qualifier: Hammond (2010), Taylor (2016) and the New Oxford Shakespeare (2017) on Fletcher and on the three layers (a Jacobean original, a Restoration adaptation, Theobald's revision)
change.prior: Every count made since Gamaliel Bradford's in 1910 finds a break in the verse at scene 3.3, with Fletcher's habits after it; Kukowski (1991), Hope (1994), Hammond's Arden edition (2010) and Jackson (2012) all put Fletcher in 3.3 to 5.2. Hammond's edition and the New Oxford Shakespeare Authorship Companion (2017) hold that the text is in three layers, a Jacobean original by Fletcher and Shakespeare, a Restoration adaptation of the 1660s and Theobald's revision of 1727, with the later layers thickest in Act 2 and in 3.1 to 3.2. The case for Shakespeare has always rested mainly on the documents. Against the standard view, Stern (2011) argued that Theobald, a practised imitator, could have written the whole thing; Alotaibi (2016) holds that Fletcher is the only author who can be recovered; Malone (1780) proposed Massinger and Pascucci (2017) found him in 2.2 to 2.4; Farmer (1767) suggested Shirley.
change.explanation: Nothing here overturns what historians already think. The measurements agree with the standard view on Fletcher, on the placement of the later layers, and on the Julio and Leonora passage of 1.2 (Julio and Leonora being the play's names for Cardenio and Luscinda) and the opening of 5.2. They read the evidence for Shakespeare differently: the Shakespeare-unique phrase links used by Jackson (2012) and Taylor (2016) turn out not to tell Shakespeare from other Jacobean dramatists, since Fletcher's and Massinger's scenes carry them as densely as Shakespeare's own, while Fletcher-unique links do. Stern's case (2011) that Theobald wrote the whole play is answered on the text at about 5 percent; her article was not read in full. Massinger and Shirley are tested at scene length against equal corpora for the first time, and neither appears.

overturn: A text by Theobald, or by any 18th-century author, that scores 0.8 for Fletcher on the impostors test would revive Stern's forgery case. None of the 40 18th-century texts in the corpus does: Rowe's Fair Penitent scores at most 0.54 for Fletcher and Theobald's own writing at most 0.63.

A scene-level model in which Beaumont, Field or Davenant beats Shakespeare on 1.2, 1.3 and 3.2 with corpora of equal size would move the answer toward Alotaibi's reading, that Fletcher is the only author who can be recovered.

Discounting the 1653 Register entry entirely, as Stern does, lowers the Fletcher and Shakespeare figure to about 50; proof of Taylor and Wagschal's argument that the play follows Shelton's 1612 translation would raise it to about 75.
fell_short: Stern 2011 and Jackson 2012 were not read in full (paywalled; no copy obtained); their arguments come through Alotaibi 2016 and Taylor 2016, both read in full. Hammond's Arden edition, Kukowski 1991, Hope 1994 and Tarlinskaja's earlier papers likewise second-hand.

Theobald's own adaptations (Richard II 1720, The Fatal Secret 1735) were not available in usable text. Davenant's adaptations other than Macbeth and The Tempest are not in the Text Creation Partnership, so the Davenant layer was not modelled as a class.
The plays of Beaumont and Field, and Davenant's plays from before the theatres closed in 1642, were too small to test as partners; the 24 percent for "Fletcher with another partner" is a judgment.

Theobald's texts are scans (legibility 0.86 to 0.98); a scanned Double Falsehood run through the same pipeline classifies the same way, but rare-phrase rates in his texts are depressed by about a fifth.
Scene-level accuracy is 84 percent for Shakespeare against sixteen other classes and lower for scenes under 400 words; no single scene label is certain.

The Rawlinson manuscript (the Bodleian Library's copy of the 1613 court payment records) and the Stationers' Register were not examined; Steevens and Malone's 1780 Supplement, the 1770 notice, the 1718 assignment of Moseley's copyrights to the publisher Jacob Tonson and the originals of Mist's Weekly Journal, the London newspaper in which Theobald replied to Pope, are second-hand.
Nobody has rerun the computation; the code and data are published with the report so that someone else can.
cases.story: In the winter of 1612 to 1613 the King's Men, the acting company that Shakespeare wrote for and part-owned, played twenty times at the court of King James I, and the royal household's accounts list one of the plays as "Cardenno"; a second payment covers "Cardenna", played on 8 June 1613, and neither record names an author. The title comes from Don Quixote, the novel by Miguel de Cervantes (1605; in English 1612), whose Cardenio loses his bride Luscinda to his friend Fernando and runs mad in the mountains; the play was never printed and is not in the First Folio, the collected edition of Shakespeare's plays put together in 1623, and the next trace is forty years on, when on 9 September 1653 Humphrey Moseley, a London bookseller, entered "The History of Cardenio, by Mr Fletcher & Shakespeare" in the Stationers' Register, the book trade's record of who held the right to print what, John Fletcher being the playwright who succeeded Shakespeare as the King's Men's chief writer and wrote Henry VIII and The Two Noble Kinsmen with him; Moseley never printed it, and no manuscript of it is known. On 13 December 1727 Lewis Theobald, a London editor and playwright who had made his name the year before by correcting the poet Alexander Pope's edition of Shakespeare, staged Double Falshood; or, The Distrest Lovers (Double Falsehood in modern spelling) at the Drury Lane theatre as "Written Originally by W. Shakespeare", its plot Cervantes's Cardenio story with the names changed, and claimed in his preface to own three manuscripts of the play, one in the hand of John Downes, prompter to one of the two London theatre companies from 1662, and once owned by the actor Thomas Betterton. Nobody else ever recorded seeing them; a notice at a revival in 1770 placed the "original Manuscript" in the museum of the Covent Garden theatre, which burned in 1808, and no account of the fire mentions it.
cases.mystery: Nothing ties the 1613 play or the 1653 entry to Theobald's text except his own word, and whatever he had has been rewritten at least once and probably twice, and rewriting destroys most of what tells one author from another, so four positions have been held since the play appeared. One side holds that Theobald wrote it himself and invented the manuscripts (Pope mocked one of its lines in 1728; George Steevens and Edmond Malone, the leading Shakespeare editors of their day, doubted it in 1780; Tiffany Stern, a historian of the early modern theatre, argued the case in full in 2011); a second holds that it is an old play by someone other than Shakespeare (Richard Farmer, a Cambridge scholar, proposed James Shirley, the leading playwright of the 1630s, in 1767; Malone, and in 2017 Giuliano Pascucci, proposed Philip Massinger, who succeeded Fletcher as the King's Men's chief writer in 1625). A third side holds that Fletcher wrote it: every count of the verse since the American critic Gamaliel Bradford's in 1910 finds a break at scene 3.3 (act 3, scene 3) with Fletcher's habits after it; Stephan Kukowski (1991), Jonathan Hope (1994) and MacDonald P. Jackson (2012), all specialists in who wrote what in this period, give scenes 3.3 to 5.2 to Fletcher; and Naseem Alotaibi's doctoral thesis of 2016 holds that Fletcher is the only author the text will yield. The fourth side, taken by the play's modern editors, Brean Hammond (his Arden Shakespeare edition, 2010), Gary Taylor (2016) and the New Oxford Shakespeare (2017), whose Authorship Companion volume sets out who wrote what, is that Fletcher and Shakespeare wrote it together and that the text is in three layers: a Jacobean original (Jacobean meaning from the reign of James I, 1603 to 1625), a rewriting of the 1660s for the company of William Davenant, who ran one of the two London theatres after the Restoration of the monarchy in 1660 and rewrote several of Shakespeare's plays, and Theobald's revision of 1727.
cases.judged: The documents (two court payment records of 1613, Moseley's entry of 1653, Theobald's licence, dedication, preface and one later statement, and the notices of 1770 and 1808) establish only that the King's Men had a Cardenio in 1613 and that a bookseller assigned it to Fletcher and Shakespeare forty years later, so the text was compared with 264 plays and other works of the period, about 5.2 million words, most of them from the Text Creation Partnership, a programme that keyboards early printed books into searchable text. The measurements were distances based on the 300 commonest words, a statistical classifier, the impostors test (how often a candidate author beats a crowd of other writers; above 0.8 counts as verified) and counts of rare phrases and of small words such as "hath" and "doth" that had gone out of use by 1727; each was tried first on Henry VIII and The Two Noble Kinsmen, where scholars agree which scenes Fletcher wrote, and on the corpus's 45 rewritings of older plays made after the Restoration of 1660 and in the 18th century, each measured for how much of the original wording it keeps, with the 39 whose originals are plays by Shakespeare or Fletcher alone scored for how much of an author survives revision, and only then on Double Falsehood scene by scene, with Theobald's own 93,000 words put through the same tests as a control. What tipped the balance is the text: the second half, from scene 3.3, carries Fletcher's habits of grammar and rhythm as strongly as scenes he is known to have written, at a level none of Theobald's own writing reaches, so a Jacobean play by Fletcher lies under it, and the first half keeps an older layer under heavy rewriting in which Shakespeare fits best of the candidates tested and Massinger and Shirley do not fit at all, though no single scene can be given to Shakespeare with confidence. Put together with the court record of 1613 and the Register entry of 1653, that makes a Fletcher and Shakespeare original the most likely source, at about 64 in 100 (the evidence supports a range of 50 to 75), and Theobald's own invention at about 5; discounting the 1653 entry entirely would lower the first figure to about 50, and proof that the play follows Thomas Shelton's 1612 English translation of Don Quixote, which a phrase count could neither confirm nor refute, would raise it to about 75.

cases.title: Hannibal's route over the Alps
cases.question: Which pass did the Carthaginian general Hannibal take when he led his army and its thirty-seven elephants over the Alps into Italy in the autumn of 218 BC?
cases.verdict: On the weights used here the Col du Clapier comes first at about 40 per cent, on condition that Polybius's Island lies between the Rhône and the Isère; the Col de la Traversette is second at about 30 and the Mont-Cenis third at about 15.
cases.confidence_label: about 40% (20 to 60, the 5 to 95 per cent Monte-Carlo band)

standing.note: Every share is a judgement: fourteen likelihood ranges, argued item by item and combined in the evidence model. The order turns on where Polybius's Island lies, the Clapier leading on the Isère reading and the Traversette with the Island at Orange. Walbank, the principal modern commentator on Polybius, and de Beer, whose books make the principal modern case for the Traversette, were read only in part.

split: A col nobody has argued for
Petit St Bernard, Montgenèvre and Grand St Bernard together
new: No manuscript, artefact, date or measurement is added to the record.

A computed viewshed (the ground in sight from a point) of the Po plain for nine cols, the eight of the route model and the Col Agnel, one of the cols nobody has argued for at length, taking in the first 10 km of each descent and the ground within 1.5 km of each col, on a single definition of "plain": only the Traversette (17% of compass bearings from the col, a 63-degree sector; 22 to 26% from the knolls beside it) and, marginally, the Clapier (a 2-degree sliver from the col, 5% from 1 km down, 8% from the ridge) see any plain from the col or the descent. The Mont-Cenis sees nothing from the col or the first 10 km of its descent and has a half-percent sliver from three cells of the terrain grid on the ridge above it; the Petit Mont-Cenis (the second col of the Mont-Cenis plateau), the Montgenèvre, the Larche, the Petit St Bernard, the Grand St Bernard and the Col Agnel see none.

A recalibration of all fourteen published radiocarbon dates from the Traversette meadow against IntCal20 (the dates are those printed by Mahaney and colleagues, with one laboratory number printed twice); a Ward and Wilson test, a check of whether two dates can be measurements of one age, showing that the two "bracketing" dates at 40 cm, which their authors say bracket the invasion year, are inconsistent with each other (T = 23.4 against a critical value of 3.84, p = 1.3 × 10⁻⁶) and both exclude 218 BC; the finding that nothing in the output of the published age model, the statistical ordering of the dates, places the churned layer in 218 BC (the words "firmly" and ">95%" of Mahaney and colleagues rest on the agreement index, Amodel = 97.6, a measure of how well the measured dates fit the model's ordering, read as a probability); the finding that the paper's own table contradicts itself, since for one date the range after modelling does not overlap the measured range, beside an agreement index near 100, which requires the two to agree; and the point that at this part of the calibration curve no radiocarbon date can separate 218 BC from 207 BC, when Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal took the same road, or from any year between about 380 and 150 BC. The dating evidence does not establish a disturbance in 218 BC and does not show whose animals made the layer.

The textual point that "Isère" stands in no manuscript of Polybius (whose manuscripts read Σκάρας or Σκώρας) or of Livy (sarar, bisarar or arar) and is Cluverius's 1624 conjecture in both, and that Livy's "1,000 feet" for the broken ledge is a Renaissance restoration of a corrupt line.

The demonstration that Polybius's 1,400 stades to the ascent and 1,200 for the crossing cannot both be satisfied by any line over the real terrain, so that neither total can be used against a candidate; and the observation that 1,200 stades is fifteen days at the 80 stades a day of the stage before the ascent (800 stades in ten days).

An explicit evidence model (14 items, 8 candidates, likelihood ranges argued item by item) with a shared-source correction (the halving of the nine items that come from one author), Monte-Carlo bands, a leave-one-out test (each item dropped in turn) and seven named sceptical scenarios, so that the disagreement between the Clapier and the Traversette can be traced to three cells of the table: the Island, the Allobrogian ambush and the practicability judgement.

Two smaller points: the morning setting of the Pleiades computed for 218 BC (true setting 29 October; first visible setting 4 to 9 November, depending on the visibility threshold assumed) with two independent astronomy programs and a check against the calendar of Columella, a writer on agriculture of the first century AD; and Pliny's geography (3.34 and 3.36) used to show that an Island in the Valence plain belongs to one of two peoples of his list, the Segovellauni or the Cavares, with the Allobroges beyond the Isère, which matches Polybius's distinction between the Island's people and the Allobroges.
cases.confirms_prior: That the Isère reading of the Island, the Allobrogian ambush at the mouth of the Maurienne and the Clapier's summit plateau fit Polybius best was argued by Perrin (1883) and by Azan (1902) and Colin (1904), who adopted the col after him, and was the conclusion, always hedged, of Walbank (1956 and 1957) and of the historians who followed him, Proctor (1971), Lazenby (1978), Lancel (1995), Hunt (2017) and Hornblower (2024), and of the reply that Kuhle and Kuhle made to Mahaney in 2012. That the Traversette fits the view, the snow and the steep descent was argued by its advocates Torr (1924), de Beer (1955) and Prevas (1998). That the Grand and Petit St Bernard fail on the Taurini is Livy's own argument. That the meadow's radiocarbon window, the span of years its dates allow, admits several armies was said by de Galbert (2016), a critic of the Traversette dating, and that the Traversette has no ground for a summit camp by Hunt (in EARTH magazine, 2016).

change.qualifier: the cautious verdict for the Clapier that Perrin reached in 1883, that Azan (1902) and Colin (1904) developed, that Walbank (1956), Proctor (1971), Lazenby (1978), Lancel (1995), Hunt (2017) and Hornblower (2024) repeated with the same caution, and that Kuhle and Kuhle defended against Mahaney in 2012, and agrees with them that the question remains undecided; shifts the Traversette from "the first direct evidence of the route", the words of Mahaney and colleagues in Archaeometry 2017 part II, with "solid evidence" in the press coverage of 2016, to a strong second whose physical case has not been tested
change.prior: There is no consensus. A count by Peddie in 1997 of twenty-four modern writers split six Mont-Cenis, six Montgenèvre, five Clapier, four Petit St Bernard, three Traversette. Before and after that count, the Clapier has been the usual hedged answer of historians of the ancient world (Walbank "hesitatingly" in 1956, Lazenby 1978, Lancel 1995, Hunt 2017, Hornblower "probably" in 2024), the Montgenèvre the scholarly alternative, argued by Connolly (1981) and by Hoyos (2006 and 2015), who follows Livy's tribes to the Durance, and the Traversette the choice of de Beer and those who followed him (1955 to 1974), of Prevas (1998), who has crossed the col many times, of Mahaney's papers (2007 to 2026), which presented the meadow deposit as "the first direct evidence of the route", with "solid evidence" in the press coverage of 2016, and of Berti and Vollrath (in the journal PNAS, 2026), whose energetics model does not engage with the deposit. Three recent writers on Hannibal, Goldsworthy (2000), MacDonald (2015) and Lendering (2022), decline to choose, and the two most recent peer-reviewed contributions, Hornblower and Berti and Vollrath, point in opposite directions.
change.explanation: No earlier finding is overturned. The result agrees with the Clapier reading at the cautious level its advocates gave it, and agrees with them that the question remains undecided: weakening the Traversette's dating does not establish the Clapier, whose share rests on the reading of the Island. It moves the Traversette from "the first direct evidence of the route" (Mahaney and colleagues in the journal Archaeometry, 2017, part II; "solid evidence" in the press coverage of 2016) to a strong second, because the meadow's radiocarbon window admits any army from about 380 to 150 BC and nothing in the output of the published age model places the churned layer in 218 BC.

overturn: A manuscript reading: the manuscripts of Polybius 3.49.6 and Livy 21.31.4, the passages that name the Island's river, read Skaras or Skoras and Sarar, Bisarar or Arar, which editors have taken as copyists' corruptions of Isara, the ancient Isère; a manuscript whose reading could be identified as a different river would move the Island, and with it the whole ranking. The Vatican manuscript of Polybius has not been re-examined for this, and the Isère conjecture has never been tested against a fresh collation, a new comparison of the manuscripts.

An artefact: a datable Punic or Iberian object (something of Carthaginian or Spanish make), a coin of Carthage, a bit from a horse of the Numidians, the troops of the army who built up the broken path in relays, or an elephant tooth, from any col or its approach, would outweigh every item in the table. None exists for any candidate: the Traversette fieldwork of 2011 to 2017 found none, and no comparable excavation has been made at the Clapier, at the Savine basin below it or at the Clarea headwall on its descent.

Ancient DNA from the meadow: DNA preserved in the sediment of the churned layer, of the kind now routine in Alpine lake cores, that showed horse (Equus) in quantity and no ruminant signal at the right depth would make the Traversette deposit an army's, but not shown to be Hannibal's; a ruminant signal at that depth would point to livestock.

A snow record: a reconstruction of the snowline (the height above which the winter's snow survives the summer) in the third century BC for the Cottian Alps, the stretch of the range from the Larche to the Mont-Cenis, 300 m below the modern mean would put old snow on the Clapier in late October and remove the Traversette's advantage on the snow item; one 200 m above would remove the Clapier's partial claim to the snow altogether.

A finer terrain model: the view test was run on a 90 m surface, and a 5 m model of the Clapier ridge and the Clarea headwall could open or close the Clapier's sliver of plain; it cannot close the Traversette's 63-degree sector of plain.

Walbank and de Beer read in full: the principal modern commentary on Polybius and the principal modern case for the Traversette were read only in part, and an argument in either that has not been met here would change the weights, though probably not the ranking.
fell_short: Not read in full (abstracts, the snippets a book search shows, or catalogue records only): Walbank's Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) and his 1956 article in the Journal of Roman Studies; de Beer's Alps and Elephants (1955) and Hannibal's March (1967); Prevas's Hannibal Crosses the Alps (1998); Hunt's Hannibal (2017); Lancel's Hannibal (1995); Hoyte's Trunk Road for Hannibal (1960), the account of a crossing made with an elephant in 1959; Seibert's Hannibal (1993); Proctor's Hannibal's March in History (1971); Mahaney's Hannibal's Odyssey (2008); Kuhle and Kuhle's two papers in the journal Archaeometry (2012 and 2015); and Mahaney's papers of 2010, 2013 and 2019 with the publisher Wiley. Their arguments are known here from what other published writers report of them, and from what they report of one another.

Livy was read in Foster's edition in the Loeb Classical Library (1929) as transcribed on the Wikisource website, with the apparatus (the record of what the manuscripts read) of the Oxford edition from scans; the apparatus of Polybius at 3.49.6, the passage naming the Island's river, is known only through Schweighäuser, an editor of Polybius in 1789, and the Oxford editors of Livy.

The terrain model is coarse, at 90 m: it can show that ground of the kind Polybius describes exists on a descent, and it cannot show that a particular ledge or the break in it existed in 218 BC; route lengths are measured along the valley floors and are lower bounds.
The bands for old snow at each col are estimates from the modern snowline and the glacier record; no autumn snow-patch series for the southern French Alps was found.
Nothing was checked on the ground, and no manuscript was freshly collated.

The input file for OxCal, the program in which the Traversette age model was built (Mahaney and colleagues, Archaeometry 2017 part I, Table 1 and Fig. 4), could not be obtained: it is printed in none of the six Mahaney texts held, and no supplementary file is deposited with the journal, with either author's university or on the Zenodo file archive. The model's structure is known only from its published plot.

Every likelihood range is a judgement, and the shared-source correction (the halving of the Polybian items) is a rule of thumb, bracketed by the two extreme treatments, every item at full strength and each source family collapsed to one item.
cases.story: Carthage, a city on the coast of what is now Tunisia, fought Rome three times for control of the western Mediterranean, and in the second of those wars its general Hannibal marched an army from Spain to Italy overland. In the autumn of 218 BC he took forty-six thousand men and thirty-seven elephants from the river Rhône over the Alps in fifteen days: the first snow was falling when the army camped for two days on the summit, from which Hannibal pointed his men to the plains of the Po, the flat land of northern Italy, and on the descent, where the previous winter's snow still lay under the new fall, a broken cliff path had to be built up before the animals could pass. The elephants came over, in Polybius's words, "in a wretched state from hunger", and three days later the army was on flat ground among the Taurini, the people around modern Turin. Two ancient historians tell the story: Polybius, a Greek who wrote within about seventy years of the crossing, questioned men who had been on it and walked the Alps himself, and Livy, a Roman who wrote two centuries later and drew, through a Roman annalist, on the same Greek account of the march.
cases.mystery: Neither historian names the pass, and the two readings that would fix it are damaged in the manuscripts: the Island, the fertile triangle of land between the Rhône and a second river that the army reached four days' march up the Rhône from its crossing, has the Isère, which joins the Rhône at Valence, as its second river only by a conjecture that the geographer Cluverius made in 1624, and Livy's "1,000 feet" for the height of the broken ledge on the descent is a Renaissance restoration of a corrupt line. The argument has run in print since Josias Simler raised it in 1574 and no candidate has a majority; the candidate passes lie along the whole frontier between France and Italy (each is a col, a gap in the chain low enough for a track to cross), and the sides divide first on the river: if the Island's river is the Isère, the army went up that valley and crossed into the Susa valley west of Turin by the Col du Clapier or by the Mont-Cenis beside it, and the Clapier has been the hedged answer of historians of the ancient world writing in English since Colonel Perrin proposed it in 1883 after seeing the view of the Po plain from it. If the Island lay further down the Rhône at Orange, as Livy's list of tribes implies, the army went east up the river Durance to the Montgenèvre, the easiest road into the Susa valley, to the Col de Larche further south, or to the Col de la Traversette, a high notch under Monte Viso at the head of the Po; the Traversette is the highest and hardest of the candidates and has the most recent support: the books of Gavin de Beer, the earth-science papers of a team led by William Mahaney (2007 to 2026), which cored a boggy meadow below the col and reported a layer churned by animals that it dated to 218 BC and identified as the passage of Hannibal's army, and a 2026 energetics study by Berti and Vollrath, a model of the energy cost of each route. The two St Bernard passes to the north, which come down into the Aosta valley, carry an old Roman tradition that Livy himself rejected.
cases.judged: Both texts were read in Greek and Latin with their manuscript variants; twelve routes over eight cols were measured on a terrain model with a 90 m grid against Polybius's day-counts and stades (the Greek unit of distance, about 180 m); each descent was profiled for ground steep and broken enough to match his cliff path; what each col can see of the Po plain was computed by casting sight-lines over the terrain; old snow, the previous winter's snow on the descent, was judged against the modern snowline and the glacier record, the dated advances of the Alpine glaciers; the setting of the Pleiades, the star cluster that Polybius says was going down at dawn during the summit halt, was computed for 218 BC; and every published radiocarbon date from the Traversette meadow was recalibrated. Fourteen lines of evidence were then given likelihood ranges for eight passes (for each line and each pass, an estimate of how likely that evidence would be if that pass were the one), argued item by item, and combined, with the nine items that come from Polybius at half strength because they share one author. The Clapier comes first at about 40 per cent, the Traversette second at about 30 and the Mont-Cenis third at about 15; the Traversette's physical evidence is consistent with any large body of animals at the meadow between about 380 and 150 BC and does not test the crossing. The ranking depends on the reading of the Island, since with the Island at Orange the Traversette leads at about 54, and a manuscript giving the Island's river another name, or a datable object from the army at any col, would move the whole ranking.

cases.title: The death of Meriwether Lewis
cases.question: Did Meriwether Lewis shoot himself at Grinder's Stand on the Natchez Trace in the night of 10 to 11 October 1809, or did someone else fire the shots?
cases.verdict: Lewis shot himself: self-inflicted about 85 percent, homicide about 15 percent, accident under 1 percent. "Self-inflicted" covers both a decision to die and a delirium in which the same acts were done without one.
cases.confidence_label: about 85% (63 to 92 across the runs that start from even odds; 32 to 97 across all priors and sceptic settings)

standing.note: The figure comes from an explicit weighing with its sensitivity (how far the result moves when the inputs change) printed beside it, and it summarises judgments rather than measuring anything. Nobody who saw the body knew what to look for, no archival work was done, and the principal opposing books (Fisher 1962, Guice 2006, Starrs and Gale 2009) were read only in snippets, though the opposing articles were read in full.

split: Self-inflicted, by decision or in delirium
under 1% (up to 17 under a flat prior)
new: John Pernier's own petition to Jefferson of 10 February 1810 (Founders Online, the National Archives' free online edition of the founders' papers, item Jefferson/03-02-02-0171), read in full and placed in the sequence of his last months. It shows him destitute and refused by the government, asking $271.50 in wages "to pay my just debts & resqued from prison"; he died of laudanum (a tincture of opium) eleven weeks later. Chalkley 2004, the fullest study of Pernier, did not use it. Gale 2016 used its $271.50 and its fear of prison as evidence that Pernier was a witness who had been silenced; the petition names no threat, and what it records is wages, debt and sickness.

Three attestations of the suicide attempts on the boat that do not depend on Russell's disputed 1811 statement (House to Bates, 28 September 1809, written before the death; Russell's lost letters as Clark summarised them to his brother on 26 November 1809; the Washington newspaper, the National Intelligencer, of 27 November 1809), as an answer to the claim that the statement is a forgery. Only House's chain is certainly independent of Russell as a source.

Forensic base rates applied to the wound pattern: multiple-shot suicides are 1.6 to 8% of firearm suicides, the first head shot missed the brain in 5 of the 11 cases in the largest series, published by Karger and Brinkmann in 1997, torso shots predominate (a series published by Jensen in 2025), unplanned complex suicide (a change of method after the first fails) is a named category, and survival with the power to act after a trunk wound is ordinary. The series were read in abstracts and are used as orders of magnitude.
The evidence model, with its sensitivity, leave-one-out and grouping printed beside the headline.

Small points about dates and documents: Wilson's visit was Sunday 6 May 1810, as the editions of his works by George Ord (1828) and Alexander Grosart (1876) already implied (the "May 28th, 1811" printed in the Port Folio, a Philadelphia magazine, misled Clay Jenkinson in his 2011 study of Lewis's character); the $99.58 Treasury check that Russell had lent Lewis at Fort Pickering, and which Russell listed in January 1810 among the money "none of which it is said could be found", did reach Washington and was forwarded to Jefferson, as the editors of the Retirement Series of Jefferson's papers note, so the missing money, one of the two items that most favour murder, did not include it; the monument committee's "assassin" (report of 1849 to 1850) rests on two stated grounds, the loneliness of the place and a story that the servant fled to Natchez, which the documents refute; and two pieces of contemporary St. Louis testimony (the St. Louis Missouri Gazette, 2 Nov 1809: fever "never failed of depriving him of his reason"; Stoddard, writing from Nashville on 28 Sept 1809 about Lewis's illness at Fort Pickering: "under the hands of the surgeons mate Dr. Smith") are not used in any of the works read.
cases.confirms_prior: The documentary case for suicide was made by Dawson Phelps (1956) and Donald Jackson (1962, 1978), and it has been the majority position among historians since; Paul Russell Cutright, a historian of the expedition (1986), James Holmberg of the Filson Historical Society (1992), the physician David Peck (2009) and the National Park Service hold it, and Danisi accepts that Lewis fired the shots and rejects the word suicide. Other lines followed here were opened by earlier writers: Holmberg 1992 on Clark's letters to his brother; Guice 2002 on the moonless night, which the calculation here confirms; the Lewis researcher Ann Rogers 2005 on the shot sequence being a presumption; Michael Carrick, a firearms historian, 2006/2009 on the pistols; Tom Chalkley 2004 on Pernier; Peck 2009/2022 on the medical answer to Chuinard; Danisi 2013 to 14 and Turnbow 2012/2015 on the Neelly dispute (whether Neelly was where he said he was on 11 October), left open; Clay Jenkinson 2011 on Mrs Grinder as a witness against her own interest.

change.qualifier: the majority of historians, who hold suicide (Dawson Phelps 1956; Donald Jackson 1962; Paul Russell Cutright 1986; James Holmberg 1992; David Peck 2009; the National Park Service), against the case for murder made by Fisher 1962, Chuinard 1991 to 92, Guice 2006, Starrs and Gale 2009 and Gale 2016
change.prior: Suicide has been the majority position among historians since Dawson Phelps (1956) and Donald Jackson (1962); Paul Russell Cutright, a historian of the expedition (1986), James Holmberg of the Filson Historical Society (1992), the physician David Peck (2009) and the National Park Service hold it, and Danisi accepts that Lewis fired the shots and rejects the word suicide. The case for murder has been made by Fisher (1962), Chuinard (1991 to 92), Guice (2006), Starrs and Gale (2009), Gale (2016), the Tennessee monument committee (appointed 1848, report 1849 to 1850) and the 1996 coroner's jury. The field is not settled: among authors who have stated a position in print since 2006, 13 are for suicide, 6 for murder in three versions that exclude one another, 3 for a self-inflicted death that was not suicide, and 6 or 7 undecided. At a panel of historians in 2009, two hundred years after the death, the historians put suicide at 96 percent and the audience voted 350 to 20 for murder.
change.explanation: The verdict agrees with that majority and with the documentary case behind it, and the question is not treated as settled. The case for murder is stated in its authors' words and answered by name in section 9 of the full report, which is linked from this page. What is added to the majority case is its basis: the weight moves from testimony about the night, which is all second-hand, to the evidence of attempts and derangement in the month before the death, reported through separate chains, one of them written down thirteen days before the death, and to base rates for multiple-shot and complex suicides from small modern series, which show the reported wound sequence to be a recognised shape of a failed-then-completed suicide.

overturn: Exhumation showing a penetrating entry to the forehead from behind or above rather than a grazing groove, a trunk trajectory a man cannot give himself, a ball of a calibre no gentleman's pistol fired, or a range beyond arm's reach. The Department of the Interior refused exhumation on 25 August 2010 as a "final decision".
A record of an 1809 inquest naming a killer. None has been found in 130 years of looking, and the county sources of 1894 to 1904 say the papers are lost or never existed.

The full text of the 1845 "schoolteacher" account (Mrs Grinder's last telling, given to a passing stranger about 1839 and printed in 1845) turning out to contain details that can be checked, instead of the additions its fragments suggest.
House's letter proving misdated, or Stoddard's informant proving to be Neelly or Russell coaching the story, which would remove the only attestation of the attempts written before the death.

A document from Pernier's last months showing money or goods of Lewis's in his hands beyond the horse of Lewis's that Neelly sent him east on and that Jefferson told him to sell and credit to the estate.
Anything placing Neelly at the stand on the night of the 10th, which would make him a witness and a suspect at once.
fell_short: Not read in full: Fisher 1962, Guice ed. 2006, Starrs and Gale 2009, Danisi and Jackson 2009 (a different Jackson from the editor Donald Jackson), Danisi 2012, Gale 2015 (her book; her 2016 article was read in full), Dillon 1965 (a biography of Lewis), Ambrose 1996 (on Lewis's opium and drinking), Kushner 1981 (on his depression), Phelps 1956, Jackson's Letters of the Lewis and Clark Expedition (the Freeman inventory and the full Russell statement), Chandler 1994 (a conspiracy theory), Peck and Peck 2021, Stroud 2018 (the Wilkinson conspiracy), Morris 2004 (for suicide), Turnbow's two books, Jenkinson beyond chapter VI. Everything on the death in We Proceeded On from 1974 to 2025 was read, apart from the two print-only issues listed below; the books were read only in the passages that searches of their digitised copies return, so the position each takes is certain and its page-by-page argument is not.

Not obtained at all, among the 20 documents listed in the working notes on the documents that accompany the full report: the full text of the 1845 "schoolteacher" account (a manuscript version is in the Draper manuscripts at the Wisconsin Historical Society, 29CC33); the 1996 inquest transcript; the Avery 1978 thesis on the death; the print-only We Proceeded On issues of Nov 2025 and Feb 2026; House's letter beyond the quoted phrases; the Clarion, the Nashville newspaper that printed the first report of the death, in its own issue (read in the Kentucky Gazette and Richmond Enquirer reprints); the 1849 to 50 Tennessee House Journal appendix, the legislature's record (read in the transcription Elliott Coues verified for his 1893 edition of the expedition's history); the Marks and Neelly letters of 1811 to 12 except as Fisher and Gale quote them.

Forensic literature read in abstracts only; modern base rates used as orders of magnitude; no archival work; the Kentucky Gazette and Missouri Gazette read from page images, so their quotations have not been checked against a machine transcription.

The working notes on the documents list 24 points on which the record of 1809 to 1813 disagrees with itself, and 20 documents that could not be obtained, among them those listed above. One point is left open: Lewis's watch is "Silver" in the letters of 18 Oct 1809 from Neelly and from John Brahan, the captain at Nashville who wrote out Neelly's letter, "His Watch" reached Washington by 5 Jan 1810 (Isaac Coles, the President's private secretary, who opened Lewis's trunks), and an unsigned 1812 note reported by Gale (We Proceeded On 42:4, n. 30, not obtained) says Neelly still held a "gold watch"; whether that is one watch or two cannot be settled from the copies read. It does not touch the verdict: no 1809 document puts a watch with Pernier.

What the numbers cannot do: the model cannot allow for collusion (if Mrs Grinder, both servants and Neelly lied together, most of the table falls away, and no number in it measures how likely that is); it cannot allow for the absence of examination, since no one looked for soot or powder marks and it gives an unrecorded finding no weight either way; it treats the different versions of homicide as one; and its ranges are wide by design, which is why the 90 percent bands are wide.
cases.story: On the evening of 10 October 1809 Meriwether Lewis, who with William Clark had commanded the expedition that crossed the continent to the Pacific and back in 1804 to 1806, and who was now governor of the Louisiana Territory at St. Louis, rode up alone to Grinder's Stand, a settler's cabin that took in travellers on the Natchez Trace, the old road from the Mississippi to Nashville, about 72 miles south-west of Nashville in Tennessee. He was 35 and on his way to Washington to defend his public accounts, since the War Department had refused to pay bills he had drawn as governor and his private creditors had closed in; he had come down the Mississippi ill with fever, and Captain Gilbert Russell, commanding Fort Pickering (the army post where Memphis now stands), had found him deranged and kept him a fortnight before he took the road with James Neelly, the government's agent to the Chickasaw nation, through whose land the Trace ran, with Neelly's servant and with his own servant John Pernier; Neelly had stayed a day behind to find two strayed horses. The innkeeper, Robert Grinder, was away; his wife Priscilla gave Lewis the house and slept in the kitchen cabin, the servants slept in the stable, and in the night she heard two pistol shots; the servants found Lewis shot in the head and in the body, and by some accounts cut with a razor, and he said he had shot himself, asked for water, and died about sunrise. Neelly came up later that day and buried him near the stand, and wrote to Thomas Jefferson, the former president, who had planned the expedition and remained Lewis's patron, that the governor had killed himself; Jefferson, Clark and the newspapers accepted it, no doctor saw the body and no inquest (the official inquiry into a death) was held.
cases.mystery: None of the people who wrote about the night was in the room: everything comes from Mrs Grinder, who told the story at least four times over 36 years and told it differently each time, and from two servants whose words survive only as others reported them, and nobody recorded powder marks, the position of the pistols or the state of his hands. The case for suicide was made by the people who knew him: Jefferson wrote in 1813 that Lewis had suffered "hypocondriac affections" (depression, in the usage of the day) from early life, Russell reported two attempts on his own life on the river, a letter that James House, a captain at Nashville, wrote thirteen days before the death, passing on what Amos Stoddard, an army major and Lewis's friend, had heard from a man just come from Fort Pickering, says the same, and Neelly found him "at times deranged in mind" on the road; most historians since Dawson Phelps, the National Park Service historian of the Trace (1956), and Donald Jackson, editor of the expedition's letters (1962), have held that view. The case for murder began in Tennessee, where in 1848 the state legislature appointed a committee to put a monument over the grave, and the committee's report to the legislature of 1849 to 1850 said that death "by the hands of an assassin" seemed "more probable"; local tradition accused the innkeeper and the Lewis family accused the servant; and since the novelist Vardis Fisher's Suicide or Murder? (1962) argued that every document was second-hand and every witness interested, the question has been argued in print by surgeons, lawyers, document examiners and historians: the surgeon E. G. Chuinard (1991 to 92) has said Lewis could not have survived and moved as described and named Neelly as the killer; the historian John Guice (1998 to 2006) has argued that the story never fitted, from the moonless night, on which Mrs Grinder claimed to have watched Lewis stagger about the yard, to the two hours she left him wounded; the forensic scientist James Starrs and the independent researcher Kira Gale (2009, 2016) have argued for a plot by General James Wilkinson, the army's senior officer, and called Russell's 1811 statement, his written account of Lewis's last weeks given two years later, a forgery; and Tony Turnbow, a historian of the Trace, has argued for a robber and a cover story arranged by Neelly. Thomas Danisi, Lewis's biographer, holds that Lewis fired the shots in a malarial delirium and that "suicide" is the wrong word; in 1996 a coroner's jury in the county where the grave lies recommended exhumation, a federal court in 1998 and the Department of the Interior, which manages the grave as part of the Natchez Trace Parkway, in 2010 were asked to allow it, and the grave has not been opened.
cases.judged: Every document of 1809 to 1813 that bears on the death was read, and so was the modern debate, from Fisher's book to 2025, in full where it is in articles and in fragments where it is in books; the events were put in date order, Mrs Grinder's tellings laid side by side, her one visual claim checked against the moon, and the reported wounds compared with modern forensic case series (published collections of similar deaths); then sixteen evidence items were scored in an explicit model, a calculation written out so that a reader who disagrees with any number can change it and see what follows, in which each item's weight is entered as a range of how much more likely the evidence would be if Lewis shot himself than if someone else did, and the ranges are combined under four starting assumptions (priors), two sceptic settings that discount every item, and a leave-one-out check in which each item is dropped in turn. The case rests mainly on the month before the death rather than on the night itself, for which there is no reliable witness: attempts on his own life were reported thirteen days before he died (House to Frederick Bates, Lewis's deputy and enemy, 28 September 1809) and are attested through three chains of report that do not depend on the disputed statement Russell gave in 1811, though only House's is certainly independent of Russell himself; Jefferson and Clark accepted the report at once; and the two men who could have robbed him, Neelly and Pernier, went straight to his patrons, while his pistols, rifle, watch, horses and two trunks of papers were all accounted for (the watch with one open question, noted under Limits). The reported wound sequence, a head shot that missed the brain and then a shot to the trunk with hours of survival, is one that suicides with a pistol are documented to produce, and every forensic pathologist who has examined the surgical claim that it is impossible has rejected it; every murder theory requires at least one of the three people at the stand to have lied about a man the servants found alive and talking, and the conspiracy version requires the record to have been false from a fortnight before the death. The verdict is that Lewis shot himself: self-inflicted about 85 percent, homicide about 15 percent, accident under 1 percent; murder keeps about 15 percent because the body was never examined for the signs that would decide a shooting and because the model cannot allow for the possibility that the three people at the stand agreed on a false story, and an exhumation showing a wound Lewis could not have given himself, or a record of an 1809 inquest naming a killer, would overturn it.
